div.head: Examiner Saturday, january 23, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, january 23, 1904.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Skirts do not vary very much as yet from the modes which have held sway throughout the earlier part of the winter. The most be- coming certainly for outdoor wear are those which fit easily but closely, immediately below the waist and are admirably moulded round the hips, the lower part from the knees down wards standing out in a rounded way, like a bell, and clearing the ground all round. The full effect round the feet is sometanes pro- duced by the insertion of pleats at the seams, together with careful damping and pressing. The result is always smart looking and is much more comfortable for street 'wear than the long trailing skirt. The latter has, however, by no means vanished from Our midst for the grace-

div.head: USEFUL SKIRT.
div.p: A USEFUL SKIRT.

ful potentialities of 'the full flowing skirt are generally acknowledged. It is, however, more seen in indoor gowns and looks very smart when expressed in sun-ray pleated material ; the pleats being either carefully graduated off into nothing at the waist or fit- ted into a shaped band covered with passe- menterie, or ornamental braiding. Skirts of this kind were greatly reduced at the sales and found many eager and willing purchasers, for a black accordion-pleated skirt of good cut made preferably over silk looks well for after- noon- or evening wear with a smart blouse. My first sketch gives a sample of this most useful skirt made in black pleated nun's veiling. _ The more dressy varieties are in the same style hut are made of silk, chiffon or crepe de chine, and show insertions of valen- ciennes lace or silk embroidery, the latter being only seen on the better and more ex- pensive skirts. Bright crimson or scarlet is a colour which is much in vogue for evening wear this season and looks most effective and warm-looking among dismal surroundings as it strikes a bright note of colour, and when not overdone is most pleasing to the eye. It is of course essentially a winter colour, as red is apt to be glaring in bright weather. At present days of sunshine do not come within the possi- bilities or probabilities of our daily life, and we

div.head: SMART BLOUSE.
div.p: A SMART BLOUSE.

therefore gaze appreciatively on all that is gay and bright. The craze for red as a colour has not only pervaded the world of dress but is a colour employed for some of the newest stock- ings. Personally, I am glad so far to have been saved the shock of even a passing glimpse of such gaudy wear out of doors and I cannot bring myself to believe that it. is a mode which will find favour amongst the best dressed women who always avoid all that is outre, or extreme in any way. Good taste is always absent when the eye of the passer-by is caught by any one item in the tout ensemble, as the acme of good dressing is arrived at when one is only conscious of a charming toilette with- out realising how the delightful result is arrived at.

The smart blouse depicted is made of cash- mere of a delicate tone, of pale turquoise green, a colour rather difficult to describe but delight- ful to behold. 'l'he whole cachet of the blouse lies in the making, which, though quite simple, is exceedingly smart and up-to-date. The blouse in this instance is unlined but could, of course, be worn over an underslip if desired. There is no trimming, but neat tucks and well- arranged drawings or gatherings obviate the
A COMFORTABLE NECKLET.

necessity of any further decorative touches. The sleeves, which it the upper part of • the arm closely; fall fully in a pouf to the wrist- band, where the fulti,ss is confined by a neatly tucked cuff. There a 4 some very pretty blouses of accordion - pleated. crepe dt, chine, in emerald green springing from a collarless yoke of fine coffee-coloured lace patterned in a floral design, a cuff of the same lace finishing the .sleeves. A piece of narrow black velvet rib- bon is threaded through the lace at the throat an:. gives a finish while it holds the yoke dose to the neck. The ribbon is tied in a little bow at the back, where the blouse fastens. • The fur necklet or stole depicted is of a lightfully comfortable order. It is finished with tails, which are most fashionable and give it a very handsome appearance. The double fur necklet seems at present to be less generally in vogue than the single shaped fur• lined with satin, which lies more on the shoul- der than the throat, and in some instances looks like a short shoulder cape finished by long flat stole ends. The fur scarf has also attained to a considerable popularity, but in spite of the fascinations of these alluring fur wraps I am inclined to think that after this season we will see little of them and that our old friend the double fur necklet. will always be well worn and never entirely disappear. , COQUETTS4

div.head: PAUL STORIONTS FIRST WIFE.
div.p: PAUL STORIONTS FIRST WIFE.
BY MARY C. ROWSELL,
Author of "Love Loyal," "he Silver Dial," "Thorndyke Manor," "The Friend of the People," "Traitor or Patriot," &c.

it was more than six years since I had seen my old school and college friend, Paul Stormont; for while destiny had sent me fulfilling sub-secretarial duties under Government into various parts of Europe, Paul, having qualified for the Bar, settled in chambers in the Temple. Is the only son of a wealthy Devonshire commoner of long and honour- able descent, Stormont enjoyed social advantages which would, no doubt, have materially aided his advance to the very front of the profession for which his talents eminently fitted him. The death of his father, however, from an accident in the hunting-field, cut short Paul's lega: career once and for ever, and he returned home to Stormont with the laudable intention of being a model lord of the Manor.

Stormont, Hall, as the old half-stone and timbered ancestral Tudor mansion was called, stood within a mile of the cliff-bound coast, and a little over double that distance from the town of Oak- •minster, of whose venerable parish church my father was rector. The Hall lay almost com- pletely concealed by embowering oaks and pine- trees some fifty yards in from the margin of a widish stream, which wound through Oakminster, where it washed the boundaries of the Vicarage garden. Then gradually broadening on between woods and somewhat isolated fields it formed an estuary beyond Stormont point, losing itself at last in the Channel waves.,

Paul, who was deeply attached to his father, felt his loss keenly, and when he tried to settle at the Hall its every stone seemed to remind him of his loss so unendurably that he decided to travel for a year or two first, leaving the management of the estate in the hands of Williams, the bailiff of many years past. From time to time letters were exchanged between us. His reached me from various parts of the world. But after about four years had passed he wrote from Nice, saying that he had taken a villa in the neighbourhood, and "congratulate me, old fellow," were the con- cluding words of his epistle, "for I have also taken a wife." Something like a regret passed over me as memories intruded themselves of the piping old days when Paul, my handsome, frank, dark-eyed chum, my Sister Felicia and I, used to make a joyous trio, scouring the woods at nutting- time, helping harvesting, or, best of all, making daring voyages of discovery up and down stream in the Lively Polly, the sturdy little Vicarage boat.

The further information that Mrs. Stormont was both beautiful and talented, was furnished by a visitor who arrived at the Vicarage some time later, armed with letters of introduction from the Stormonts. He was, it appeared, a Pole, one Count Stanislas Solenski, owning an estate near Warsaw. now travelling in England for his pleasure. Yes, "it was small wonder, he said, that ce cher Paul had been captured and bound in the chains of matrimony by such an enchanting lady as Madame Stormont."

Oahminister folk seemed to regard Solenski with a similar sort of admiration. That I did not share in it, proved the rule, nor did I think Felicia felt in the least disposed to yield to the fascinations the undeniably handsome Count brought to play on her. Felicia, in fact, had of late grown strangely quiet and thoughtful, some- times even to melancholy. It was not for want of polite attention from the other sex, for a loving godmother had dowered her with the comfortable little sum of twelve thousand pounds. But she sturdily announced that her mind was not set on marriage, and Solenski, after twice attempting to brinc, her to change her resolve, left Oakminster with almost startling precipitation. This took place during one of my prolonged absences from England. "And he was so terribly upset," said my mother, when she told me the tale the next time I was home for one\ of my flying visits, "that he would not stay 'to see Paul, though lie had tele- graphed that he was coming home the very next day." "Paul's return was quite unexpected ? " I said. "And sudden. Oh, absolutely. And he has grown altogether so—so eccentric—no, not that exactly, but he isn't the old Paul a bit. -You'll see that directly, John, though he's very nice— isn't he, Felicia? " "Yea," said Felicia, whose back was turned to us, feeding the canary with a bit of groundsel. "And it's all very curious, isn't it? And his hair is heavily streaked with grey. But it's not unbecoming, is it Felicia ? " "No," said Felicia, as she disappeared into the conservatory. "Don't go down in the boat to Stormont, dear," added my kind, anxious mother. "I know there's going: to be a storm." "Perhaps, hut not yet awhile, mother " ; and kiss- ing her good-bye I made my way down to the Lively Polly's moorings, and put off into mid-stream for Stormont Hall. And I was to see Paul again at last, for he had come back. Come alone, except for a magnificent Mount St. Bernard dog, who was, Felicia said, his almost inseparable companion. No mention of his wife had been heard to pass his lips. A hesitating inquiry made by the house- keeper as to whether preparation was to be made to receive Mrs. Stormont had been met by him with a calm, level negative: and he had spent his time since his return almost entirely divided between his books and long rides in the neighbourhood attended by Basco.

Hoping that for me my old friend would be unchanged, I planned, as I rowed on, to steal a surprise on him if he should be—as I gathered he usually was at this late evening time—in the library, whose windows were bayed, opening within a foot of the ground by tall mullioned lattices.

When I came in sight of the little peninsula, clothed to the margin of the water with the well- remembered pines and oak trees, the last rays of sunset were fading from their tips, leaving grey shadow and a faintly moon-silvered mist covering the water, which hereabouts was brackish, and took on something of the motion of the sea, where it tided up to an expanse of sandy mud below the grass-grown banks bounding the Hall grounds. In a sheltered miniature creek under the trees on the further side of the point lay the little landing- stage of the Hall. But as I swept forward into the midst of the curve I neared a huge black object lying_ upon the fringe of the mud. Paddling closer I found it to be a stranded, vessel, no uneom- mon sight about that storm-beaten spot. She was a mere hull, a deplorable Heaven-abandoned thing; not a vestige of anything on her deck, sate a few feet of her torn mizzen-mast standing up in a sheaf of splinters, and a portion of the gaunt framework of her companion stairs blanched by the rays of the misty moon to sickly white contrast against her heavy black bows. She had been a barque of fair size, and must have lain where she was for some time, judginc, by the tufts of coarse grass sprouting here and there among her sodden, fast-- rotting timbers, which were coated from stern to prow with a greyish, fungus-like film. She lay heeled over, .but at no sharp angle, on her leeward side. Her keel was under water, save up by its extreme forepart, which seemed as if it had been forced forward into the mud, and in this manner held in place. I could almost fancy as I looked, that she lent herself h i the faintest of movements to the gentle forte of .the rising tide, but that might have been the mere delusion of the moonlight stealing across her bows and pmetrating in at the portholes, that yawned in vacant blackness like empty human eye-sockets. Shiverinc, a little in the chill, dank breath of the coining night, I turned from the castaway barque and paddled on till I ran the Lively Polly lip apinst the landing-stage, and tying her to a stake, passed up with swift but soundless tread by the zigzag path which ran to the low stone steps of the library windows, Paul's name upon my lips and my heart bounding with content, for he was there. I could hear the dear remembered music of his voice.
As I framed my lips to utter the word it broke from the lips of a woman within the room, in such a discord of mocking emphasis that I shrank back into the screening laurels.
"Paull" - And the rest she seemed about to speak he cut short with a malediction. •

"Leave this house!" he went on. "Go! Do you hear me? Before I do you a mischief. Alt, fiend! temptress!- What are you that you should have crossed my path ? " "It was you," she interrupted him with a mrickina lauph. "you, Ma Caro. 10-- went out of

your way to cross mine. And how prettily you spoke then! If every stone '-,—ah, yes, you remember, don't you ?—` had been a diamond it would not nave been good enough for foot of mine to tread on.' But now--"

"Yes. Will you go ? " '"Now we are not compatible, are we ? " and the speaker forced a chuckling mockery of ,a sigh, "Not compatible. Yet you took me---" "Hush! I took you for what you seemed, a pure, good woman, consummate minx that yot are!"

"And ? " she cooed softly. "And I found you—yes—too late," he went on as again the little triumphant cackle escaped het, -4that there is no vice of which your dark soul it tot capable." "Guilty, do you mean, dearest?" "And if I do can you not spare yourself tilt vord ? Will you go now? Or by—" "Sposo Alio," she broke in softly. "Yes, -I am going. Your generosity is too- great for me to refuse you any—any little fancy, and so adieu darling. But one minute first," and I could hear the soft, crisp rustle of bank-notes in her hand as if she were counting them. "Yes, quite right, and so farewell, Paul. You will keep the bargain. Ah! but you must not scom I so. It makes your handsome face look quite ugly. Farewell. Only if you fail to keep the bargain it will be au revoir. Yes, address to Monte Carlo, don't forget dearest, and you know now I am going to—" "Ah!" he cried, with another half-smothem* word of loathing that sounded strange and terrible to me on Paul's lips: "Go!" And as he spoke the lattice was flung open to its widest width, arid the tall, graceful figure of a woman momentarily filled the space. The mingled rays of moon and lamplight Tell full upon her face as she turned, and stepping down, caught close about her the sheeny silken wraps enveloping her from head to foot, with a hand sparkling with diamonds. There was just the froze-3'7r= of her drapery as she brushed past me with a light, swift step. Then she was gone. I, too, turned away. This was no time to intrude on Paul,. but leaden disappointment and pained perplexity so weighted my steps that I took no heed whither I bent them, and arrived only by a circuitous garden path at the landing-steps once

more. My boat was gone! And though I peered right and left up stream and down, and along the banks till I was wearied out, I saw no signs Of her. It was long past the Vicarage bed-time when I knocked up Jobson, our butler, and Crept to my room, but hardly to any sleep; and the household was only just getting astir when I stole out again to reconnoitre for my missing boat. No long search was needed, for when I reached the landing-stage at Stormont, there she lay, well in and as secnrely hitched, as 1 had left her On the previous evening, among the reedy tanglee covering the sides of the steps. It was unaccounte able, unless in my pre-occupation of mind I had passed her over. Then I went up to the house, to learn that the master•was gone to London, and would not be back till quite late. Sick at heart, 1 strolled down again towards the banks, to pace back to Oakreinster only to decide before I had gone many steps, that I could not stand the ordeal of inquiry concerning my visit to Stottnont, and would instead go by the train to Southampton where I had a little busi- ness to transact at the docks, and take my chance of finding Paul at home on my return in the evening. Scouring to and fro along the verge of the banks, I came upon the St. Bernard. Ile paused for a moment in his restless movements, and eyed me with disconsolate, uneasy gaze, sniffing unceasingly all the while into the heavy sunshiny air. His tawny coat was spotted with mud, and nand encased his limbs like stockings, and I had Only to glance at the stretch of mud below to see that it was indented with his paw-marks, mostly in the direction of the derelict boat. In such an insistent manner the dog intimated to me that I should oblige him by adventuring on—or more correctly into—the treacherous slime below, that I humoured him to the extent of walking to the utmost verge of terra firma above. The train to Southampton was not far from due. I then walked on, followed by a reproachful appeal- ing look from the dog's eyes, which haunted me all through the day. After transacting my small affair at Southampton Docks, I loitered on the pier to pass the time watching the departure of the steamers. Among them, the Havre steamer was putting off, and not half a minute too soon a belated passenger pushed on deck through the crowd about the gangway, and dropped spent and breathless into the nearest vacant seat on board. It was Solenski. There was no mistaking the outlines of his hard, relentless chin, or the glint of his hawk-like eyes, covertly glancing on all sides from beneath the close down-drawn brims of his felt hat. After all, then, he was not eating his heart out in Poland for disappointed love. Towards sunset, instead of the noisy train, I took a little coasting steamer which set me ashore within a couple of miles of Stormont Creek. Thence I walked on by the cliff path, till I descended by the sheep track, winding down into Stormont Woods, following the bank paths to make sure the Lively Polly had gone no more astray., She lay safe enough as I had left her, and there as I had left him was Basco, except that now he sat fateful-looking and marble still in lion-like pose, his black nnizzle uplifted and pointed direct upon the derelict boat across the half-submerged mud tinged with patches of blood-red reflection from the lurid clouds overhead, to the turbid shallows sullenly lapping round her bows. The dog sprang up at sight of me, 'and clearing the bank, splashed forward. Then as suddenly turn. ing he scrambled back crouching to my feet, utters ing a volley of hollow, distressful, howling barks, and fixing my gaze With eyes that impelled me to obey his wish, his will that I should go out to the castaway boat and seek whet I might find. "Come then, Basco," I said, and together we turned, and untying the Lively Polly, 1 steered her for the wreck ; Basco, standing mute, expectant, his deep flanks heaving, his jaws eagerly opening and closing as he watched every stroke of the sculls. I drew them in as I came aloneside, under one of the largest port-holes, which was widened still more 'by many a breach in its surrounding timbers ; but the splintered marks, soiled and stained, bore the look of being freshly made, wrought by violence, not by damp and decay. Clearly too, Basco had already attempted to gain entrance by the aperture, for his huge paw-marks impressed the trails and smears of fresh mud, and of-e-something in the clinging, clammy quality of what I touched, prompted me to strike a match. The stains were red, as I suspected. But Basco left me no time for thought. He was up the barque's sides before I could 'Make my boat fast by the stout line of rope she always carried, and clawing and scrambling he disappeared irfto the hole. I succeeded in loop- ing the rest of the line round a sufficiently firm looking stanchion near the vessel's prow, and holding by this I set foot in a short ladder hang- ing over her sides. • The rune's shivered to powder ' immediately, leaving me hanging midway, but Basco now craning head and shoulders through the port-hole, lent me the support of his big strong neck, and casting one arm round it, I let him draw me into the hole, which he did with a sturdy gentleness, letting me drop to a shelf not more than a foot below. It was strewn with mildew, reeking shreds of mattress and blanket. The place had probably been the skipper's cabin. From this eminence I scrambled down as I might, to find myself standing on the floor in the full light of the moon flooding in through the yawning gaps in the a wooden partition whose deck above, and facing rotted-out panelling 'lay scattered around upon the floor. Through this the dog's head was look- ing at me like a picture painted on a black canvas, beckoning inc onwards with his insistent eyes, and approaching the broken panel, I crept through it into the cabin beyond. Just as I got to my feet a cloud darkened out the moon, and it was by a forkine flash of lightning that broke in a crash and crackle of thunder, that I caught a glimpse of the place I was in. It was enip',.; save for an overturned broken bench 'or so, and the row: of doorless lockers lining the wall. There was nothing to be 'seen lave at the extreme end a heap of lierldled drape.y lying flung upon , the bench, silk aid -satins that gleamed and shimmered gorgeous', in the unceasing lightning flashes: Nothing to be seen but the unmistakable outlines of a human form under the torn and bedraggled silken felds trailing down into a Ovrk stain upon the floer. With a tight clutch upon Basco'r collar, I stumbled forward to find myself meeting the dead face of the woman I had seen leave Paul's room the night before. Through the glaze of the eyes staring beneath their lone fringed lids, pierced a look of mingled horror and hatred and amazement that for the moment paralysed me. Then I lifted a fold of the mantle, and drew it over the stark, livid face, and took one of the icy hands fallen to the floor, laying it across the dead woman's breast upon the other clenched about her heart,

as I did so 1 noted . i.,1 mocked th,3 ghastly hues of the straining dis,olonreti fingers. Then with a sign to Basi.o, ho. ielded strict but somewhat sullen obedience, 1 turned, and the dog and I left the derelict. i. Bow. I canno tell if I would, any more than I could describe a nightmare dream, only that as I dropped into the brave little boat tossing in the rush and roar of the water, a flash of steely light caught some gleaming thing which had caught in her wooden foot-grating. I wrenched it away with some. difficulty. It was a small gilt-hilted stiletto, like a dagger. I laid it away in my cigarette-case, and when I examined it later that night I found it bore the initials, P.S. And one thing besides, I remember, as we touched the landing-stage, that I thought I heard *3 voice calling through the storm. Basco seemed t3o have no doubt of it, for, with a joyous bark, he bounded to the bank and was gone.

"No, sir. We wern't the least anxious about you," said Jobson, when I reached home in the small hours. "The mistress was sure Mr. Stormont wouldn't let you leave the Hall, and you were not expected for hours yet. But, maybe, 'tis as well you've come back now, as this arrived last night," and Jobson placed a telegram in my hands. It summoned me to town by earliest train next morning, and thence almost at once to proceed to Paris. I had no more time than to make ready and depart with hurried good-byes. There are times—sufficiently rare, of course— when a man finds even his newspaper distasteful. Such a time was that next day to my pre-occupied mind. The horrible experience in the storm, the haunting remembrance of the murdered woman's interview with Paul, the initials engraved on the dagger•hilt. Oh, no! it was not possible, and yet if he had been goaded, driven till reason • had trembled on her throne? No! Ah, no, the instincts of.bloddshed were not in Paul Stormont's nature. And I argued with myself till my brain grew dazed, and to screen my haggard face from the keen and slightly apprehensive observation of my fellow-travellers, I plunged it into the newspaper I bought at Swindon. "Terrific Storm on the South Coast." This I read mechanically, letting my eye run down the brief paragraphs anent the mishaps that had befallen all along the coast. "Nowhere," stated one of these reports, "was the violence greater than on the Dorsetshire Coast. At Stormont Hall, near Oakminster, which lies at the head of a small estuary, the force of the elements dislodged from the mud bank in which it had seemed hopelessly embedded, a derelict barque. The hull was to have been broken up in a few days, but last night's tempest has saved this trouble. Not a vestige of her remains, and she has probably been swirled out to sea, and gone under." Gone under! Lost for ever, and with her all chance, in every probability, of the crime being known. Whatever hue and cry might ensue after the missing Mrs. Stormont, only I—and in my breast-pocket, hard and inexorable, stained to the hilt, lay the accusing weapon. Only I was cognisant of the crime. _ _

_ I was to sleep that night in Paris, thouzh sleep and I were likely to be sworn foes. Anything was better than to be alone, and I turned into my club, a Franco-English community of well-born Bohemianism, and found a seat in a corner of one of the card-room sofas, where I sat absently watching the lights upon the Seine. The room, which was deserted when I entered, had gradually filled, and suddenly the voices of a group of men in heated discussion uprose. I turned to see in their midst Count Solenski, pale, contemptuous, glaring down at a little Frenchman with whom I had some slight acquaintance. He was an agree- intelligent man, something of a virtuoso. "Pah," said Solenski. "I tell you the thing is not unique. Don't flatter yourself, Vicomte." "But .1 tell you--" began the Vicomte. "Tell me what you like, but not that lie. I have —I had had the counterpart of that stiletto. It had been'in our family for generations. It bore my late grandfather's initials, P. S., on the hilt." "Can't you produce it then? " defiantly asked the Vicomte.
"No," said Solenski, with a hard laugh. "You must take my word for it. I—lost it." "Nom de Dieu!" said the Vicomte, in sym- pathetically compassionate tones. "And you can smile?"
Solenski turned with whitening lips. "Ah I a bagatelle," he said lightly, as he pushed through the group. "I dropped it—in the sea—a couple of years ago."
, - "TivO' nights ago you mean," I said, rising from the couch, and facing him as he advanced. "Put it is not lost."

-He drew a step back staring at me and mechanically muttering my name. "I have it here," I went on, taking out my cigarette-case, and drawing forth the little stiletto, "There is your weapon. You dropped it in my boat, which you borrowed at Stormont a night or two

-"Ah, "he said, forcing a ghastly smile. "No--" "Yes—here it is, stained as it must have 'alien from yourtmurderous hands.' Ah, yes, hold him, gentleman! " I shouted, "hold him fast. Stanislas Solenski, I charge you tvith the murder of Giulia Stormont, whose body you secreted in the cabin of the derelict barque." "It is a lie!" he shrieked. "It is the truth. Hold him fast, gentlemen • I cried, entreatingly. But whether their arms failed them, or his tremendous strength of desperation conquered, he Woke from them, and bounding to the window, sprang from it with a yell of defiance, and in. the supervening silence, the sound came up of a heavy thud on the flags of the courtyard below, and we knew that Stanislas Solenski had escaped human justice.

. . - Felicia is Mrs. Stormont now. The happiest, woman in the land, but the tragic event a that night when the derelict barque was swept Out to sea, has left its shadow upon the memory of all concerned. The worthless woman Paul had married, was but an instrument to work the ends of Solenski. Since the wretched man died a suicide, and unconfessed, the exact manner in which he carried out his hideous design, was never certainly known. That he followed the woman to Stormont Hall, knowing that she was to receive Money from Paul, a handsome maintenance conditional on her living abroad, was patent. That Solenski stole my boat to decoy her to some solitary spot on the "'her side of the river seemed almost certain since rue marks of a struggle and traces of foul play were found in a field near the banks, and the deed must have been done. What more secure hiding-place than the derelict? practically ina.ccessible and too dangerously rotten to board. And even if the crime had come to light by that means, what more natural than to fasten it upon Paul ? The insulted, injured hushed. Solenski was not known to he in England, and apparently was there only for the few hours needed to perpetrate the crime. Most of the diamonds he had stolen from his victim were foupd in his valise at the hotel he had put up at. Hay came he to drop the dagger? Well, it was clear from his own words that he be.ieved he had flung it in the deep, brackish water of the estuary, not daring to keep it, and it had missed aim, bounding back, falling soundlessly, probably, into the coil of rope. Solenski was clever. After his death many other crimes of theft and forgery were tracked to him, but the cleverness of evil found its bitter ending. Basco too was clever, and the good dog's reward is the one thing he. values, the one thing wor'ah winning, boundless love. [Tile END.

div.head: GROCER'S TRIALS.
div.p: A GROCER'S TRIALS.

A young lady employed by the West Ham Corporation called on Edwin Garland, a grocer, of 'Plaistow. and asked for coffee. "Coffee, or chicory and coffee V? said Garland, anxious to keep within the law. The young lady's reply was to the effect that she would have coboa. "Cocoa or chocolate powder ?" said the honest grocer. "Half a pound of butter," replied the young lady. Then the grocer made the mistake which cost him .£3, including costs, at West Ham on Monday. He supplied margarine.

div.head: NTS OF THE WEEK
div.p: NTS OF THE WEEK
COUNT INOUYE.

JAPAN'S LEADING DIPLOMATS. r Few men in the world have of late been talore in the public eye and more prominent in the papers than the Japanese statesmen who have been sitting in council with the Mikado on the all-absorbing subject of the war with Russia. In our Constitution there is no exact parallel to the "..Genro,' or elder statesmen. They are the men who helg the reins of power in more feudal days before the present form of Administration came into use, and now they are like a small Privy Councll without Constitutional powers, combined with a sort of unofficial "Committee -of Defence." It consists at present of five members, who are convened at critical times by the Mikado, and they are selected for their services in peace and war, so that they are competent to give their ruler valuable advice ,on any or every subject, representing as they do nowa- days the flower of the experienced and tested intellect of the country. The names Of this august little group are the Marquis Ito Hiro- humi, the Count Inouye, the COunt Matsu- gata, the Marquis Yamanata, and the Marquis Oyama. Of these the first-named is the best 'known at home and abroad. Sixty- three -years of age, he is the man who modernised Japan and was for years its leading statesman. As ex-Premier he enjoys the confidence of the whole nation. Count Inouye was also one of the leading reformers and a prominent foreign diplomatist. Count Matsugata was twice Premier and for fourteen years Minister of Finance, and is certainly the greatest financier Japan has produced. The last two are the country's most famous soldiers. Thus the " Genro " is as representative as it is valuable.
-UNT MATSUGATA MARQUIS YAMAGATA.

what sooner but for the death of the mother of the Earl of Warwick; and more recently still the bridegroom, Viscount Helmsley, broke his collar-bone in the hunting field. It was a very pretty wedding, widely attended; and th e house party was a large one, as of bridesmaids alone their were fourteen! Of these none was prettier than Miss Ivy
Gordon Lennox, the brides first cousin. But, as a matt, - of fact the feature of the wedding

VISCOUNT AND AND VISCOUNTESS HELMSLEV • •s the good looks of all concerned. I'ady hirjorie Greville, young and charming, is the 1 cautiful daughter of a beautiful mother and is far more than what is understood by the commonplace word, "pretty." On his side Lord Helmsley comes of stock famous for their good looks, and is no exception. His sister, Mrs. Gervase Beckett, is a great beauty, aud his aunts, as the Ladies Duncombe, excited and, as married women, still excite extraordinary admiration. Viscount Helmsley, who is twenty-four years of age, was the only son of the late VisN)unt Helmsley, son and heir of the first Earl of Feversham.

div.head: NEW MEMBER FOR NORWICH.
div.p: THE NEW MEMBER FOR NORWICH.

Mr. Louis Tillett, the new member for Nor- wich, is a grandson of Mr. Jacob Henry Tillett, whom nobody in Norwich called any- thing but "Jacob Henry" in the days when he sat for Norwich. Mr. Tillett is a solicitor, thirty-eight years of age, has a long record of municipal work, and has been for some time leader of the Liberal party in the Division. The figures were as follows: Mr. Tillett "(L.), 8,576; Mr. E. Wild( U.), 6,7 56 ; Mr. G. H. Ro- berts (Lab.), 2,444; majority, 1,820. Speak- ing after the poll, Mr. Tillett confined his re- marks to a few sentences. "My friends,"he said,
MR. LOUIS TILLETT, M.P.

-we have fought an uphill fight, but we have won. We have had strangers here from all parts, including the Tariff Reform League, and I venture to think you like the local article the best. Gentlemen, I wish to take this oppor- tunity of expressing my thanks to my op- ponents for their courtet'y t 9 me. Politics ought never to sever friendships, and I hope we can now all shake hands and go home and feel we have done a good day's work. I thank you from the bottom of my heart for the magnificent work you have done."

div.head: LATEST SUBMARINE.
div.p: THE LATEST SUBMARINE.

A new submarine has been invented by an American named Simon Lake, which pro- mises to be very generally adopted. It is called the Protector, and looks as though she were intended to be a very diminutive battleship,- provided with . a turret a number of sizes too large for her. She is unlike the general run of submarines, which vary from egg form to the longest kind of cigar shape, although it is true there have been a few designed in this style. The Protector is a vessel of 115 tons displacement, with a length of 65 feet and a beam of ii feet. She has two means of propulsion. When at the surface gasoline engines are used to aCtuate her _twin screws, and these engines are capable of recharginc, the storage batteries which are used to 'drive her when below water at the same time that they are pro- pelling the vessel. Her speed is said .tb be from ten to --eleven knots when at the surface, but, like all submarines, this will doubtless be considerably reduced when below.

div.head: PROTECTOR.
div.p: THE PROTECTOR.

She has a number of appliances and arrange- ments which are quite peculiar to herself. The big, roomy, oval-shaped conning-tower, from its position, size and weight, is said to have a steadying or counter-balancing effect on the boat when diving or ascending, *prevent- ing her from rising or descending at too sharp an angle. ' At the top of this is a species of sighting hood, which can appear above water without exposing the whole of the conning-tower. Another remarkable point about the Protector is that she has wheels sunk into the lower part of her hull which .can be utilised for propelling .her when on the bottom of the sea, and she has also facilities for divers to leave and return to her while below water. The Protector has three ways of diving. She can either sink by admitting water into tanks provided .for the purpose; she can plunge down by the use of horizontal rudders or hydro-planes; or .she can descend by making use of weights.

div.head: SOMALILAND.
div.p: SOMALILAND.

We have had so much bad news in the past from Somaliland that many had begun to fear the worst, and the success of the com- bined efforts of Generals Egerton and Manning and Colonel Swayne has come as a great relief. After months of preparation and care, ful manceuver-

ing three thous- and of our men a ttaaked five thousand Der- vishes at Jid- balli and routed them with great loss. The ene- my as usual charged with great ferocity, but our infantry broke theirS. frontal attack with , a heavy fire, routing them hopelessly
and then pursu- ing them. In THE LATE CAPTAIN THE HON. this way the T. LISTER, D.S.O.' forces of the , _

Mullah, who was not present in person, lost over a 'thousand killed to our losses of twelve killed, including three officers, and thirty-one wounded, including nine officers. At the first report it was announced that Captain the Hon. T. Lister, D. 5.0., of the ioth Hussars, was missing, but he was subsequently found to have been killed.. His loss is a consider- able one, as he was a most gAllant and rising young officer, and the deepest symPathy is with Lord and Lady Ribbler=dale. His father is one of the Liberal peers , and popular any- Where, not least of all at Court. He was a Lord-in-Waiting for some years, and from. 1892 -189 s• Master of the Buckhounds, of which he wrote a history. : Captain Lister. who was only five-and-twenty, Was his heir, and served through the South. African vial with great distinction, earning special men tion from Lord- Eitchener and a D.S.O. for "conspicuous coolness and gallantry under fire" with Colonel Alexander's column in Cape Colony.. Upon his return from the front he was drafted into the Provisional Regiment of Hussars at Aldershot uncle] Colonel de Lisle, until he was selected for special service in Somaliland and gazetted to the loth Hussars, of which the King himself is the, C.lonel. " THE FATHER or THE MET."

Admiral Sir Henry Tieppel, who passed away after a few days illneFs at his chambers in the Albany en Sunday afternoon, had lived to the age' of , ninety-five—his passion for the sea undiminished, 1. is vitality unchecked, his menial vigor little impaired by the burden of years, :Born in .180 9—t h e year which gave Gladstone, a great statesman and • , Tennyson, a great poet, to England— the " Father of the Fleet'' joined the Navy At the age of thirteen, when Queen " Victoria was but three Years old. He was born in the reign of George 111., :ived through the reigns of

THE LATE SIR H. KERP),-.L. George IV., William IV., and Queen Victoria, and witnessed the accession and coronation of King Edward VII. For fifty-seven 'years he seved his country in the Navy, and retired as Admiral of the Fleet in 1879. Keppoll came of a well- known family. His grandfather's grandfather was the original Arnold Joost van ' Keppel who came over to England with the Prince of Orange, nursed the future William HI. through the small-pox, and was his Sovereign's most faithful and trusted friend and servant till that monarch's life's end. King William left him 200,000 guilders and created him Earl of Albemarle. Sir Harry Keppers fathet was the fourth earl, and was born as long ago as 1772. Two of the old admiral's brothers fought at Waterloo.

FIRST DIVISI3N.
WARRINGTON v. BATLEY.

A crowd of about 5,000 assembled at Warrington on Saturday to witness the downfall of Batley, who, though they beat Warrington at Mount Pleasant were expecied to prove easy prey at Wilderspool. The home team turned out as selected, with the exception of Hallam, for whom Knight appeared at full back. Batley were well represented. Good weather prevailed and the only fault With the ground was that it was on the soft side. Mr. Renton (Hunslet) was the referee and the players lined out as follows: Warrington.—Knight, back.; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and Hockenhall, three-quarter backs; Bate and Davies, half backs; Boardman. Morrison, Swift, Cook, Thomas, Jolley, Naylor, and Edmondson, forwards. Batley. --Sutcliffe, back; W. Davies, Fenton, Wafters, I and H. Davies, three-quarter backs; Hodgson and Calvert, half-backs; Spurr, Shackleton, Phillips, Wolstenholme, H. Hodgson, Clayton, W. Philips, and Judge, forwards. Batley had the advantage of a stiff breeze, but laxity of combination spoiled several openings made by Calvert and Fenton. Eventually Warrington took up a strong position, and a round of passing between Isher- wood, Dickexson, and Bate resulted in Davies racing over at the corner. Batley continued on the defensive though Sutcliffe got the visitors out of several tight corners. From a fine run and cross kick by Fish the home forwards passed with remarkable precision, and Morrison, Naylor and dollo handling rapidly, Hocken- hall took the ball over, ‘Varrington leading at the interva. by six points. Turning round, Batley were compelled to adopt defensive tactics, and Sutcliffe was early called upon to save in quick succession. Fish made a bold effort to cross until stoutly challenged by Fenton. Calvert, one of the Batley half backs was ordered off/ for kicking Fish, and with their depleted force Batley fell off and exchanges between Bate and Davies ended in the latter scoring, Fish adding the goal. Diokenson next passed to Hockenhall, who raced in at the corner, whilst shortly after, Bate added the fifth try on the blind side of the scrimmage. Hockenhall scored just before the close, and Warrington won by 1 goal 6 tries (20 points) to Batley nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. HUNSLET.
div.p: RUNCORN v. HUNSLET.

This match was played at Runcorn before a very poor attendance, the recent bad form of the home team hav- ing resulted in a loss of public interest. On the Huns- let side Albert Goldthorpe played full back, and there were also several changes in the forwards. The Run- corn team had been re-organized. W. Goldthorpe kicked- off for Hunslet against a strong breeze. Hunslet soon got well into the Runcorn half, where VV. Goldthorpe made a fine attempt to place a goal from a penalty, the ball falling just under the cross-bar. A. Goldthorpe effected several fine clearances, and finally sent the ball into touch near the centre flag. Jackson, Hannah, and Whiteley made a good attempt to break through, but tlie defence was safe. Runcorn were then in difficulties until Harrison relieved by kicking into touch. The Hunslet backs frequently got possession, but Jolley and Butterworth played a smart defensive game. For an infringement Hunslet were penalised, and Jolley had an easy chance of placing a goal, but failed. A minute fromthe interval Jones was almost over, but was splendidly collared by Ramage. ' The second half was started with the game pointless, Hunslet having now thd assistance of the wind. Richardson and Butterworth got away, and the latter seemed to have a good chance, but was stopped by A, Goldthorpe. Runcorn then pressed, and Binks was collared before he could return. With only a few minutes to play, the game was keenly contested. J. Richardson made a good return, when his side were be- ing pressed, but A. Goldthorpe caught the ball and dropped a fine goal for Hunslet. Runcorn made des- perate attempts to score in the last few minutes, but could not get through. Result :—Hunslet 1 goal (2 points), Runcorn nil. Hunslet—A. Goldthorpe, back; W. Goldthorpe, H. Whiteley, Hannah, and Binks, three-quarter backs ; Everson and Jackson half backs; Glow, Barraclough, Wilsen, Brooke, Wilcox, Ramage, Wray, and Uttley, f orwards.

Runcorn—Harrison, back ' • Jones, Butterworth, J. Richardson, and Flanagan, three-quarter backs; Jolley and Faulkner, hhlf backs; Walker, Moulton Houghton, Dixon, Tomlinson, A. Richardson, Washburn, and D obson, forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Edmondson, Bradford.

div.head: WARRINGTON COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON COMMITTEE.
Annual Report.
We have received the following report of the first year's work of the Warringtoa Labour Representation Committee.
"TO THE MEMBERS OF THE ABOVE, AND TRADE UNIONISTS IN WARRINGTON."

In presenting to you this report, your Committee has pleasure in congratulating you on the progress made in Labour Representation in Warrington. It is necessary in submitting this, our first report, to refer back some eighteen months prior to this present time when a con- ference was convened in July, 1902, by the Trades and Labour Council, to take into consideration the forma- tion of a Workers' Election Committee. This confer- ence was fairly representative and was addressed at some length by Mr. John Hodge, who dealt forcibly with the need for Labour Representation, and pointed out very clearly how it could be brought about. The following resolutions were unanimously carried at that meeting :—(1) "That this conference is of opinion that the time has arrived when the working classes ought to be strongly represented on all local governing bodies, and in the House of Commons." (2) "That this meet- ing is in favour of a Workers' Election Committee being formed in Warrington, for the purpose of securing direct Labour Representation on all local governing bodies and in the House of Commons."

A short tine elapsed before a second conference was called by the Trades Council of a like nature, when a code of rules was submitted and a,i.opted and the present Labour Representation Committee took form- ation' several important societies at once becoming affiliated.

After the usual procedure of election of officers, the Committee immediately got to work to try and educate the trade unionists. All societies were written to 'appealing to them to join. the Committee, and asking them to receive dpputations, so as to put our views before the members, and to prevail upon them to take an interest in Labour Representation. Several socie- ties requested to have a deputation sent to them, and in every instance where this took place the trade unionists displayed a keen interest in the work of the Committee. In course of time other societies joined, and the Com- mittee grew in numbers and finance. The most important feature of the work has been the edtiLational part, and in connection with this we have issued a leaflet, entitled "A Lesson to Trade Unionists," which showed how the employers were federated together, and the steps they were taking to have their views expressed on local governing bodies and in the House of Commons. This leaflet also appealed to the trade unionists to take notice of what the employers were doing and to join the local committee s as to I hold their .own against the Employers' Federation. I Also, as a means of educating the workers, a large ' demonstration has been held during the past year for which the assistance of the Trades Council was sought and given. Mr. D. Shackleton, M.P., spoke at this , demonstration, dealing at length with the fullest I details regarding the present state of the law as it affects trade unionists, and Mr. A. Henderson, M.P., also gave a very interesting and instructive address on Labour Representation. The nudience,which numbered about 1,200,,was very enthusiastic, and at the close of the meeting when asked for a collection they responded very willingly and nobly, showing that the workers not only wanted Labour Representation' but were prepared to pay for it; on the whole, the demonstration was ' very successful. Afterwards,the opinion of Mr.llender- son and Mr. Shackleton was sought on the chances of I a Labour Candidate for Warrington, and acting upon I their advice and taking into consideration the feeling at the demonstration, the Committee at once took steps te circularise the societies asking them to send dele- gates to a conference, who must come prepared to vote whether in favour or not of a Labour Candidate being nominated for the Borough of Warring- ton, and the committee also decided to invite Mr. Alex Wilkie, of Newcastle-on-Tyne to attend. This confer- I ence has been held and was attended by a large number of delegates, representing about 2,000 trade unionists. Mr. Wilkie addressed this conference on general labour topics, and the following resolutions were unanimously carried :—(1) "That this conference recognizing the importance and necessity of direct Labour Representa- tion in the House of Commons, views with satisfaction the prospect of a Labour Candidate for Warrington." (2) "That this conferenee heartily and unanimously invites Mr. Alex. Wilkie to become the Labour Candi- date for Warrington at the next election and pledges itself to actively work for and use every legitimate means to ensure his return to the Imperial Parliament" This conference also,was a decided success,every delegate being instructed to vote in favour of a Labour Candidate being nominated. At the time of writing this report we have not yet received the official intimation that Mr. Wilkie accepts our invitation, but .we take this opportunity of appealing to the trade unionists for their assistance. The work of organization will be pro- ceeded with, and in this every trade unionist can help. Let us hope that before long we shall have the satis- faction of knowing that Warrington is represented by a genuine and direct Labour Member. The last, and one of the most pleasing items the committee has to report, is the endorsement of Mr. F. Scott's candidature, who was nominated by the Inde- pendent Labour Party for the municipal election in Orford Ward, and whilst Mr. Stott was unfortu..ately last successful at the first time of trying, he contested again at a bye-election, and we are pleased to record that he was returned at the head of the poll by a majority of 80, and we can now boast of having a Labour Mem- ber on our Town Council. Your Committee ventures to express the hope that you will soon send more Labour Members to help Mr. Stott. A lesson is to be derived from this eleetion, in that Labour had to fight a powerful organisation. assisted by a section of another organisation, who are usually found fighting one another as to which shall secure the workingman's vote. They were on this occasion work- ing hand in hand to try and defeat labour. It is to be hoped that the trade unionists will not forget this, and will cease to place their trust i these political parties, and will themselves do what work they require to be done. With all best wishes for the future, I remain, Yours fraternally, 0. BUCKLEY (Secretary).

div.head: STILL MORE PROOF.
div.p: STILL MORE PROOF.

At last, I heard of Doders Kidney Pills and, after taking a few doses,l felt so much better that I decided to keep on with there. I have not had a doctor in my house since then. div.head: INDESTRUCTIBLE PLANT-GROWS ON NOTHING,
div.p: INDESTRUCTIBLE PLANT-GROWS ON NOTHING,

There is a creeping moss found inJamacia, in Barbados and other islands of the. West Indies which is called the " life tree," or more properly the "life plant." Its powers of vitality are said to be beyond those' of any other plant. It is absolutely indestructible by any means except immersion in boiling water or application of a red-hot iron. It may be cut up and divided in any manner, and the sthaliest shreds will throw out roots, grow and form buds. The leaves of this extraordinary plant have been placed in a closed, air-tight, dark box, without moisture of any sot, and still they grow.

div.head: NEW DANGER TO FIREMEN.
div.p: A NEW DANGER TO FIREMEN.

Attention is drawn to the fact that a new danger has been added to the fireman's calling by the existence of electric wires carrying high tension currents. The danger is not extreme in Great Britain, where, except in the case of the overhead wires of a trolley-system tramways, most currents of high tension are carried underground. Wires sometimes bar access to a burn- ing building, and the fireman who has to chop them away is .confronted often by an extremely dangerous task. But a more peculiar danger than this exists, which is that the water from the nozzle Of the fire-hose that the fireman holds in his hand may, if the high tension wire b 3 near enough, convey a shock to him.-

div.head: BY L. VILLARI
div.p: BY L. VILLARI

It is not easy for people who have always lived in Western Europe to realise the hopeless confusion of divers races and religions which obtains throughout. the greater part of the Balkan peninsula. In Western Europe we have well-defined, groups of nationalities Ang,lo- Saxons, Frenchmen, , Germans, Italians—which only overlap at the extremities, in such regions, for instance, as Alsace-Lorraine and the Alpine :valleys, where two races come into conflict. But as we move towards the south-east we find large countries inhabited hy two or more hostile peoples, not dwelling apart in separate areas, but scattered all over it, and intermingled, though not amalgamated, in the same provinces, towns, and villages. Whim religions differences in- trude themselves as well, they help to make confusion worse confonnded, and the bitterness of race hatred still more bitter.

European Turkey is peculiarly unfortunate in this respect, for in a comparatively small e L we have no less than six races, all of whom can be said to be more or less indigenous to the soil—Turks, Greeks, Bul- garians, Serhs, liutzo-Vlaelis or Roumanians, and Albanians. To these we may add two more peoples, who, although not exactly indigenous; nevertheless form important com- munities—the Arinenians. who are practically limited to Cons(antinople so far as Europe is concerned, am! the Jews. In many parts of the country, and in most .of the towns, all these divers races are represented. There are, of course, many districts where one particular race really is predominant, and it would not be impossible to divide up the country into provinces based roughly on national lines; but the exceptions are every- where so numerous that it wotild be extremely difficult to say where the predominance of one race ends and that of another begins. Even as regards statistics of the various races, it is impossible to find out the numbers ofi each one with any degree of accuracy. The figures vary by hundreds of thousands, according to the 'views of thc: persons who have compiled them.. One thing, however, can be stated with certainty: the actual division of Turkey into vilaycts does not correspond iii any way to the division according to race. On the contrary, it , was expressly designed for the purpose of placing the warring elements into conflict with each other as much as possible, so as to govern them more easily. When we speak of Macedonia we usually mean the three viiayets of Salonica, Aonastir, and Kossovo. which correspond in some sense to the Macedonia of the ancients. But in modern times the name has no real signifi- cance, either ethnically or as an administra- tive division. There is no race which may be called Macedonian, for in that region we find half-a-dozen different races intermingled. If we try to didide it up according to the piedominance cf each, we may say roughly that the northern .and eastern part of the vilayet of Salon ica, the north-eastern,part of that of Monastir, and the southern part of EOSPOVO are inhabited chiefly by Bulgarians. South of Salonlca and Monastir the Greek element predominates; west of Monastir, in the north-west of Kossovo, and throughout the vilayets of Scutari • and Yoannina, the population is almost wholly All?enian. In the north of Kossovo, • as far, south as Ueskiib, there are Servians. - But, as I nave said, the various races everywhere overlap, and we find Bulgarians at Salonica, Greeks at Ueskiib, Servians at Ochrida, and Albanians at Serres. Over the whole country two other races are scattered about—the Turks and the Kutzo- Vlachs.

The Turks are all Mohammedans; and of the Albanians, from one-third to three-quarters, and a small proportion cf the Bulgarians, Serbs, and Kutzo-Vlachs, are also of that religion. The rest all belong to the Orthodox Church, save a small number of Roman Catholic Albanians.

The Turks, to whom for all practical purposes all the other Mohammedans not of Tin kish race may be assimilated, although not a majority, constitute the strongest element of the population. The . army is composed. exclusively of Mohammedans, and the Govern- ment, in spite of the presence of a few power- less Christian officials, is entirely in their hands. Above all, every Mohammedan can carry arms, whereas for a Christian to do so is a crime. Some of the worst atrocities have been. and are still, committed in the periodical searches for arms in the Christian villages. The Turks, as I have said, are scattered more or less all over the country, but there are several 'largo patches of them, such as the one round Yenidji-Vardar, another round Servia (between Salonica and 11.1onastir), and one in and about Uesktib. A considerable number of villages are half-Mohammedan and half-Christian, and in every large town there is a strong Mohammedan ciernea. Asa rule, the Moliannnodans are found in the plains and the Christians in the highlands. It is easy to imao;ine. in this state of affairs that the Nioliarnmedans will almostirievitably persecute the Christians, for to differences of race and religion are added village feuds, disputes about the ownership of this plot of land or the rights of pasture on that, quarrels caused by jealousy, and so on. Where a single village is mixed the feeling is exceptionally bitter, especially if the Mohammedans are Poniaki, i.e., renegade Bulgarians. The Mohammedans cannot be said to have any definite political views beyond a desire and determination to maintain their predomi- nant position in the country. This even the more educated and progressive Turks would never abandon unless forced to do so. They, too, suffer like the Christians from oppression and grinding taxation, and their privileged position consists in the right to plunder and outrage their Christian neighbours, and force them to labour on their farms for nothing

From the Mohammedans who are.ideaified with the Turks we must distinguish the Albanians. These people, who . are supposed to be the last remnants of the ancient Illyrians, the original inhabitants- of the Balkan peninsula, are in many ways a fine race— sturdy, brave, hospitable, and independent. But owing to an utter absence of education, at least as far as coucrns the Mohammedans, they have reMained in a ,zate of primitive harharism, and, in (7calinu. with their Slavonic and Greek neignue.ur§, are capable ot the greatest cruelty .As I have said, they occupy the whole of the vilayets of Scutari and Yoannina, and parts of those of Kossovo and Monastir. In Kossovothey are Continually driving back the Serbs, whom they despise and persecute unmercifully, so that many districts which were fornierly Servian, and, indeed, 'formed the nucleus of the great Servian Empire of the fourteenth century, hays now become almost wholly Albanian. This movement has been hastened by the emigration of Serbs into the kingdom of Servia and by the immigration of Albanians from that country into Kossovo. The Turkish Govern- ment has found in the Albanians a most useful instrument of oppression against its Christian subjects. Any future settlement that is made

for Macedonia will have to provide for the exclusion of the purely Albanian districts from the scheme, as what is suitable for Greeks and Slays and Kutzo-Vlachs would not do for the Albanians, wbether Christian or Mohammedan.

The Christians, unlike the Mohammedans, aro divided by race into a number of rival nationalities with distinct nationalist aspira- tions, of which the most incompatible are those of the Greeks and those of the Bulgarians. This quarrel has for over 1,000 years been one of the chief political features of Balkan politics. From the days when the Slays threatened Constantinople, and when a Greek Emperor earned the terrible title of Bulgarok- tonos, or Slayer of the Bulgarians (a title which might not inaptly be applied to the present Sultan), down to the dispute between the Patriarchate and the Exarchate, it has raged. But, whatever historic foundation the Greek claim to Macedonia may have, there is no doubt that to-clay the Bulgarian element is the strongest, at all events in the central part of the country, and the most full of vitality. Some of the larger • towns, like Salonica, may present a Greek appearance to the casual obserFer, but the villages all round art• purely Bulgarian._

The Greeks have always claimed to be the so'.e representatives of civilisation in the Near East, and as, long as the Slays remained_ ignorant and barbarous no cna disputed it. But the nineteenth century has seen the revival of tho Bulgarian language, and the Bulgarian people, having once shaken off the thraldom of the Greek influence, have become the dominant people of Macedonia. As, how- ever, the ethnical lines of division are con- stantly ,crossed by lines based on ecclesiastical distinctions, those Bulgarians who did not join the Bulgarian Exarchic Church, but continued to adhere to the Patriarchate, are described by the Greek party as "Bulgoraphone " Greeks. As a matter of fact, they are pune Bulgarians, who speak not a word of Greek, and it is certainly not among theta that any enthusiasm for the Greek cause to be found. Individuals, and even whole villages in Macedonia, often change from the Patriarchate to the Exarchate, or 'vice-versci, and with their change of Church they also change their political nationality. Of late years it is always the Bulgarian element that has advanced, pushing back Hellenism; and even at Salonica Bulgarian influence is on the increase. Not only is th;s the case in Macedonia, but even in the Adrianople vilayet, of which the northern part along the Bulgarian frontier is almost entirely Bulgarian. This race is, on the whole, the mast solid and reliable in the whole of the Balkan peninsula, and five centuries sLf Turkish misgovernment and persecutionVfave failed to destroy its vitality and spirit. The 'Macedonian Bulgarians look brutalised and dejected, but education and propaganda have galvanised them into activity, as has been proved by the hard fight the insurgents have been making. If any race in the world has earned its right to independence and national existence it is the Bulgarian. The astonishing progress they have made, the real political instinct of which they have given proof in the Principality, and their •incredible vitality and activity in Macedonia, shew that with time and oppor- tunity they are capable of great things. The Greeks are in a majority only along the coast, to the south-west of Salonica, and in the southern part of the Adrianople vilayet. nut scattered settlements of them are found e;sewhere, chiefly in .the towns. To them are assimilated the Kutzo-Vlachs, who, although numerous and wealthy, have hitherto had no distinct nationalist aspirations, but were usually regarded as Greeks. Of late years attempts have been made to arouse in them a feeling of Roumanian patriotism, and this, too, has helped to weaken the Greek cause.

The Serbs are found chiefly in the vilayet of Kossovo, although even there, as I have said, they are being slowly pushed back by the Ailmnians. They lay claim, however, to the whole of Macedonia, and pretend that the Macedonian Slays are not really Bulgarians at all, but Serbs. But their adherents in the country are very few in number, and there is no chance of their aspirations ever being realised unless they have powerful foreign assistance. The hostility between Serbs and Bulgarians has had most unfortunate cense- qiienct.s, as it has weakened both parties. Lately, however, a tendency towards a rni-procbement has manifested itself, and there i, a chance that the two Slav peoplDs will co- operate for the common (rood. The various nationaliset propagandas have ratio-ally been fostered and made more active 1.% the creation of the independent Balkan l. a tes, uhose frontiers are in no .case con- terminous with the ethnical limits of their populations. The ultimate object of all these poiitical movements is, of course, to prepare tile way for the time when the Turk shall I awe left Europe and Bulgaria, Greece, and ;._ervia will be able to annex those districts eyond their frontiers where their kinsfolk m the predominant element. 1-.:tit for the present nothing further is aimed at than to keep up and propagate national fee:ing and the national language, while the immediate object of the revolutionary agita- tion is to secure a decent government for the country. In spite of the rivalry between the various Christian - races there is among them nfl a longing for any change that will end the present intolerable state of things. Political agitators may contribute to these jealousies, and the agents of interested foreign Powers may foster them and magnify their im- portance; but the only thing that the bulk of the inhabitagts of Macedonia really want is refc2m—genuine, sweeping, honest reform.

div.head: UNDERGROUND WIRES.
div.p: UNDERGROUND WIRES.
Connecting Warrington _ with London.

Between the years 1897 and Itioo the Post Office engineering officers were engaged upon the work of laving an underground telegraph line from London to Birmingham, the route being Watford, Leighton Buz- zard, Fenny Stretford, Weedon, Southam, and Leaming- ton, and so en to Birmingham Post Office. Shortly after it was completed there occurred one of the most serious breakdowne of the overhead system that has ever been known in this country, and the underground line during that breakdown was found of great utility, as the telegraph service between London and Birmin- gham was uninterrupted at a time when Liverpool and Manchester were quite isolated from the Metropolis.- / The Postmaster-General was urged to ,extend the underground wires in other directions, and deputations were informed that it was intended to do so. Last year an experimental cable was laid between Birming- ham and Warrington, and this cable was in use until May,1903. Since then men have' been engaged pulling out the experimental wires and .putting in a main per- manent cable between the Midlamds and Lancashire.

The cable which is laid in a 3in cast-iron pipe con- tains 103 wires, enclosed in a leaden sheathing; 74 of the wires are twisted in pairs, and the remainder are single wires ceparately wrapped with a tape of coppet for the purpose of screening the wires from inductive action. The pairs of wires may be used for telephonic purposes, but it is believed that their primary use will be for high-speed telegraph circuits. The route from Birmingham is via Walsall, Cannock, Stafford, Eccleshall, Woore,and Nantwich. At the pre- sent time the cable has been completed to Eccleshall. The whole of the cables have been pulled into the pipes, but between the last-named place and Nantwieh the lengths of cable still require to be jointed together. The operation of jointing up the cable is one which requires very great care. It is hoped to have the cable completed to Warring- ton before the end of next March. At Warrington lines connecting Liverpool and Manchester can be tapped. It will then be possible to work from London to those cities by means of underground wires. During the De- partment's next financial year probably the section be- tween Warringion and Carlisle will have attention. A line is also being laid north- east from Manchester to serve the large Yorkshire towns.
