THE situation of THE END OF LIBERAL- the L i beral- UNIONISM. Unionists is a

sight to make the angels weep. It seems to the DUKE of DEVON- SHIRE that under the present conditions the Liberal-Unionist organisation had better be dis- solved. That is not the view of the Executive Committee of the Metropolitan Liberal-Unionist Federation. It may be taken for granted that no political body likes the idea of dissolution. Such a catastrophe must have the effect of adding a number of blameless officials to the ranks of the unemployed. Think ot the Wight which must descend upon a secretary's mind when he is deprived of his wonted routine of organ ising meetings and drawing up agenda papers! Such a prospect is naturally dis- tressing to Mr. NETrLEFOLD, who shepherds the Liberal-Unionist machinery in Birmingham itself. He is not in agreement with Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN, but he is not going to relinquish the post of secretary if he can help it. Nor will he sign any cheques for the " Protectionist prop- aganda." The funds were not subscribed for that purpose, and Mr. NETPLEFOLD Will not let them be diverted. But what, then, is to be done with them? A Liberal-Unionist organiser is either for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN or against him. There is no Unionist ptopaganda now which is wholly un- connected with the fiscal iSSUe.IF,Mr. NETTLEFOLD will not sign cheques for 31r. CHimaiintrArs's cam paign,how can he sign them for the opposite policy "We wish the Liberal-Unionist Association could be kept in being," counsels the Standard "and would continue to devote itself to the objects for which it was formed. Properly speaking, it has nothing te do with Protection and Free Trade. It has no/right to employ its funds and machinery to assist either side." But this overlooks the elementary facts. If the funds are employed at all they must assist one side or the other. There is no such neutral thing as the Liberal-Unionist who is neither Protectionist nor Free Trader. Either the organisation must break up, or it must Choose between the Fiscal principles of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and those of tl.le DUKE of DEVONSHIRE.

Nothing is gained by these efforts to tinker up a party which is utterly distracted by the main issue before the nation. "It is not," says the Standard," as if there were no longer any occa- sion for the Unionist party to be kept together. There is still abundant work for it to do, and work of precisely the kind which was intended by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and the other dissentients from Mr. GLADSTONE'S rolicy in 188 G- The value of this opinion may he judged from the assump tion of our contemporary that Mr. BALFOUR'S . Ministry" on a raft," as Mr. MoRLEY aptly calls it is engaged in this very policy. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN is anathema to the Standard ; but Mr BALFOUR, who is just kis much a Protectionist as his colleague, is claimed to be the pillar of the only original Unionism. " Unionist disunion," says the Standard, "is the Radical oppor- tunity" and this dreadful mischief can be cured only by a rally of the party to Mr. BsLroun's scheme of "deep and genuine change:' in our Fiscal system. Free-Trade Unionists who do not relish unity on such terms are told that they need not worry. Let .them apply their minds to the "abundant work" which belon2s to the statesmanship they created in 1886. But what chance is there for that when all the party machinery falls into the hands of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN? Mr. BALFOUR will meet Parlia- ment next month as a Protectionist Minister, at the head of a Protectionist party. The old shib- boleth of Unionism is dead, and the belated mumblings of the Standard merely reveal the embarrassment of politicane who find it difficult to adapt themselves to the new situation. No follower of the statesman who has openly aban- doned the principle of Free Trade can persuade the country that he is not a Protectionist. Every by-election is fought on the question deliberately raised by Mr. BALFOUR and Mr. Criambsnrairr,and the General Election will show the determination of the country to reject their Fiscal heresies.
THE preservation of THE CZAR'S: RE- peace in the Far East SPONSIBILITY. now seems to depend

upon the CZAR. Will he give efiect to his pacific desires by an exercise of autocratic authority? There is very little doubt that Japan will refuse to recede from the position she took up at the outset of the negotia- tions. She will not consent to a "neutral zone in Cores, and she will :not waive those rights in Manchuria which are embodied in her coracnercia

treaty with China. At a crucial moment China has asserted her authority over her own province authority which Russia has hitherto scouted as a diplomatic figment. By her commercial treaties with Japan and America, China has com- pletely outflanked the Russian diplomacy, and provosed M. DE PLANCON, Admiral—A-lexeieff's agent, into an unguarded expression of irrita- tion. According to this oracle, Russia will ignore the treaties, and refuse to accord consular status to the American representative at Mukden. Of course, M. DE PLANCON will be disowned by his Government, not for the first time. He was detected on a former occasion in the act of endeavouring to extract from the Chinese Govern- ment conditions flatly opposed to the 'public pro- fessions of Russia. When this little game was shewn up M. DE PLANCON was thrown over. He is used to the process. Russian agents are never sensi- tive. With a very bad grace Russia will acquiesce in the position which America has acquired in Manchuria by treaty ;and if she resolves to avoid war for the present she will acquiesce in the precisely identical claim of Japan. Some Optimists, indeed, anticipate a complete collapse of Russian aggression in Manchuria. The Moscow correspondent of the Standard says: "Russia will retain her West to East railway across Manchuria direct to Vladivostock, but will have to give up the southern branch, from Khorbin to Port Arthur, either to China or to an International Board of Control, or possibly to certain Powers selected to act on behalf of all." Then there wil be a truce for ten years or so, until Russia has an opportunity for " another attempt against a less formidable combination of odds." That such is the view of Admiral ALEXEIEFF does not seem very probable, for it means a se-ious blow to Russian prestige. It was scarcely for th a result that Russia ejected the Japanese from Port Arthur. She did that with the help of France and Germany, who are not likely to join an International Board of Control for the purpose of taking Port Arthur away from her. On the other hand, the CZAR cannot keep the peace ex- cept by overruling his Viceroy. A correspondent of the " Tinte;• " gives an interesting sketch of autocracy in practice. There is no Russian Cabinet, and the CZAR opposes or rejects the proposals of each Minister in turn. But the Ministers tell him what they believe to be the national conceptions and aspirations, "and he would be a very bold Czar who would sacrifice a great national interest to love of peace or any other personal feeling." So if Admiral ALEXEIEFF who corresponds with the CZAR quite independ- ently of the Foreign Office, where apparently, Count LAMSDORFF sits and twirls hi 3 thumbs should represent to his Imperial master that national interests forbid any concession to Japan, then peace will depend upon thelparticular degree of boldness which belongs to Nicholas 11. "If he desires peace in the sense of being 'ready to sacrifice to itcertain material and political interest he should lose no time in transferring the conduct of the diplomatic negotiations from his Viceroy to his Foreign Office." But he has already lost a good deal of time. Moreover, he made !Admiral ALEXEIEFF Viceroy with very largo powers,which would have to be withdrawn if the CZAR should decide to take the very bold course laid down for him. Is there a single instance of his having , Withdrawn any powers from a minister in deference tO prudent counsels? M. DE WirrE was super- Ceded by 31. PE PLEHVE, who is certainly not a model of prudence. Europe awaits with anxiety the first real manifestation of personal will from NICHOLAS IT.

We are pleased to learn from the numerous lettersfand verbal messages we have received this week that our readers greatly appreciate the im- proved quality of paper now used in the produc- tion of the " Examiner." Owing to a lengthy con- tract we were unable to make the change sooner. Some of our correspondents have also favoured us with suggestions for improvement in other direc- tions, for which evidence of friendly interest we -cordially thank them. The suggestions shall not only be considered, but carried out where practicable.

In another column we publish the first annual report of the Warrington Labour R3presentation Committee,which shows that a good deal has been done during the year to further the objects of the committee. The principal achievement—or per- haps we should say the only achievement—is the return of Councillor Stott to the Town Council as a representative of Labour, and on this success we congratulate the committee. Their endeavour to secure a Labour candidate for Warrington we have no sympathy with at the present juncture, because there is already an excellent Liberal candidate before the constituency and a three-cornered contest would be to the disadvantage of both. We have always believed so at any rate, but the result of the election at Norwich leads one to think that per— haps a Labour candidate would greatly enchance Crosfield's chances in Warrington. Mr. Roberts the Labour candidate at Norwich, received a tremendous thrashing from both his opponents, and the result of this experiment in three-cornered contests should not be very encouraging to the Labour party. If they desire directrepresenta- tion they should oppose Conservative non-pro- gressive candidateq, who are the men before all nthers antagonised to the reforms Labour demands. "There are plenty of opportunities for the Labour tearty to try its strength up and down the country without intervening awkwardly and tactlessly at Warrington. We are glad that, judging from Mr. Buckley's report, the prospect of a three-cornered fight at Warrington is remote. Mr. Wilkie has not jumped at the chance and Norwich is not likely to spur him on.

We are sorry to have to involve the Water Com- mittee in more trouble, seeing the sore tribulation -they have passed through during the past year. hut there is a serions fault to be remedied. From a chat which on of our reporters has had this -week wich Mr. Skelland, the esteemed superintendent of the Ragged School, we I.3srn that this valuable institution is seriously hampered in a very important ilranch of its work by the arbitrary action of the Water Committee. One would have thought that the members of this committee would have been particularly alive to the fact that " cleanliness is next to Godliness," and that there is no more important consideration affecting the public health. Yet they have stopped the bathing of the great unwashed at the Ragged School. For three years it has not been possible to give the children the weekly bath they so sorely need and iised to have. Mr. Skelland believes that some of the youngsters have not been washed since the Ragged School ceased to perform their ablutions. The sole reason is that the Water Committee,with fine disregard for the public health, persisted in levying an extra charge for the use of the big tub at the Ragged School—and the charge was more than the school could afford. This is an example of short-sighted policy and niggardliness such as we have not met with for a long time. The committee ought to have been only too pleased to let Mr. Skelland have for a nominal sum all the water he desired for cleansing the.. neglected children of the slums, instead of send 'ner in their bills for £lO and £5. What does our Medical Officer think of this? He is usually a stickler for cleanliness and sanitation. We should advise Mr. Skelland to see the Water Committee

once more andlif they remainrobdurate, t °resume the bathing of the youngsters in defiance of the committee and its bills. We will pledge the credit of the " Examiner " that the Rigged School does not lose by such action.

There are not many business concerns, either co-operative or otherwise,in such a sound position as the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-opera- tive Society, whose forty-third annual meeting we report elsewhere. From very humble beginnings it has risen to a remarkable position of prosperity and influence in the town, over 5000 families benefiting by the periodical dividends. The balance sheet is a pleasure to behold, though the stated assets and liabilities do not adequately represent the value of the Society. Properties have been written down to such an extent that the figures do not indicate anything like their worth. We do not wonder at the pride Mr. T. Birchall,J.P., takes in his co-operative protegee. He was one of the original founders and no man is entitled to greater credit for the magnificent suc- cess which has followed upon those early elf )rts nearly half-a-century ago.

Many Warringtonians will appreciate the im- proved passenger train service from and to Warrington which:the London and Nortii-Western Railway Company proposes to inaugurate on the Ist of February. For many years this powerful railway company has done little to meet the wishes and conveniences of the inhabitants of this important district. To judge by the treatment meted out to Warrington by the London and North-Western Railway Company,this County Borough might be but a small, insignificant town on a branch line, instead of being the busy centre of a district on the main line with 100,000 inhabitants. The passenger services have been poor and iutarenittent and the complaints of manufacturers with reference to goods traffic have been loud and deep, and at times have found expression at the meetings of the uhamber of Commerce. Baek Quay station itself has long been an eyesore'and it is a wonder that any self-respect- ing railway company has allowed it to remain in its present state for so long. It may have been ade- quate to the needs of Warrington a quarter of a century ago but it .is altogether inadequate to-day. On the high level the platforms are too low and too narrow, whilst the low level platform is a perfect puzzle-cfardsn to passengers. If it be true that everything comes to those who wait,then may be some living at the present day who will see a new, commodious and convenient station at Bank Quay.

, Notice has already been given of an application it is intended to make at the forthcoming licensing sessions for a licence in connection with an entirely new house it is proposed to erect on a plot of land at the junction of Lovely-lane and Delamere-street. The owner of the land is His Worship the Mayor (Alderman William Bolton) who proposes to erect and construct the house in question. Without in any way wishing to express an opinion on the merits of the appli- cation itself, we think His Worship has taken an' ill-advised course in associating himself with such an application during his Mayoralty. What can be said of the spectacle of the Chief Magistrate of the Borough asking a fa- vour—for the granting of a licence cannot be con- sidered as anything else—ot his brother magis- trates ? Warrington's close connection with the drink traffic is already notorious, and such an application will only serve to accentuate it. Under the circumstances we think the Mayor's action is not to be commended.

The smallpox outbreak has not yet subsided, four patients having been admitted to the Great Sankey sanatorium during the past week. Yester- day afternoon aregrettable incident which aroused strong comment occurred. An ordinary cab,which does not appear to be in particularly good condi- tion, is used for the conveyance of persons suffer- ing from the disease to Sankey. Shortly after two o'clock a patient from Winwick-road was being removed, and when tne vehicle had proceeded almost as far as the crossings in Tanners'-lane one of the wheels came off. Of course, the usual interested.spectators soon assembled and consider- able time °Lapsed before the cab could resume its journey.the wheel having to be re-fixed. It is not very long since we heard of a patient escaping from this improvised fever van and rambling about the country-side for a while, eventually being secured at a farm-house. The authorities would do well to consider the advisability of providing a specially-adapted vehicle. for the removal of patients. At any rate, it is to be hoped that such unpleasant incidents will not have to be recorded again.

By far the worse reverse hitherto sustained by the Protectionist agitation has been inflicted by the overwhelming victory of the Free Trade party at Norwich. It is hardly too much to say that the circumstances were such that the capture of the seat held until the other day by Sir Harry Bullard seemed out of the Tiestion. With the Free Trade forces divided by the ptesence in the field of a Labour candidate, the bdst thing to be expected was that the votes of the combined Free Trade candidates would be greater than those of the Concervative. But the result shows that the anti- Protectionist stream is running so strongly that all obstacles to success are being swept away. Mr. Tillett's enormous poll of over 8,700 votes is not only the largest vote ever cast for a candidate in the capital of East Anglia—it indicates that hun- dreds of Conservatives have deserted their candi- date, finding his support of Mr. Chamberlain in- tolerable. An aggregate majority of 4,400 votes for Free Trade on a poll of 17,000 is an over- Nhelming proof of the determination of the workers of Norwich to have nothing to do with Protection.

While this sensational electoral message was being delivered Mr. Chamberlain was opening his expert Commission. The Norwich result published side by side with his speech in the next day's papars made his optimistic expressions with regard to the outcome of his agitation road rather foolishly. No one has ever denied to Mr Chamberlain the gift of being a consutn. mate tactician, and it would have been poor tactics to have confessed that the labours of the Commission were bound to end abortively. None the less, certain passages in his address suggest than his expressions of confi- dence do not harmonise with his real convictions. Mr. Balfour, who spoke a day or two earlier struck a still less cheerless note. He at all events has no illusions about the popularity of the food- tax. Lord Stanley, the Postmaster-General, who spoke at Great Lever on Saturday, quoted the advice of a working man, that the food-tax should be dropped and the tax on manufactures parse- vered with. But, as Lori Stanley pointed out the food-tax is the very heart and kernel of the Chamberlain policy. Without a tax on wheat, he has told us, the Empire cannot be held together.

Swinton (surveyor)- -Farrington (inspector of nuisances), and Hough (deputy clerk)—The committee approved plans of six new houses in Carlton-street, submitted by Mr. James Strange—The Chairman said be had received a letter signed by owners and ratepayers in Ellesmere-road calling attention to the condition of the footpath and asking the committee to recommend the responsible authority to flag it similarly to the footpath in the adjoining Fairfield-road.—lt was stated that the road belonged to the County Council and the committee decided to request the District Council to approach that body with a view to the work being carried out. —On the suggestion of Me. Coming Events. To-morrow (Sunday) special trust sermous will be preached at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church by the Rev. John S. Simon, Governor of Didsbury College. Mr. Simon is now the leading authority in Methodist law! and history, and is one of the principal ministers in the Connexion. lie will undoubtedly be.,s President of the Conference at an early date.
At Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church to-morrow (Sunday) evening, the Rev. j. Garciham Reed will preach " The ladder of character, and how to climb it."

An open meeting of Wycliffe P.S.A. Society will be held to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon. The Rev. .T. Yonge will preside, and the speaker will be Mr. W. Beecher Smith, of the Y.M.C.A., Manchester. The Apollo Male Voice Choir will give selections. A social arranged by the Free Church Council will be held in Bold-street school on Thursday even- in, when brief addresses will be delivered by Mr. Charles E. Parker (president), the Revs. John Yonge, 6-. H. Carnson and J. F. Matthews. There will also be a musical programme. The annual Congregational tea party and entertain- ment in connection with Emmanuel Church will be held on Thursday evening next .11 the schoolroom over Arpley Station. The annual Christmas treat to poor children will be held in the Drill Hall on Friday and Siturday next. The girls will have their treat on Friday and on Saturday the boys will be entertained. A subscrip- tion list is published in our advertising columns. The second subscription concert of the season in connection with the 'Warrington Musical Society w ill be 'held in the Parr Hall on, Wednesday, February 10th i when Dr. Elc,,a,r's "King Olaf'' will be rehdered. The annual ball in aid of the Infirmary and Dis- pensary will be held at the Parr Hall on 'Wednesday, February 10th. Personal. - - -

_ Lady Croft, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. Charlton Parr, of Grappenhall Heyes, gave birth to a daughter on the 14th inst. We are pleased to hear that mother and daughter are doing well. The trustees of the living of St. Helens have selected six clergymen, and invited them to attend a meeting for the purpose of seeing the church and vkaxage, &c. The Bev. Inspection of Hackney Carriages. The annual inspection of hackney carriages by the iWatch Committee took place on Thursday afternoon n front of the Town Hall. Inspector Taylor and Detective Barlow (hackney carriage inspectors) were in attendance. About twenty vehicles were carefully examined and found satisfactory.

Mr. S. Brighouse's 20th Anniversary as
Coroner.

On Saturday:- ii;t7 -Nix. S. Briliouse completed his twenty yearns coroner for South-West Lancashire, having been appointed by the freeholders on January 16th, 1881. This election was the last coroner ever elected by freeholders in the country, for afterwards the County Councils took over the right of appoint- ment. Mr.Brighouse has held over 10,000 mquests,and of special interest were those he held ia the Maybrick case and the Deeming case. He has travelled on an average about 7,000 miles a year. In 1884, in his first year of office, 539 inquests were held, "and of these 476 were held in public-houses. Mr. Brighouse has always desired to hold his inquiries in other places, such as schools, institutions, etc. Last year, of the 453 inquests, only 179 were held in public-houses, and almost all the 179 were in country places where there was no other accommodation. This fact is worthy of record, and Mr. Brighouse is certainly deserving of the thanks of the public for his action.

Warrington P.S.A. Society. There was an excellent attendance at the open meeting of the above society on Sunday last, in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street. Mr. E. Wynne- -Tones presided and in a short address, said the P.S.A. movement had done much for the spread of moral ideas. He trusted the influence of the members of that P.S.A. would always be on the side of purity, temperance, right, and truth. He hoped each member would take a deep interest in the welfare of the society. If they put heart into it, and brain into it, and prayer ,into it, good, and good only would be the result. The Rev. .John Yonge was the appointed speaker and he delivered a most helpful and interest- ing address. Mr. Yonge said he had great con- fidence in the P.S.A. movement; it had great possibilities at Wycliffe. Much good had been done, the drunkard had been reclaimed, young men who were fast drifting away from religious influences had been rescued. It was impossible to tabulate the results because they are moral and spiritual results.Mr.Albert G-arner,of Widnes, rendered in excellent style two solos entitled " There is a green hill" and "The lost chord." Air. Wadsworth was the accompanist. Mr. Brown and Mr. Warham also took part in the service.

Death of Mrs. Brabazon, of Lymm.
After a long_illness,_Mrsl BrabTizon, wife of Dr.

Brabazon, of —Brook House, Lymm, passed away on Sunday. Mrs. Brabazon was the 'daughter of the late Mr. Benjamin Pierpoint, J.P., of St. Austin's, War- rington, and was well known in the neighbourhood, having spent the whole of her life in Warrington and Lymm. She had resided at Ly mm for thirty years and will be much missed by all classes, especially by the poor, who esteemed her for many acts of sympathy and kindness. The funeral took place at St. Mary's, Lymm, at noon on Wednesday. The chief mourners were Dr. Brabazon, Miss Brabazon, Dr. and Mrs. Burrows, Mr. Charles Brabazon, Mr. R. On Wednesday evening, the weekly session of the Temperance Mission Lodge of the T.O.G.T. was held in Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street. Bro. Merlin C.T. presided and there were also present Bro. J. Parr C.C.T., Sister Battersby C.V.T. and Bro. P. Hulme C.M. (of Leigh), Sister Miss Woods and Bro. Smith (Earlestown). One new member was initiated and one restored to membership. The visitors gave a capital programme consisting of earnest addresses by Bros. Parr and Hulme, solos by Sisters Woods and Battersby and gramophone selections by Bro. Smith. Refreshments were served, and a happy time wa,,, spent. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS NfINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Liberal Club Euchre Competition.

Death and Funeral of Mr. David Pickton. The death took place oa Sunday of Mr. David Pickton, who has been connected all his lifetime with the firm of Messrs. David Pickton awl Sons coach builders, wheelwrights, &G.; of Allen-street. He was 62 years of age and had been lying ill at his residence. 40, Bewsey-street, about IQ, weeks. He was of a quiet unostentatious disposition,but his lona residence and business connection. with Warrington had caused him to be well-known among a wide circle of 'friends and acquaintances. He is survived by two sons and three daughters. The funeral took place on Wednes- day afternoon at the Cemetery and was attended by sorrowing relatives and friends and workpeople. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. W. Bracecamp. • St. Mary's Dramatic Society._ •

div.head: London and North-Western Brakesmen's Dinner.
div.p: London and North-Western Brakesmen's Dinner.

The brakesmen employed on the London and North- Western Railway at Warrington held their annual dinner at the Railway Taverif on Saturday. After an excellent meal, provided by Mr. W. Longmore, a pl6asant evening was spent, toasts, songs, recitations, and vocal music being given: Mr. R. Bolton, station- master, after' some encouraging words to the men, proposed the toast of "The King and the other mem- bers of the Royal family." A song entitled "Stand by your countrylstand by your King," was given by Mr. A. Hindley. Mr. Diggory proposed the toast of "The London and North-Western Railway, its officers and men," and Mr. Longmore the toast of "The Army and Navy and reserve forces." Mr. C. Williams gave "The donors of the feast and to the collectors." Songs and recitations were contributed by Messrs. J. Gordon, P. Rigby, J. Sankey, A. J. Wickhain, J. Wainwright, T. Lowe, W. Cope, J. Ditchfield, M. Burke, E. Williams, E. Slater, and R. Scarisbrick.

div.head: Cow Throws a Goods Train Off the Line.
div.p: Cow Throws a Goods Train Off the Line.

The traffic on the railway between Chester and Liverpool (Lime-street) and Manchester Was consider- ably delayed on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning owing to a cow which had strayed on the line near Dunham Hill, getting in the way of a London and North-Western goods train drawn by two engines. —As a result of the impact the cow was, of course, killed, and no fewer than twenty-five waggons were thrown off the line and badly smashed,, whilst the permanent way for a distance of something like three- quarters of a mile was torn up. The damaged part.is on one of the busiest lines in the vicinity of Chester, and the heavy traffic between .Manchester and Liver- pool has had to. be diverted through Helsby and -via Hooton. Despite the efforts of a large breakdown gang, it was only possible at ten o'clock on Wednesday morning to work one line via Dunham Hill. The engine-drivers, stokers, and guards were unhurt.

div.head: Professor Timson at the Druids' Hall.
div.p: Professor Timson at the Druids' Hall.

Professor Timson, of Leicesier and Southport, and assistants commenced a series of lectures and enter- tainments at this Hall on Monday. In the afternoon Nurse Cox gave a lecture to ladies only, and in the evening the hall was filled, when Professor Tinason gave a lecture on phrenology and mental science, illustrated by views thrown upon a screen by means of a limelight lantern, manipulated by Mr. Langhana. The address was followed by a number of "living pictures" and vocal and instrumental selections. Miss Pemberton gave an effective rendering of "0 dry those tears," and Miss• Cook of Southport, was applauded for her song, "Get a wife, -young man." Mrs. Bracewell, also of Southport, gave very effectively the recitation, "The King's Picture," and an instru- mental quartette (piano, mandoline, guitar, and violin) was capitally rendered by Miss Holdcroft, Miss Cook, Mrs. Bracewell, and Mrs. Langham. Mr. Timson closed by delineations from photograph and hand- writing and an examination of the " bumps " of two gentlemen from the audience. On Tuesday evening during the entertainment Miss Furness sang in a pleasing manner. " Thn6hildren's home," and several delineations were given by Mr. Timson. Further lectures were given on Wednesday and Thursday.

div.head: Manchester and Liverpool District I Banking
div.p: Manchester and Liverpool District I Banking
Company.

At a meeting Of th-e shareholders, held on Wednes- day, at the head office in Spring-gardens, Mr. Abel Buckley in the chair, the report of the directors recommending a 'dividend for the half-year of 21s. per share, free from income tax, was adopted. The Chairman referred in his speech to the proposed amalgamation of the bank with Lloyd's Bank. Opposition to the propossl came, he said, from shareholders and customers, and from many who occupied neither of these positions. It was associated, however, with such tributes of appreciation and even of admiration and regard towards the District' Bank as could not but be gratifying to those who had the conduct of it. It was mutually agreed that it 'would be better to close the negotiations, and the directors of that bank were thus left free to proceed on the old lines as a separate institution. (Applause.) In reply to a vote of thanks accorded to the chairman and directors and the staff, Mr. Buckley stated that he had occupied the position of a director for 33 years, and of chairman for 21 years, and that he now desired to retire from both- positions, and therefore he would not be able in future to address them from that chair, an announcement which was received with much regret. At a meeting of the Board of Directors sub- sequently held, Mr. Edward Donner was elected chairman, and Mr. James Halliday deputy-chairman for the current year. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the XING OP ToNics.--63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt.
The Appointment of Tramways Manager.

For this appointment, 72 applications were clu- sidered at the special meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee held last evening. The follow- ing applicants were placed on the short list to appear before the committee at an early date :—Mr. T. Tate of Shipley, Mr. J. Teller of Rotherham, Mr. C. Warnersley of Huddersfield, Mr. J. Worrall, of New Brighton. The commencing salary is £l2O per annum, rising by early increments of £lO to £l5O. H. M. AsrrroN's LIFE Tone is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. "The Idler." At the Parr Hall on Saturday evening the members of the Warrington Dramatic Society gave their con- cluding performance of this comedy in aid of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children and the Children's League of Pity. The attendance was disappointing but the highly credit- able production of the pliy met with cordial appreci- ation. It is to be regretted that financially the per- formances have not been as successful as was desired but the members of the Society 'can at any rate rest assured that they put forward their best efforts in a worthy cause. It may be mentioned that as a result of the performances of "Our Boys" early in the autumn over £5O was distributed to charities, but the proceeds from "The Idler "—a far superior production —will hardly pay expenses. "The Right Little Island."

This is the title of a successful temperance operetta which was given on Monday evening ;in Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street.The performers were the members of the" Young Mission " juvenile temple of the 1.0.G.T. Councillor Thornton presided. The scene is laid in temperance Island where Queen Teetolia (Miss Ada Littlewood) reigned supreme. The inhabitants all lived happy together until the arrival of a band of drinkers headed by Lord Brewer (Master Sam Hughes) who try to generally disturb the peace of the island. Lord Brewer being out with his com- panions one day, is separated from them and loses his way. He is met by one of the Queen's attendants, Clara (Miss J. Hughes) who is also lost. While they are mutually trying to find their way, Lord Brewer falls in love with Clara and in return for her hand and heart she asks him to sign the temperance pledge. He does this and his followers, rather surprised at his action, follow his example. They are all welcomed as members of Temperance Island and the scene closes. The various characters were creditably taken and a good time was spent. During the last scene a miscellaneous entertainment of songs, duets and re- citations was given by Misses E. Ryder, F. Littlewood L. Warburton, G-. Fry, A. Clough. F. Egerton, A. Warburton, and A; Edwards. At the close, a hearty vote of thanks to all who had taken part *as moved by Paster 3". Grady (who has commenced a good work in the district), seconded by Mr. J. W. Roberts, and unanimously carried.

div.head: EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.
div.p: EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.
Modern Enterprise.

Enterprise is the keynote of modern business life and the manufacturers of foods and household com- modities—in fact of requisites of all kinds—are ever on the alert to discover fresh means of bringing their productions before the notice of the purchasing public. One of the most popular mediums-7-and one of which Warrington people, at any rate, never seem to tire -- is the trades exhibition. Since Tuesday last the Parr Hall has been the scene of a very representative exhibition of this description, promoted by a syndicate comprising some of the leading firms. It is due to the management to say that every effort has been put forth to make the arrangement of the stalls bright and artistic, and the general effect is pleasing to the eye. Admission to the hall is free, and each day there has been a steady stream of visitors,particu- larly in the afternoon and evening. A great variety of goods is on view and so alluringly are they dis- played that it is almost impossible to resist the temptation to buy. Moreover there are cheap and free samples galore and for a very modest outlay one can obtain delicious confections as well as handy labour-saving produCtions which the busy housewife can fully appreciate. A glance at the following list of exhibitors will enable our readers to form a pod idea of the scope of the exhibition :

Messrs. Bird's (custard, blanamange,baking egg and jelly powders. , Edwards' (dissicated soups, &c.) - The Cannon Iron Foundries, Limited (gas cookers and fires.) The Nugget Polish Company Limited (waterproof boot polishes). The Shredded Wheat Company. "Matchless "Metal polish and other preparations. Hovis bread and flour, baby food, and invalids' food.

Cadbury's (cocoa and chocolate.) Sapon, Limited (self-acting washers.) J. Mackintosh, Limited, (toffee). Palethorpes' (sausages and pork pies). Icilma soap, &c. Mr. B. Wadsworth, Warrington, (pianos and gramophones). Mr. J. Horton, Warrington, (confectionery, &c). Messrs. B. Podmore & Co, Warrington. (" Oliver typewriters). Mr. J. Marsh, Warrington, (ironmongery &c.) E. Davies, Liverpool,. (electric flash lamps). Apart from the exhibition itself there are numerous attractions. A ladies orchestra discourses sweet music and in one of tile ante-rooms cinematograph entertainments are given at intervals The cookery and laundry lectures have been well attended, and various interesting competitions have proved a success. A beautiful oil painting" Peace at last" is on view, and has been much admired.

div.head: LOCA.L EXHIBITORS.
div.p: THE LOCA.L EXHIBITORS.

One of the principal local exhibitors is Mr. B. Wadsworth, of the Music Depot, 59, Sankey-street, and at his well-arranged stall in the entrance hall, no fewer than eleven of the best pianos, as well as a beautiful organ by Sames, are on view. Particular attention is drawn to the pianos of John Broadwood and Sons. This firm, which was established in 1732, has by far the oldest business of its kind in ~the country, and we suppose there are very few persons who do not know of the supreme excellence of their instruments. The late 'Sir Charles Halle wrote 7 "I can highly recommend the Broadwood pianofortes, as I have used them in public and private for the last forty-two years, and prefer them to any others." Every instrument is fully warranted, and is sold at the very lowest possible cash price, although arrange- ments are made for easy payments at a slight increase on the "prompt cash" price. All the instruments have the check repeating action and the celeste pedal, which gives a very soft tone without injury to the piano. A number of smaller musical instruments are also exhibited, and the collection does Mr. Wadsworth great credit. Mr. James Horton, of the Park Machine Bakery, is also to the fore with a stall laden with choice edibles. The exhibit is well worth inspection, and good busi- ness should be the order of the day.

In the large hall, Messrs. B. Podmore and Company, of Bevvsey Chambers, have a very creditable exhibit of the well known" Oliver " typewriters, which have been skilfully manipultated in the presence of many interested spectators. One of the great advantages of the machine is that it writes in sight of the operator, and it is already used by many local firms. Mr. J. Marsh, ironmonger, of Sankey-street, has a very attractive exhibit, and his stall has been well patronized. The exhibition will continue until Friday evening next.

div.head: DESERTER OR NO DESERTER?
div.p: DESERTER OR NO DESERTER?

At Runcorn, on Tuesday, Augustus Lewis, a yonnz man, was charged with being a deserter from the Royal Navy. P.C. Preston, who apprehended the prisoner, said he had admitted that he was a deserter, but now the prisoner said he did not know whether he was a deserter or not. The prisoner's father informed the Bench that when his son came home he wrote to the Admiralty, but as he had not received any reply he thought the Navy had no need of him. The prisoner was remanded.

div.head: LE.A.P FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE.
div.p: THE LE.A.P FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE.

On Tuesday at Runcorn, S-iirn-Wei.-dOa-,-;f.f'rederick - terrace, Ditton, clerk at Gaskell Deacon's works, Widnes, was charged with having on the 7th January unlawfully attempted to commit suicide by jumping from Runcorn Bridge into the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr. F. J. Poole appeared for the prisoner.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. .Tohnson)said the question was whether Cook was fit to bear the inquiry.—Cook : lam perfectly well.—After further discussion, the Chairman (Mr. Fred .T. Norman) said the best thing would be to remand him for a week.—Cook was remanded for seven days, and liberated on his own recognisance of •£lO, and his brother's surety of a similar amount.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

There was no interruption of Warrington's victori- ous career on Saturday, when Batley were the visitors to Wilderspool. The "gallant youths " are gener- ally found stubborn opponents, but Warrington had booked them as among the slain before they arrived. It is easy to prophesy when you know, and one was as sure of Batley's defeat on. Saturday as it is possible to be of anything in football. They came with a very poor resord, whereas Warrington have proved their mettle in no uncertain way of late.

There .is really not much to say of Saturday's match. Warrington.'s superiority was so soon made apparent that it was only a question of the number of points the visitors would succumb by. It took the home backs a while to find their feet, but once :they got going points accrued. Davies was the scorer of the first try, after neat com- bination, and Hockenhall got the second. This was the product of a rather remarkable movement. Davies, Isherwood and Fish got away on the left in the War- rington half, the wing man running speedily to the Batley quarter and then punting into the centre. Here Jolley fielded smartly, and a series of transfers among the forwards sent the ball to Hockenhall who finally grounded on the right wing. The cheering was loud and long, and the forwards in particular deserve praise for smart handling such as one does not often see in their department. At half-time thegscore was two tries to nil in favour of Warrington.

Early in the second half, Calvert,the most energetic of the llatley halves, was caught in the act of kicking Fish, with the result that Referee Renton gave him marching orders. Warrington completely overran the visitors after this. Hockenhall notched a couple more tries as the result of clever back play, Bate and Davies getting one each. Fish kicked a goal and the total finally reached 20 points to nil. Perhaps the most remarkable feature of the (Tame was the fact that Fish failed to get one out of six tries. He put in all he knew, but for once in a way Fate was againSt him Sutcliffe, the Batley full back, tackled him three times when he had beaten everyone else., and he deserves every credit for what is a somewhat uncom non achievement.

The Batley men were. thoroughly well-beaten. From the commencement they played like a team without much hope and one never expected them to trouble the scorers. Turton at centre was about the only back who did his duty, and this diminutive three- quarter played good football throughout. Wattie Davies was very lackadaisical and-did nothing at all calculated to enhance his reputation. Calvert at half played an energetic game until he was sent off, and the full back likewise played a fair game. Though slow he defended surely and punted well into touch,

On the home side there was much ragged football relieved by brilliant flashes. The forwards showed ' plenty of dash, easily holding their own in the packs and quite outclassing the Batley men in the loose. There was more speedy following up than usual, a feature I was glad to note. Only a few seasons ago few teams could compete with the Warrington for- wards when chasing the bill. Alereweather.Nlorrison, and Masoã were a trio who gave the defending side little rest. There is plenty of ;speed in the present eight and it might well be utilised oftener in following up.

Hallam was. missed at full back, where Knight deputised. He preferred to give his injured shoulder a long rest, thus the call on the "A " team back. Knight was not in his best form, and it is fortunate he was not severely pressed. • Only in kicking a good length did he do himself justice. Davies played a grand game at half, quite coming out of his shell. The speed and cleverness be displayed were streets ahead of anything he has done under the Warrington colours previously. On Saturday's form he is a half back to be feared. The threequarters all played a fair game, though Dickenson was uncertain in his passing at times. Hockenhall astonished the croivd with scor- ing three •tries, and displaying more dash than usual. Fish's disadvantage was his opportunity. -

Oldham still lead the way, and it is much to be regretted from a Warrington point of view that the return match is not down for decision at Wilderspool.. Still it is not impossible to check their Victorious career at .Watersheddings, as Widnes and Broughton Rangers proved. On Saturday, for the first time this season, Warrington got ahead of Hull Kingston Rovers, and they ought on form to certainly finish in the first three. •
The League table up-to-date is as follows: For. Against.

Warrington's fixture for to-day does not appear a very serious one, on piper, but the men of Keighley have several times proved that on their own peculiar battleground they take some beating. Salford were only able to draw there quite recently and Warring- ton will have to play their hardest to secure the maximum of points. Fish will be absent owing to an injured thumb, and this fact increases the necessity for the Warrington men to strain every nerve. Kenyon gets his chance to-day, and I shall be delighted if he proves that his scoring ability is not Confined to junior football. Cook is reported missing, and Lunt will fill the forward vacancy.

The Warrington team will be: Hallatn, full hack; Kenyon, Isherwood, Dickenson and Hockenhall, three- quarters; Bate and Davies, half-backs; Boardman, Morrison: Thomas, Lunt, Naylor, Jolley, Swift, and Edmondson, forwards.

An important capture has been made this week. Fielding, the captain of the Ponty-newydd team, and an old club-mate of Thomas's having been signed on. He is a forward standing nearly six feet high, had weighing over 13 stone. He will be eligible for the Broughtln Rangers match next Saturday. A young forward from the Wigan district has also joined the club, and receives a trial with the " A " team against Pendlebury to-day.
Though deprived of Knight and Mahoney, the " team won easily at St. Helens on Saturday. Kenyo and Short were the principal scorers, each notching points.
Harris is practically fit again, and there is a pro- bability of Warrington putting the strongest team they have had this season in the field against Brouc,rh- ton Rangers next Saturday.

It is not often that one of my correspondents favours me with a Limerick, but this week " S.W.T." sends me a few lines anent the" slippery Fish" which are above the average in point of rhyme and appropriate- ness. This local Limerick is as follows There are many team managers fish, But they don't always cltch what they wish; Let them try Wilders—pool, And they will, as a rule, Gat a," bite " from the "'slippery Fish."

div.p: GRAPPENHALL

DAY AND SUNDAY SCHOOL PARTY.—The children attending the day school, together with those of the Sunday school, had their annual tea party on the Friday last and afterwards games and dancing were indulged in. During the evening oranges and crackers were given to the scholars. The Rector, the Rev. R. Green- all, and the Rev. E. E. Farrel', the teachers of the day school, and other ladies and gentlemen interested in the , schools were present. The pr ^ ecl ings went on merrily until nine o'clock, when, tired but happy, the little ones Idispersed.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

div.head: Annual Meeting. THE COMMITTEE ENLARGED.
div.p: Annual Meeting. THE COMMITTEE ENLARGED.

It is now forty three years since the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society, Limited was established and at the annual meeting on Monday evening the members were able to review the gratify- ing progress which the organization has made, particu- larly of late years. Mr. T. Birchall presided and was supported by Mr. W. Jeffrey and Mr. A. H. Rathbone (managing secretary). There was a large attendance. THE PRESIDENT AND THE ADVANTAGES OF COMBINATION. The PRESIDENT alluded to the great progress which the society had made since they held their first meeting. At that time it would have taken only £lOO to pay their dividend. This year £24,000 would be required and 5,000 families would benefit. The growth of the so-operative movement was one of the wonders of the world, and when they looked at the great advance co- operation had made and its ramification surely it ought to be an object lesson to working men, showing what it was possible for them to do when they combined. (Hear, hear.) Theirs was the biggest commercial con- cern in the country; and it had brought to its present state of perfection:--increasing year by year— by working men. If only working men would but realize their power, and dispense with the mill-stones hanging round their necks in the shape of drink, gambling, and debt! (Hear, hear.) If working men would turn the money they spent in drink into other channels they would settle once and for all the fiscal question without the aid of protection. The object of the society was to make workingmen independent and when they considered the advantages it was a wondei that so few people seemed to be aware of the existence of the society and that there was, comparatively speaking, a small membership.

CO-OPERATIVE CONVALESCENT HOMES. THE AMERICAN COTTON CORNER. THE 'PRESIDENT AND HIS POSITION. The SECRETARY reported that at a meeting of the Committee a letter was read from the Wholesale Co- operative Society suggesting the erection of taro con- valescent homes for co-operators in Lancashire and Yorkshire. It was suggested that societies should sub- scribe at the rate of .£1 for every forty members. The Committee decided to ref9r the matter to the general meeting. The Secretary had also received a letter with reference to the encouragement of cotton growing in. the British colonies, and the Committee had decided to grant £3O to the British Cotton Growing Association, the donation to be spread over a period of six years. Mr. Robert Cooke, who had served on the Committee for forty-three years, and Mr. William Jonas, who had acted for an almost equally long period, had tendered their resignations. The new members admitted to the Society (raring the last quarter numbered 1,003, and the number of withdrawals was 917. The CHAIRMAN said that at the last meeting there appeared to be some misconception on a matter which aroused considerable discussion. Up to forty years ago the secretary took his own stock, but the members thought that ISMS not desirable and appointed him (Mr. Birchall). He had discharged the duties ever since. Fifteen years ago he was granted an annual honorarium for his services, and although since then the business had more than doubled, the honorarium had not been, increased at all. Of course, he was not complaining about the smallness of the grant. With regard to the convalescent homes, the amount required to build them would be £24,000. The Whole- sale Co-operative Society had agreed to pay pB,OOO if the other societies of the United Kingdom would raise the remaining £lO,OOO within a reasonable time. Alluding to the Cotton Growing Association, the Chairman pointed out that English cotton manu- facturers suffered through the " cornerinr, "of cotton by speculators and the association had been formed to encourage the growing of cotton in the colonies. He moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. JEFFREY seconded. In reply to Mr. MayburY the CHAIRMAN sdid that if the sogiety contributed to the convalescent homes at the rate of Ll for every 40 members the subscriptions would amount to about £175.

Mr. LOWE pointed out that the Cotton Growing Association urgently required support and he suggested that the grant of £3O be paid at once. Mr. HAIGH moved that a grant of £lOO, to be spread over a period of four years, be made. Many co-oper- ators and their families were dependent to a great extent upon the cotton industry, and he would like to see the time when England would be independ- ent of other nations in regard to her cotton. supply. Mr. Timperley seconded the proposition which was carried.

There was considerable discussion in regard to the convalescent homes, Mr. J. W. Bouchier eventually moving that the proposal of the Wholesale Society be entertained. He thought they could rest assured that. anything undertaken by the Wholesale Society would be properly carried out and that the homes would be managed as successfully as the huge business which the society conducted. Of course, if the scheme did not pay the society would be liable but at the very outside their liabilities would be only £3OO or £lOO. He did not for a moment think there would be a loss; on the contrary the homes might possibly pay adividend. Mr. Crowther seconded. Messrs. G. WALLINGTON and B. FARRAR suppntecl and it was carried unanimciusly. The minutes were then confirmed. THE BALANCE SHEET. The report and balance sheet, which were approved, showed that the scales of the quarter amounted to £36,216 Lis. 4d.; which was the highest on record, and showed an in crease over last quarter of £4,332 15s. sd. In comparision with the corresponding period of last year, the difference was £3,811 3s. Id. in favour of the presene' quarter. The committee were pleased to note that the shoe department was having more attention from the members, the sales showing an increase of £3B over the cbrresponding quarter of last year. THE OFFICIALS THANKED. Mr. ENGLAND proposed a vote of thanks to the officials and committee for their services. Mr. B. FAR.RArt seconded, and said that seeing that Messrs. Cook and Jones, who had just resitned from the committee, had been with them for such a great number of years it was only fitting that the society should make some substantial recognition- of \their services. (Applause.)

WALLINGTON seconded, and added that the matter should be placed in the hands of the committee for thew. to decide what form the testimonial should take. This was agreed to. In returning thanks, the PRESIDENT said he had never been connected with a committee which worked more. harmoniously. He emphasised the facts that the balance sheets were genuine ones. ENLARGEMENT OP THE COMMITTEE. Mr. 'MAMMY, in accordance with the notice he gave at the last meeting, moved that the committee should be increased from eight to twelve members, and that the additional members be appointed that night. The PaEstDimr explained that it would be necessary to obtain the sanction of the registrar to the altera- tion before the four extra members could be elected. Arguing for the enlargement of the committee Mr. I.IIA-YEURI7 alluded to thelgreat increase in the business of the society and said that as the sales, liabilities, and capital had increased, the committee ought also to be enlarged.

Mr'.' B. FARRAR seconded but pointed out that there was no desire to displace old committee-men. Mr.Boucif LER suggested that the additional members ornight be appointed that night, subject to the approval of the registrar._

There was a long discussion, in which the personal element at tinxes asserted itself, and the enlargement of the committee to 12 was can ied by a large majority. At this stage Mr. Birchall was unanimously re-elected president on the motion of Mr. WALLINGTON seconded by Mr. 130UCHIER. Mr. J. Green Chappell was elected auditor. - Voting then took place to elect the four additional members of the committee and also to fill the vacancies caused by the resignation ,of Messrs. Cook and Jones and the retirement in rotation of Messrs. Dunbobbin and Critchley. The following were elected : Messrs. S. Critchley, S. Dunbobbin, J. W. flouchier, B. Hall, F. Timperley, H. Maybury, B. Farrar, and -W. Bibbv. The others nominated were Messrs. E. England P. Winskill, S. Blythe and J. Crowther. Mr. MAYBunv then introduced a resolution that the committee.be paidat the rate _of £2 12s Oct each per year. The CHAIRMAN: We don't ask you for any pay, but if you are going to pay us we are not going to call that. pay. The Runcorn Society pays £8 per annum and at St. Helens the committee men receive 2s per meeting and there are two meetings each week. One member suggested that each committee man be paid £lO per annum. . Mr. MAMMY pointed out that in the summer tha committee had a picnic which cog £2O. Ultimately the consideration of the matter was ad-. journed.

A PAUPER'S COMPL IINT AT RUNCORN. A pauper named Minnie Price, made an accusation against the Matron of Runcorn Union Workhouse on Tuesday, at the Runcorn Police Court, in answering to a. charge of absconding from the Workhouse with clothing worth I ss. Louis Anthony,Assistant Workhouse Master deposed that the prisoner and another woman named Johnson climbed the high wall of the houseand escaped They had had great trouble with the prisoner.—The Prisoner: There is no comfort in the workhouse. IC you say anything the Matron will smack- your face with her fist. It's not the first time she has done it to me,and. I told her I would not stand it any longer.—The Chair- man (Mr. Norman) : Have you ever complained? The , Prisoner; No, sir, because I dare not speak. She is always present with the Guardians, and she would punish us in some way.—The Chairman : She did not do anything of the sort on Saturday ?—The Prisoner: No, but she had been agate" of me.—The prisoner was committed for a month's hard labour.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
TIIR')WVG A KNIFE-A WARRINGTON Ms INJURES

His CHILD. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, Joseph Clancey, Stoney-yard, was charged with making use of threats towards his wife Catherine Clancey at 11.30 on Saturday night and with assaulting and exposing his .child, aged seven/months—Mr. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. and said the prisoner, who was a furnace man, earned39s. a week. At 2.30 on 'Saturday, afternoon he came home from work and gave his wife some money. He went out and on returning again at 10.30 went to sleep Whilst he was asleep, his wife not having receivedj suMcient money from him, tank some out of his pocket. On finding out what had happened prisoner began to upbraid her and struck her with an ashpan. He then ordered her out of the house, threatening that if she did not go he would murder her. The woman was standing near the door when prisoner picked up. a knife and threw it at her. The weapon, however, missed her, and -struck the baby on the top of the head, inflicting a wound which bled. Mrs. Clancev went to Market- gate where she saw Superintendent Monaghan and Sergeant Barnett, and the sergeant went to the house. He found the prisoner was not drunk but in a temper, and he threatened that if the officer kit his wife and children in the house he would cut their heads off. Prisoner was consequently taken into castody.—The Chief Constable said the police were satisfied from the threats prisoner made use of that the woman's life was in imminent danger.—Superintendent Monaghan said the child was very poorly clad and it was screaming.—Other evidence was given and it was stated that Prisoner had been before the Court twice previously. The Chief Constable described him as "a dangerous man when in a temper."—The Mayorsaid the case might have resulted very Seriously. Prisoner committed the offence whilst in a temper and the Bench had decided to deal leniently with him. He would be fined 10s. and costs and bound over to keep the peace.

AT WARRINGTON. At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday. Arthur Jones (16), errand boy, and George Henry Daniel (35), broker, were indicted together, the youth for stealing a quantity of toys hnd smallwares, the property of Thomas taker, toy and smallwares dealer, Warrington ; and Daniel for receiving the goods, well knowing them to have been stolen, during the months of September, October, November and December last. The youth Pleaded guilty, but Daniel pleaded not guilty. For the prosecution, Mr. Crireaves Lord (instructed by Messrs. Browne and Crompton) explained that Jones was in the employ of Taker, and occasionally sold articles at the markets on commission. Finding that his goods were disappearing from his warehouse, Taker watched, and on December 12 he visited Widnes mazket, and there found a quantity of his goods. valued at E 7 10s- being sold by Daniel nada boy named Samuel Jones. The two were arrested, but at the police court the case against Samuel Jones was withdrawn. It was alleged, in evidence, that Daniel said at one time that he bought the goods from Arthur Jones and again, that they had been ." pinched." For the defence, Mr. Maxwell (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) stated that Daniel carried on business as a broker, and in this case he took these goods evenly from Arthur Jones to sell on com- mission at the market. Jones told him he had pur- ,hased %iota lot. Daniel corroborated this statement, and evicrence of good character was given.—The jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty," and Daniel was clis- charged.—Jones was bound over under the First Offenders Act to come up for judgment when called upon.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Alderman Bolton (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, 1 Messrs. Birchall and Wright. ' No VISIBLE MEANS.—EmiIy Worrell, Rush Green, Lymm, was charged with having been found at Orford . Barracks at twenty minutes past twelve on Sunday •morning,without having an visible means of subsistence —Police-constable Clarke said the prisoner was handed over to him by Corporal Maginniss, who described her as "a nuisance about the place." She went to the barracks nearly every night.—She was sent to gaol. for a month. DISTURBING AN INVALID.—TweIve boys named James Tranter, 2, Warburton-street; Edward Stokes,3B, Warburton-street; Ernest Stevens, 8, Watkin-street ; : Robert Dutton, 18, Warburton-street; William Penketh. 1237, Winwick-yard ; Samson Green, 237, 5 inwick-road ; Henry Marklove, 255, Winwick-road ; Alexander Jones, 1, Taylor's-yard, Winwick-road ; Edward Casey. 239, Winwick-road; Alfred Casey,239,Winwick-road; Wilson Fox, 230, Winwick-road : and James Cowell, 10, Warbur- ton-street ; were summoned for having played "shinty" I.in Winwick-roai on Friday, the Bth inst.—Stovens Stokes, Tranter, and Cowell pleaded not guilty.—Agnes Baguley 142, Winwick-road, stated that at about 3.45 on Friday, the Bth inst., she was ,at home attending to her husband, who was very ill. He was being greatly annoyed by a noise in the street at the front of the house, and witness I found the defendants playing "shinty." Upon asking Ithem to go away- some of the boys commenced to use very bad language. She went to the Police Station,and , complained.—P.C. Lewis said that upon seeing Tranter, , Stokes and Stevens, they admitted the offence.—The Chief Constable said it seemed a very lamentable thing that lads of that class would usually tell the truth when seen before their parents had had time to manipulate , them, but after their parents had drilled them they said , what they were told by them to say. In fact, he over- heard several of the parents drilling the boys. Tranter, Stokes and Stevens had been summoned previously. . The muistrates ordered the three defendants named to pay sslhcb, and the others were fined 2s. 6d. each. TUESDAY..—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair) and . i Hutchnson,andpr,Fox.. „ _ __ .

"CAUGHT HIM ON THE HOP."—Daniel Cox,a stranger was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, at 11-15 the previous night.—P.C. Whalley said he saw prisoner trying the doors of three separate boot shops in Bridge-street. He then went into Rose and Crown-street, but returned to Bridge-street shortly after. He stood for about three minutes in front of one boot shop, looked round, and then tried the door. Witness went to him and prisoner remarked: "You have caught me on the hop. I intended to get a pair of boots from somewhere, and I might as well have them from Warrington as anywhere else." The mail was under the influence of drink.—Prisoner denied that he had tried any doors, but admitted he was drunk.— The Chief Constable asked if it was worth while adjourn- ing thecase to inquire into prisoner's antecedents.—The Bench decided to deal with the case at once and fined prisoner 10s. and costs with the option of fourteen days' imp-isonment. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. H. Roberts and Hepherd. THEFT FROM A. FORGE.—Thomas Barlow, Fea.rnhead- lane, a youth, was summoned for having on Monday last stolen 161 b. of scrap iron of the value of H., the property of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd.—Mr. F. S. Taylor, soliaitor, prosecuted, and said defendant whilst loading a cart ,with cinders took away the scrap iron which . was lying about the. premises and would shortly have been removed V. the scrap heap. The felonious intent was undoubted, because defendant was observed to put the iron into a hag which he placed on the cart. The firm instituted the proceedings ad a warning-and he sug- gested that defendant might be dealt with under the First Offenders' Act.—The mlgistrates imposed a penalty of 10S. EXPENSIVE SIA.P.-10bort Reid, 215. Knutsford road, was summoned for stealing two packets of dry soap of the value of VA, the pronertv of Messrs. Joseph Cros- field and Solis, Limited.—Nfr. 11. Evans watched, the proceedings on behalf of the firm and Mr. Steel appeared for the defendant who pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said the -charge might seem a trivial one, but Niessrs. Crosfield very seldom prosecuted with anything ' like severity and in many cases did not prosecute at all. He was afraid advantage was taken of that leniency. The firm felt it was their duty in this caseto ask for the assistance of the magistrates in putting down pilfering which had become a frequent occurrence. At the same time they did not wish the defendant to be made a scapegoat in the matter and left the disposal of it entirely in the hands of the Bench in the hope that they would deal with him in that lenient way which so often characterised their decisions.' It appeared that on Friday morning last, Joseph Flood, a night watchman, in consequenre of information of previous thefts, cpncealed himself in a place commanding. a view of the pkcking room. At 5.1 n he saw defendant come through a trap door and , deliberately take two packets of dry soap from the table. He was in the act of raw:ming down the steps when Flood called him back and told him that the matte: would be reported—lr. Steel said the defendant was a married man with three young c'aildran and had hitherto borne an irreproachable character. He said he had never taken anything before, and as he had lost his situation he (Mr. Steel) suggested that the magistrates should deal with him as a first offender—A fine of 10s. was inflicted.
