and Mr. T. Hilton.

CRUE;TY TO Hs .—W titer Peare?. Whitefleld- road, Stockton Heath, was summoned.. for illtreating two horses at Rixton on the Bth inst.—Tames Blundell, of Cidishead. stated that he saw defendant beating the horses severely and making them gallop. They were so exhausted that they came to a standstill and would not start a second time although defendant continued to thrash them.—P.C. Clarke said the horses were sweat- ing and completely ethausted. There were weals on their backs inflicted by the .chip.—Defendant stated that one of the horses W s "jibbing" and he could not get it to go.—A fine of 23. Gd. and costs was imposed. WARRINGTON MEN SENT TO GAOL FOR THEFT.— Arthur Rowlands, 'it Crossley-street. and Arthur Lomax, 3; Spencer's-yard, Warrington, were charged with steal- ing 1191bs. of potatoes, of the value of 4s. 3d., the pro- perty of Isaac Warburton, farmer, Woolston.—P.C. Clarke, of the Warrington nolice, stated that at mid- night on Sunday he met the prisoners in Manchester. road. When he approached them Rowlands dropped something bulky from his back and made off. Witness gave chase and caught him, and Rowlands admitted that he had dropped a sack containing potatoes, which had , been stolen from Mr. Warburton's farm. Witness took , Rowlands to the Police Station, and subsequently appre- hended Lomax at his residence.—The Chairman said prisoners were exceedingly badcharacters, And had been fined many times.—Lomax had been to prison before. They would each. have to go to gaol for a month with hard labour.

div.head: FATAL FALL INTO ACID AT WIDNES. The Coranar anri Insarantle Companies.
div.p: FATAL FALL INTO ACID AT WIDNES. The Coranar anri Insarantle Companies.

.\lle. S. Brighoase, caunty • clronex, conducted an inquiry on Tuesday evening, at the Accident Hospital, Widnes, into the circumstances attending the death of William Platt, aged 20 years, of 70, DaYies-street, an employ 6 of the Chemical Manufacturing Company, who died on Sunday last as the result of being scalded in a -vat of soda liquid on Christmas Day. Mr.. Evans, H.M. Trilpector of Factories, was present: also Mr. Linacre, who watched the proceedings on behalf bf the insurance company.: and Mr. C. Poole representing the Chemical. Manufacturing Company. At the.outset, theCaronerasked Mr. Porde whom he represented, and he said he appeared on behalf of the company. The Coroner replie-1 that Mr. Linacre, of Manchester also appeared on behalf of the company, so they must arrange between themselves. Mr. Poole replied that he represented the chemical manufacturing company. The Coroner said the insurance company, who were called upon to pay, had a perfect right to be repre- sented and hear che evidence at the inquest, but they came in a sneaking sort of way and said they repre- sented the company, yet, at the same tune, they repre- sented the insurance company. Mr. Linacre: Excuse me, sir, I said in the interests of the company. • The Coroner: It's all right : it's only a quibble of words.

The matter then dropped. The evidence given showed that on Christmas Day the decemted was directed to attend to two vats qf soda liquid. The vats were large ones, about 2ft. deep, one of which was Planked over in order to make ;platform for barrels. Platt's duty required him to make a test of liquid, and he mounteg the ladder to test one vat, and crossed over on to the planking for the purpose of testing the second van, when, owing to the steam and smoke issuing from the vat, he placed his foot in an aperture between the planks, and his leg went into Ole liquid as far as the knee. The inry return.i a ver-liet of " Accidental death," and added that they were of the opinion that if the planks were used they should be put so close together that an accident of the nature described could not occur.

div.head: ELEPHANT HUNT AT WOOLWICH.
div.p: ELEPHANT HUNT AT WOOLWICH.

An elephant Chase in real life has been causing excite ment and consternation at Woolwich. A cattle truck was specially reserved on Sunday morning, at the Arsenal Station, for taking four of *Captain Lockhart's performing elephants to Norwich. The . animals were just entering the truck when the keeper suddenly rattled his keys and chains startling the beasts, ,who scampered out of the station wildly trumpeting. The crowd in the vicinity of the station scattered with surprising celerity and the elephants, apparently enjoying their new-found liberty, did not stop until they had run for half a mile. Eventually the keeper secured his charges but not be- fore one had backed into a photographer's shop front, and anotherhad broken down the iron railings rounda front garden. ,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 23, 1904 LIBERAL MEETINg AT STONTON HEATH.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 23, 1904 LIBERAL MEETINg AT STONTON HEATH.

the borough. It would be within the recollection of , the committee that some little while ago they received a letter from the Board of Education asking them to let the Board know what steps they were going to take for the provision of secondary education. The Director of Education and himself were deputed to draw up a memorandum of suggestioas on the subject, and that had been done. He should like to take the opportunity of saying that the credit of that report was due almost entirely to the director. His (Mr. Stevenson's) part in the matter had been a very small one indeed, and only consisted of various suggested verbal alterations, and he wished it to go forth publicly that the real credit of the thought of the scheme, which he ventured to say was a very excellent one, was entirely due to Mr. Murray. The scheme had been placed before the School Management Committee and approved by them with practical unanimity. It was well known to all that on Thursday the School Management Committee would have a conference with two representatives of the Board of Education who would give them their expert stdvice upon the scheme, and after considering that advice the Committee would be able to present their scheme to the Board of Education for approval. He hoped it would be clearly understood that it was not for a moment contemplated that everything which was embodied in the scheme should be immediately carried into effect. (Hear, hear.) What the Board of Educa- tion asked them to do was to formulate a plan, but it did not press that every detail in the plan should be carried out immediately. Such a demand would be un- reasonable and inadvisable. In that plan they had, when it was finally passed, the steps which it was hoped and thought the committee would take in due course, and each after due deliberation. The co-ordination of education was one of the most difficult questions occu- pying the minds of educationists at the present moment. They were in a position of groping in the dark. Almost every town had the question before it, and no town had yet made its final decision. Therefore they were Without the guidance of other people and had to think those things out themselves. He was one of the committee's representatives who attended the Northern Educational Conference at Leeds, when the subject of co-ordination was discussed. He came away very much in the same state in which he went—deeply in the dark. It did not seem clear that any of the gentlemen who addressed the meeting by papers and speeches had thor- oughly thought the whole thing out and were prepared to say "This is the right thing to to and we must do it." That being the case he thought it was advisable that they should move slowly and thoughtfully and they hoped the scheme was worthy of consideration and of being carried out step by step, unless they saw, as time went on, cause to in any way modify it. It would be noticed that the Grammar School Governors had been in communication with the Board of Education, as the committee would naturally and rightly suppose they would be. They were all proud of the Warrington Grammar School. (Hear, hear.) They all wished to see it retain that honour- able position in the town which it had held for such a longtime, and they were quite sure that in the hands of the governing body, when they had taken the advice of experts, they would find the school would step into its niche in the educational plan of the borough and hold the position it was justly en- titled to occupy. Mr. Stevenson alluded to the con- sideration by the School Management Committee of an application from the honorary secretary of the associa- tion of Foundation Managers of Church of England schools in Warrington, for two rooms in the secondary school to be used each morning for the purpose of giv- ing religious instruction to the Church of England ohildren attending thtt school. In view of the terms of section 4 of the Education Act, 1902,the committee were unable to entertain the request. The section named expressly provided thatanyrerlnest for religious teaching must emanate from the parents of the children, otherwise it could not be entertained. The committee had therefore no option but to come to the:decision recorded. Should a request emanate from the parents it would, of course, receive that very careful consideration which the subject would justly demand. Councillor CRNIK seconded. , OTHER PHASES OF TETE SCHEME.

The Rev. E. J. Wir.r.cocics said he had taken a very great interest in the provision of higher education and he had thought the matter out carefully. It seemed to him that there were three points for their considera- tion and the first was the formulating of a scheme fer the grading of the schools such as was before them that sight. The next point was an inquiry into the educa- tional needs of the borough and the co-ordination of the existing institutions in the town, and the last was that if necessary they ought to call in outside expert advice. He looked upon the scheme as an honest attempt to solvea most difficult pro 31em. Their thanks were due to the Rev. Morley Stevensonand the director for the time and trouble they had devoted to the deve- lopment of the scheme. In regard to the Grammar school his hands were rather tied at presentand he was perhaps not. able to give full expression to his opinions In view of the inquiry which would he held on February 4thand sth. He would like an explanation in regard to the upper standard school.

The Rev. IVIoRLEv SrE% ES'ON said that by the scheme it was intended that at the age of ten years children should enter the upper standard school which would commence at about the fourth standard. Mr. IL T. learßcLouGH emphasised the importance of elementary school works being followed bya course at the continuation school and expressed the opinion that the instruction should be given free of charge in order to encourage boys to take advantage of it. The CFIA.IRMAN : If it is free it ought to be com- pulsory.
Mr. 111AIRCLOUGFI : I think it ought to be free in any case.

Aldecman BENNETT desired to add his testimony to the words already employed in reference to the scheme. The praise which had been given had been high but it had not been one jot too high. He certainly thought they had every reason to be proud of the gentlemen to whom they deputed the framing of the scheme and they were thoroughly satisfied with the result. Mr.Steveason said the impression he got from the ethic ttional con- ference wan that not many gentlemen appeared to have thought the matter out,but his (the speaker's)impression was th it the gentlemen who had drawn up the scheme at Warrington seemed to have thought the matter out—he did not mean in all its ramifications and details, that could not be expected, but the general principles and trend of the scheme appeared to him to be logical and to bear investigation. If they adopted it he thought they would have a schema that would admirably meet their requirements and do a great deal to carry out the ideals of many members of the committee. It was a statesmanlike survey of practically the whole field, and he rejoiced that for the first time in his life he saw a Possibility of the poorest and humblest lad in Warring- ton climbing, if he had the ability, to the highest educational facilities it was possible to attain in this eotrntry. He hoped the necessary scholarships would be forthcoming in due time. He felt very strongly that this country had been severely handicapped °wino' to the fact tiat there had been a tremendous realm of bun- exploited brain power that we had not been able to tap and make use or. There was no doubt that there were thousands of lads in all classes of society who, given full opportunities, woul9l develop greater capacity and help the progress of civif zation not only in this town and country but throughout the empire. We could not afford to ignore that brain power. We wanted to make the best use of it for the town and for the State. The ideal of the system they hoped ultimately to evolve would make that not a dream, a vision or an ideal, but a matter of actual practical', politics. He thought that thanks to the labours of the Rev. Morley Stevenson and the director they saw for the first time in their lives the way to the consummation they devotttly wished.

Mr. I.llAv asked for an explanation of thelucid scheme which none of them could object to. He believed in the open door, but there were two tales to it. Was the Grammar school coming to them for funds or would it provide its funds for carrying out the scheme and co- operate with tha Education Committee?
Alderman. SUTTON suggested that Mr. May should wait for the report..

The CHAIRMAN observed that the scheme presented to the committee was complete from beginning to end, and that was the advantage. They started with a child, and it worked its wayiup to the university if it had brain power enough. There was a large proportion of children who did not go beyond the sth 6th standard,but were sent to work, and under ordinary circumstances dropped out altogether. A good many of these children had presented themselves at the Technical schools utterly unprepared, and a great deal of the work the Technical Committee had had to do was to Ire-educate the children w:ap ware unable to take advantage of the opportunities offered to them. By this scheme, when a child left the elementary school to go to work, continu- ation schools would be provided in order that their education might be continued,and if they wished it they would be qualified, after passing some preliminary examination, to enter the Technical school like anyone else. For higher education provision was made. There was a complete scheme for taking a boy or a girj not only through the Technical school, but through the Grammar school into the University, if necessary. With reference to Mr. May's inquiry, all he would say was that he was certain the Grammar school would give the committee a great deal more than they could give the Grammar school. If they' made an arrangement with the Grammar school it would be favourable to the educational interests of Warrington, and not be a burden on the ratepayers. (Hear, hear). Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said in view of one or two remarks Which had been made he should like in the most stren- uous manner to urge every member of the committee to study the chart in connection with thq scheme. Every member should realize that while it indicated the lines of the complete scheme, it was a definite plan, repre- senting a great deal of thought and work, and indicated the lines on which any well considered plan of educa- tion, if it was to be really useful, must be carried out. It was not an ideal that was too remote, and the sooner it was materialized, and the various steps indicated were brotight into actual existence and operation, the better it would be for everyone. He quite appreciated the Rev. Morley Stevenson's caution in suggesting that the whole scheme could not be carried out at once but he (Mr. Jolley) would urge upon the committee that there were some suggestions which it was desirable to carry out as quickly as possible. I (Hear, hear.) The Rev. E. J. Willcocks had referred to the need of obtaining outside expert advice, but he (the speaker) did not think it was wanted. (Hear, hear.) Speaking with some knowledge of the move-

THE TEMPERANCE CAUSE. Meetings at Warrington. A PLEA FOR UNITY OF FORCES. 11 Mr. A. PERKINS made a strong plea for unity of action in the temperance cause at a well-attended public meeting in connection with Wycliffe Temper- ance Society held in the Memorial Buildings, Edge- worth-street, on Wednesday evening. It had, he said, been one of the features of their wont, or lack of work in Warrington that they did not unite. He thought most of the Nonconformist churches had recognized in years gone by one Sunday in the year as temperance Sunday, and on that day temperance sermons were supposed to be preached in all the Nonconformist churches. He did not want to find fault with anybody or with any organization; but what a splendid opportunity it would have been, if some Band of Hope Union, the temperance federation o:'a committee appointed from among the various temperance associations of the town could have •taken the Parr Hall on that day and have had a great tem- perance meeting in the afternoon and P, monster tem- perance meeting at night. He believed an effort of that kind would do far more (rood than the multitudes of smaller meetings at which they only spoke one to another and made no aggression. What they needed in Warrington was aggression but first of all they must have unity. He did not want to give his hearers the impression that he was a pessimist, but sometimes he felt that the bands of hope were not do- ing the kind of temperance work that they hoped and longed for them to do. It seemed to him that often thelenergy and resourcefulness of th-ir band of hope workers were almosticast to the wind, because they were operating again and again upon merely a handful of children. If the same qualities could be brought to bear in a great united effort which would extend over the whole year, the results would be far-reaching and would have a far greater influence upon the people of our town. Then again, temperance workers required conviction as well as unity. Many people who were total abstainers were not absolutely convinced as to the awfulness of the traffic in strong drink. They wanted to stimulate, to fire the hearts of people and bring them to the solid conviction that what was really needed was one great effort to thrust back the jugger- naut car which was crushing so many thousands of their fellow creatures. Mr. Perkins made a brief allusion to Mr. Justice Grantham's recent strong and pointed remarks, for which, he said, some people would almost apologise. In his opinion •no apology was needed, as the remarks had come from a man who had seen through many years of experience the awful- ness of strong drink, and who, spoke because he wan convinced and felt the matter deeply. Mr. Perkins spoke at some length against any compensation to the trade from public funds. If compensation became law he contended that the houses that would be closed would be those which were not paying. Let the brewers arrange a scheme of compensation among themselves, for that would be the only course which could be sensibly and reasonably considered by the country. (Applause). In the uuavoidable absence of Mr. P. O'Brien the chair was occupied by Mr. J. W. ROBERT, who asked his hearers to pray for the success of the temperance cause. He also expressed the hope that the churches would take united action and that at no distant date they would have the blessing of a "sober Sunday." It was stated that a Bill would be introduced in Parlia- ment to put a gag on the magistrates and take away , the power which they had held so long, of 'reducing the number of licences when they were not required. He hoped Mr. Balfour would never have the pleasure of carrying such a measure. (Applause). A most enjoyable musical programme was submitted by the members of Legh-street Primitive Methodist Choir under the conductorship of Mr. Spruce. The voices blended sweetly in the glees "Blow, blow thou winter wind" and "Strike the Lyre" and the part songs " When evening's tailight and "The sea hath its pearls." Another Pleasing item was the humorous song and chorus " Holstiener's band" by Mr. Philips and the choir. Mr. Barnes gave a creditable interpreta- tion of "The guiding light" and Mr. J. Corrin's solo .` Mona" was much appreciated. Mr. F. Podmore supplied the accompaniments. The usual votes of thanks concluded a successful gathering.

AN EVENING_ WITH THE JUVENILE RECHABITES. The "John Dimond " Tent. It is.lpleasant to see young people being trained in the principles of total abstinence and there is certainly cause for gratification in the flourishing iondition of the "John Dimond" juvenile tent of the Independent Order of Rechabites. At the annual meeting and dis- tribution of prizes held in Friars' Green schoolroom on Tuesday evening a satisfactory report was presented and words of encouragement were addressed to the large band of children which assembled. Brother W. Higginson (juvenile superintendent) presided and was supported on the platform by Bro. R. Campbell (High Secretary of the Order), Brother W. A. Platt (member of the Board of Directors) and Brother Smith (late of the indianEmpire district of the Order;) The SF:CRETA.RY (Bro. S. Gallop) in his annual report said he was pleased to state that the tent showed an increase on the previous year, both numerically and financially. During the year out tent meetings had been fairly well attended, and some very pleasant meet- ings had been held. The juveniles had entertained them with recitations, songs and readings which had been interspersed with temperance addresses from the superintendent or some Rechabite visitor. In August they held their annual picnic to Frodsham. and a very enjoyable day was spent, on Mersey View, the weather being delightful. The balance sheet showed that the income'on the various funds during the year, including £8 9s. 10d. in hand on December 31st last year, was £6O Bs. ld. After making all payments the funds in hand amounted to ,C 9 Bs. 10!id. The total consolidated funeral fund was £268 Bs. 2d. Forty six new members had been initiated and the total member- ship of the tent now stood at 185. _

I Brother CAMPBELL delivered an interesting address I in which he pointed out thatethe tent was instituted in November, 1901 with 21 members. Up to the present time 32 members had been transferred to the adult tent and 30 to other !juvenile tents. It was about thirty years since he commenced working for juvenile tents. At that time there were not 10.000 juvenile members in the whole order When he came to Manchester to take up the secretarial duties eighteen years ago they had 24,000 members,and now they had 125,000. ''The order was doing a splendid work for the young, and the young had helped them shrrreat'ly in building up the adult tents. Bro. Campbell owed how the operations of the order now extended all over the world and tents had been established in the army and navy. One tent was in Ladysmith through, out the siege and during that time doubled its member- ship. A vast amount of good was done to emigrants by the tents in the colonies. The speaker briefly re- viewed the life of Brother John Dimond and asked the children to emulate his example. Instancing honours which sometimes fell to the lot of Rechabites Bro. Campbell pointed out that it was through his official connection with the order that he was enabled to attend the Coronation and to visit Germany with a deputation. He proceeded to deal with the amount of wages paidin various trades in relation to the turnover. He, pointed out that brewers paid only £7 in wages out of every £lOO ii turnover and this, he considered, wns, fa. ' miserable sum compared with other trades. If the money spent in the brewing business was diverted to some other trade employment would be found for thousands of people who needed it. In conclusion he urged the members of the tent to put their shoulders to.the wheel and advance the time when the great drink business would be annihilated to a great extent, for this would mean better times for the country. (Applause). Later in the evening Bro. Platt distributed twenty:, six book prizes, and Presented Sister Elsie Wright and Bro. Alfred Pridden with juvenile Past Chief Rulers' sashes.

The evening WaS very pleasantly spent. The gramo- phone selections by Bro. George Lawless were thoroughly appreciated by the youngsters. Songs by Sisters C. Gallop and M. Fletcher were well received, and Sisters H. Hill and E. Gallop acquitted themselves well in a duet. Recitations were creditably given by Sisters Florrie Noble, Elsie Wright, and Ada Furnival. Sister M. Gallop accompanied.

div.head: DISCUSSION ON THE FISCAL QUESTION.
div.p: DISCUSSION ON THE FISCAL QUESTION.

A public meeting was held in the Providence School- room, Stockton Heath. on Tuesday evening, under the auspices of the Knutsford Division Liberal Association. Considering the short notice which had been given of the meting, there was a satisfactory attendance. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. W.H. Sherburn, who briefly introduced Mr. John Taylor of the National Reform Union.

Speaking on the subject of " Free Trade v. Protection," Mr. Taylor referred to the increased cost of living at the present day owing to the war taxes. Twenty-five shillings a few years ago, he said, would buy about as much as could be bought for 30s. to-day. That intant that every man had had; his wages reduced by ss. a week owing to the increased cost of living. Were they prepared, he asked, for a continuance of this kind of thing by the adoption of protection. In defining free trade, he said it was the unrestricted opportunity of exchanging goods for goods. They had been treated to a great deal or nonsense on this fiscal question by Mr. Joseph Chamberlain. He had been telling us that the country was going to the bad and that the exports were not keeping Race with the imports. The lecturer pro- ceeded to point out that a country was enriched by its imports, inasmuch as they .were in exchange for what was exported. Wages, he said, did not depend upon the price of the article produced but upon the law of supply and demand (Hear, htar,) The editor of a socialist paper had recently said that so far as protection waslconzerned it did not matter whether they taxed corn or meat or tea and sugar. It mattered a great deal, said the becturer. They could grow corn in this country and they could raise cattle; but they could not grow tea and sugar. If they imposed a duty on tea and sugar they did so for the purpose of raising revenue, but if they imposed a duty on corn and meat, it was not to raise revenue but to give the English producer an advantage over the foreign producer. (Hear, hear.) Indirect taxation always pressed heaviest on the poor, and there- fore every social reformer advocated a system of direct taxation. The lecturer proceeded to attribute the pre- sent fiscal discussion to a desire on the part of Mr. Chamberlain to divert the attention of the people from other things. According to Mr. Chambertain we had lost the American Colonies because they would not let us tax them and now we were going•to lose the other Colonies if we did not let them tax us. (Laughter.) Protection was a grand thing for millionaires but an evil thing for workingmen. (Hear, hear.) Where pro- tection had been tried it had produced millionaires and millions of paupers. As Free Traders we had had an enor- mous advantage in being able to get our raw material cheaplyand he contended that workingmen had everything to lose and nothing to gain by adopting the plan of Mr. Chamberlain's. (Hear, hear).

, . . 1 The CITAIRMAN said the matter under discussion was primarily a workingman's question. The reasons given for the success 'of our competitors in trade might be summarised under five heads. In the first place it was contended that foreigners had an advantage owing to the action of trades unions in this flO intry, which led men to work less hours and demand higher wages than their competitors on the Continent. There was perhaps a little truth in these charges. The decay of the glass trade in this country was due to some extent to the rigid conditions laid down by the Trades Unions connected with that industry. Trades unions were right in their place, but they must take care that they were not tyrannous. Then the second charge was brought against manufacturers. It was con- tended that we were losing trade owing to the antiquated methods of manufacturers and their un- businesslike way of dealing with customers. It w,s one of the dangers of protection that i manufacturers would lack enterprise and initiation if they were cer- tain of the home market. A third reason was that we were behind Germany and America in technical educa- tion. Some progress had been made in this respect but we were still a long way behind. Then in the fourth place it was contended that opr progress was hindered because we had so many lazy people to keep. (Hear hear.) When it was understood that a royalty of six shillings was paid on a ton of finished iron or steel to people who had not lifted a finger they would see what a drag it was on the industry. Then there was the land question still undealt with. Commissions had been held on the questions he had mentioned and they were now to have a so-called Com- mission on the tariff question. People who were convinced Protectionists were going to inquire whether protection was needed or not. (Laughter.) Many of the best known Manufacturers were not sitting on the Commission. He looked in vain for such names as Sir William Mather, Sir John Brunner, Mr. Crossley, Mr. W. H. Lever, Mr. Cadbury, Mr. Tangye and Sir William Holland. If this tariff question was the question now to be'dealt with, he contended that the present Govern- ment had proved itself unfit to deal with a business matter. (Hear. hear.) Mr. E. Lloyd Jones moved the following resolution: —" That this meeting affirms its unabated confidence in the principles of Free Trade, and protests against any attempt to tax oar food or the raw material of our manufacturers or to interfere with the fiscal principles that have brought so much comfort and prosperity to the nation, and that this meeting pledges itself to use every legitimate means and endeavours to return a Free Trade representative for this division at the next elec- tion." Mr. Jones pointed out that even the best Con- servatives were giving the matter the attention it deserved. He thought he might venture to say that they would welcome any Conservative Free Trader who would co-operate with them intarrying out the resolu- tion. The election in that division would be fought ex- clusively on the tariff question. The member who mis- represented the division had stated definitely that he preferred to ride on the fast horse. They Knew what that meant. It meant Joseph Chamberlain in preference to Arthur Balfour. There were several well-known Conservatives in the dtvision who had definitely promised to vote for the free trade candidate. It was necessary to unite the Free Trade forces in order to combat the great enemy to our commercial prosperity. Mr. England seconded the resolution, and said that. on this tariff question he preferred to take the opinion of old men rather than young men. Old men, who remembered the evil days of protection in this country wendered at young men really arguing this question. In every Protectionist country the hours of labour were longer and, with onp exception, the rate of wages was much lower. With regard to our exports, the increase per head of population, was greater than in Protectionist countries. Mr. Chamberlain would not face figures. There were more momentous matters that affected the workingmen, continued Mr. England, than this fiscal question. The question of the taxation of ground rents and site values was a pressing one. (Hear. hear.) The Chairman invited expressions of opinion from those in the audience. 1

Mr. McDermott contended that under the present trading conditions, we had not got Free Trade, which according to the lecturer, meant unrestricted oppor- tunity of exchanging goods ,for goods. Our markets were open to every other country butjthese other coun- tries closed their markets against us. That was not freedom of trade. What was wanted was equality of conditions and equality of opportunity. Given equal conditions the British workman feared no competition. In discussing this question it would be better to stick to the fiscal question. They had heard something that night about the taxation of land values and the imposition of mining royalties, but these did not affect the question. Even when steel works had their own mines they were unable to com- pete against the artificial barrier which countries raised against the manufacturers of this country. It waeonly fair for this country to be in a position to say to other countries "if you will give us a free market we will give you a free market." The discussion was continued, several in the audience taking part. ' __ _ •
The'dhairnan briefly replied to some of the points raised, aud the meeting terminated.

div.head: COLLIER . KILLED AT BOLD.
div.p: COLLIER . KILLED AT BOLD.

Phillip Lennon, a pit-4nker. aged 26. of 42,Edzworth- street, Sutton, died in the St. Helens Hospital on Friday from terrible injuries received the previous evening at the No. 3 pit of the Bold Collieries, belong- ing to the Collins Green Colliery Company, through a heavy iron slipper falling upon his head during pit- sinking operations.

div.head: COMPLETE SCHEME OF EDUCATION.
div.p: A COMPLETE SCHEME OF EDUCATION.
ADOPTED BY THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
From the infallts' Scholl to the
University.

A complete scheme for the supply of education in Warrington, whereby it will be possible for a child to pass from the infants' school by progressive gtages to the highest branches of education, has been formulated by the Rev. Morley Stevenson (chairman of the School Management Committee) and Mr. J. Moore Murray (director of education). The scheme was submitted to the Education Committee on Monday evening and ap- proved. In introducing the scheine, it is stated that it has been drafted in accordande with part 2, section 2, sub-section 1 and 2 of the Education Act, 1902, and is intended to co-ordinate all forms of such education, having reference to the existing supply of efficiept schools and colleges. The scheme embodies what is considered a complete system of higher education, which it should be the ultimate aim of the committee to establish, and has been arranged to meet the children of various aged and social positions in life, and to prevent any overlapping or competition between the schools. When established, it will be possible for a child to pass from an infants' school through the various grades to the Grammar school or the High school for girls, and on to the University:rne Scheme is placed before the committee for their adoption in order to comply with the section of the Act quoted above, and is not intended for immediate aecomplishment, as each part will require careful consideration before it is put into effect. There are, however, certain portions of it—the completion of the Secondary school, the co- ordination of the Grammar school, and the provision of more Training College accommodation—which should be undertaken at once. The re-organisation of the Evening schools and the Technical schools will receive the attention of the School Ilanagement Committee before the next Session commences. The committee have also considered the relation of the elementary schools to such scheme, and tney suggest, on grounds of economy and ecaciency, that accommodation should be provided in.the proposed new school in the Cock- hedge district for an upper standard department, in which the 7th and ex-7th standard children from the surrounding schools (which are situated in an artisan district Nvhere most of the children leave school between tile ages of thirteen and fourteen) could be collected for instruction in well-staffed classes. ' EVENING SCHOOLS.

The Evening schools should be re-organised, and opened for instruction on three evenings a ;week. The , instruction should be of such a character as to form a 1 continuation. of the work being done in the elementary day schools. Efforts should be made to secure the attendance of children leaving the day schools between the ages of thirteen and fourteen, and the courses of instruction should be such that the students may, between t4e ages of fifteen and sixteen, pass an en- trance exa/hination to the Technical school. The sub- jects of instruction should be limited to English, arithmetic, algebra, drawing (for boys), and needlework, ! domestic economy or cookery (for girls). The syllabus I might, with advantage, be that of, the Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes, for which examination the students ; could be presented, and on passing them, be transferred ; to the Technical school.

div.head: DAY TECHNICAL SCHOOL.
div.p: DAY TECHNICAL SCHOOL.

The fortunate position of Warrington with respect to Manchester and Liverpool makes it unnecessary to suggest the formation of a day Technical school at present, and, until such time as the general education of the children is improved, little use could be made of it.

div.head: EVENING TECHNICAL SCHOOL.
div.p: EVENING TECHNICAL SCHOOL.

The evening Technical school has suffered in the same way as most from the want of preparation of the pupils wishing to take advantage of the instruction offered. Few children are prepared to undertake techni- cal training before the age of sixteen. It is proposed to hold an entrance examination, or require seine proof of an applicant's ability to profit by the instruction. The standard of this examination would at first bs low, but as the supply of better qualified material increased, it could be raised. Such a proceeding will sacrifice numbers to efficiency. An attempt has been made, with some degree of success, to arrange the curriculum of the school in groups to meet the requirements of the students. The courses at present are building, engineer- 'electrical, chemical, textile, domestic, and general. As occasion arises, these groups might be extended, and new ones introduced. It is suggested that facilities should be offered to students who have passed through. the Evening Technical school to attend either Man- chester or Liverpool schools to complete their studies. SCHOOL OF ART.

The School of Art, in order to be more successful must be brought more closely into contact with the local industries. The evening classes should be arranged to meet the requirements of students engaged ía the artistic trades, and designing should form a strong feature of the school.

div.head: SECONDARY SCHOOL "A."
div.p: SECONDARY SCHOOL "A."

A school is necessary for the children of parents who, for financial reasons, cannot take advantage of the Grammar school, but who intend to keep their children at school until fifteen or sixteen years of age. A depart- ment or division preparatory to such a school, contain- ing children from eight to twelve years of age, should be attached to the Secondary school " A,".the children of which would, at the age of twelve, pass on to the Secoiadary school or bydmeans of scholarships to the Grammar school or Girls' High school. The curri- culum to be of such a character as to prepare them for these schools. The number of children in this prepara- tory division would not be very great, but, in towns where one has been established, it has been found tc meet a want. The Secondary school "A " already requires more accommodation. it is filling a want, but its usefulness would be improved if the Board of Educa- tion could see their way to amend their requirements in respect of such schools. It is proposed to arrange the second and third years' courses to meet local requirements preparing the boys for the engineering, chemical and other trades, whilst the girls will receive instruction in household and domestic duties. The boys on leaving this school, and entering upon their trades, would be well prepared to study in the evening Techni- cal school. PUPIL TEACHERS' TRAINING.

For the present it is proposed to continue the Pupil Teachers' classes in conjunction with the Secondary school "A," but it will probably be found advisable, when the complete scheme is working, to attacri the classes for boys to the Grammar school and thos2 for girls to the High school. GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
It is hoped that, by agreement with the Governors of the Grammar Schoo}, it may be co-ordinated with the Secondary* and Elementary schools and take its place in the system.

div.head: GIRLS' HIGH SCHOOL.
div.p: GIRLS' HIGH SCHOOL.

This school, charging considerable fees, will occupy the same p mition in relation to the other schools as the Grammar school. It would receive girls from eight to eighteen years of age, those from eight to twelve years of age forming a preparatory division. At twelve years of age they would pass into the upper division, the curriculum of which would be arranged to fit the pupils for the various walks in life which they intend to follow. A strong feature of this school should be the domestic training. TRAINING OF TEACHERS.

This probably the most pressing of all our needs, would best be met by the establishment of hostels. 2y conference has recently been held, and wilt meet again probably this month, at which joint action will, no doubt, be taken for the establishment of hostels in con- nection with the existing training colleges and the establishment of more training college accommodation it is recommended that a hostel for girls be established in connection with the Warrington Training College either by this committee or jointly with the surround- ing authorities, and that arrangements be made with the Liverpool and Manchester Day Training Colleges for the retention of places in those colleges for students from the town.

div.head: SCHOLARSHIP SYSTEM.
div.p: SCHOLARSHIP SYSTEM.

If such a scheme as has been outlined above be adopted it will be necessary ,to institute a scholarship scheme to enable the best girls and boys to make their way through the schools. These scholarships may be founded by voluntary effort, and could be assisted from the Education funds.
SPEECH BY THE REV. MORLEY STEVENSON. THE QUESTION OF RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION TN THE SECONDARY SCHOOL.

In moving the adoption of the minutes the Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON said the nubject which had princi- pally occupied the attention of the School Management Committee since the last meeting was the very import- ant one of the provision of secondary education within

div.head: " I WILL HAVE VI-COCOA."
div.p: " I WILL HAVE VI-COCOA."

Your grocer and every other grocer, too, can tell you of men and women who week after week regularly use Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa, and who, to use a common term "swear by it." as a nourishing and stimulating Food Beverage. Are you a regular drinker of Vi-Cocoa? If not, why not? . _ _

Dr. Tibbles Vi-Cocoa, by taking the place of stimu- lants of an ardent nature, has made happy many a home which otherwise to-day would have been wretched, and the ultimate effects of which it is impossible to foresee. For breakfast, dinner, supper—indeed at any hour of the twenty-four—Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa will be found light and refreshing ; it leads the way among all bever- ages, and nothing can equal it..

ments in the educational world, he ventured to think that in Warrington they could give advice to many authorities, and that thay had in their Director an educational expert who knew how to apply the general principles which had been accepted by anyone who had given serious thought to education, to local needs. Considering the short time Mr. Murray had been in Warrington, the report was an admirable testimonial to the Director, and he had shown how he could apply accepted principles to local requirements. In a measure, of course, as Mr. Stevenson had said, they were groping in the dark, but there were gleams of light illuminating the track. . The Cailttm As: Moonlight. (Laughter.) Mr. A. J. JOLLEY (continuing) said he hoped Warrington would maintain its position and would be a pioneer in education., (Elear, hear.). He particularly wished some members of the Council, who after al/ were their masters in regard to financial matters, would recognise that ttie scheme meant the expenditure of money, but perhaps one of the best investments any modern community could Make wasP on education con- ducted on sound lines. (Hear, hear). _ _

/ Alderman PIERPOINT slid:that as one of the mem- bers of the Corporation who would have a final voice in the scheme, he should like to point out that every pupil who went through the scheme would cost so much to the county borough. Every .elementary scholar, every scholar moving up to the Grammar school, would cost a certain amount of money. When Mr. May referred to the open door, it struck him that anyone who went through the open door of the borough—he was referring more to the country pupils from Lymm, Thelwall, Grappenhall and other districts outside the Borough—the cost of their education should be estimated and they should be made to pay in ac- cordance with the cost. He had no objection to people coming from Grappenhall and Lymrn, and other places, so lone. as they paid their fair share of the cost to the borough. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON pointed out that the cost of pupils from outside the Borough, either on the Lancashire or Cheshire side, would be paid for by the county authorities. • Colonel BUCKTON called attention to the fact that the scheme set no two new schools._.. a Girls High school, and an Upper Standard school. They had already established a Secondary school on a small scale and this under the scheme would develop into something much larger. These schools would relieve the pressure on the accommodation in the elementary day schools. The present Secondary school had already relieved the pressure °winc to the want of education in some schools upon which the inspectors had reported for some time. It might be that when the scheme was developed there would be a still greater relief. RePerence had been made to the evening Schools, and he contended that they should be carried on in every day school in the borough during the winter months. There were many who could not aspire to the higher education which was proposed, and he did not see how they would get on with the ordinary work of the world if 'everyone did. (Hear, hear.) These needed further education in evening schools. At the present moment there was no evening school on the south side of the river and those who lived there had to face that terribly crowded Warrington Bridge. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the scheme included the provision of evening schools all over the town.

Mr. UPSON in referring to a remark by the Rev. E. J. Willcocks said he was of opinion that they did not need any outside expert advice. (Hear, hear) He was beginning to think that the members of the School Management Committee were experts. (Hear, hear, and laughter). He did not think they needed any inquiry as to the need of secondary education in the borough, as they were all convinced of the great need for the pro- vision of some such scheme as had been put before them that night. He contended that the evening schools were not fulfilling the purpose for which they were established throughout the country, as the work was a repetition very largely of what was done in the ele- mentary schools. But by the present scheme, they would carry on the work of the primary school when a child went to work. They ought to make the evening schools free and have compulsory power over the children when they left the primary school to compel them to go to a continuation school, so that the moment they left the day school their education could be continued. Some children,perhaps a small proportion of the poorest had remarkable brain power. and even the charge of a few pence per week might prevent them availing then- selves of the continuation school. He thought the thanks of the committee were due to the Director of Education and.the Rev. Morley Stevenson for the Admirable scheme. .(Hear, hear.) The R9V. E. J. WILLCOCKS : I said, call in outside exnert advice "if necessary." That makes all the difference. -

Rev. 311. STEVENSON, in reply, said that however desirable it might be.and it was desirable, that evening schools should be made free, under the present state of the law it was not possible. At the present they were bound to charge a fee of some sort. With regard to children who came from outside the borough, their expense would be charged partly to the county from which they came. It was gratifying to Mr. Murray and himself, and the School Managment Com- mittee as a whole, to find that the scheme, which naturally lent itself to any amount of criticism, should have received such a kindly handling at the bands of the committee. It augured well for its future. He was perfectly sure of this that whether they adopted exactly that scheme, or whether it might be modified, the importance of the work of higher educa- tion could not possibly be over-estimated. Whatever the fiscal palicy of the country was to be in the future— and that was a matter about which he should say noth- ing. not being an expert—(laughterl—he was perfectly satisfied that they must educate, educate, educate, if they were to hold their own in the world.*And it would largely depend u-on the support which the higher education received from the great employers of labour in the borongh, how successful it would be. (Hear. hear.) He was delighted to heir that one firm had already offered to give one shilling a week extra to boys who had passed standard seven. When that was clone it created a demand for higher education. If all emnloyers of labour would take such action as that and back up the labours of the committee by substan- tial support, then their labour would bear fruit. (Hear, hear). The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: ifiIIKIRTANT C9NFERENCE.
div.p: ifiIIKIRTANT C9NFERENCE.

A conference was held at the Education office on. Thursday morning between the members of the School Management Committee and representatives of the Board of Education in accordance with a desire ex- presied by that Board with reference to the -scheme for higher education which was approved by theEduca tion Committee at its meeting on Monday. Most of the membors of the School Management. Committee were present, as also was tile Mayor, and the repre- sentatives of the Board of Education were Mr. A. Cardew, senior examini,r, Mr. J. Parry Laws and Mr. H. M. Richards, H.M. inspectors, and Mr. A. T. Kerslake, H.M. sub-inspector. The discussion turned chiefly upon the future position of the Grammar Schp )1 in its relation to the scheme as submitted. .No decision was arrived at, but the interehanga of views and opinions will be of considerable assistance to the Education Committee when the time 'comes for them to consider the pro- posals of the Governors of the Grammar School. The other matters touched upon were the provision of scholarship 3) the training and supply of pupil teachers, the preparatory division of the Secondary school, and the establishment of a Girls' High school; the necessity for the latter being 'strongly urged upon the Committee. The scheme as adopted by the Education Com- mittee has been sent to theßoard of Education for their approval, but this will probably not be obtained until •the Governors of the Grammar school have ' decided the lines upon which the re-organisatio n of that school should be effected, in order that it may fill that position in the scheme which the - Committee hope to see it occupy.

div.p: THE LICENSING QUESTION. Mast not be a Show Bill.

The promised Bill to deal with the licensing question "was discussed at the annual meeting of the Cheshire, Shropshire, and North Wales district National Trade Defence Association held at Chester onyMonday. Mr. T. J. Down, of Warrington, who presided, com- plained that some magistrates did not hesitate to inter - few with the freedom of contract, always considered a. sacred thing, and override agreements between land- lord and tenant.

Mr. Ne-w—t-o-n--;"manager of the National Trade Defence Association, London, said that the promised Bill must ILot be a show Bill, but a measure over which the Government meant business. The trade. he added, were not prepared to submit to further burdens, and any compensation fund must come Iforu Imperial sources. Until that were done tho duty of Parliament was to prevent confiscation.

div.head: EDUCATION IN WARRINGTON
div.p: EDUCATION IN WARRINGTON
MONTHLY MEETING OF THE LOCAL AUTHORITY.
MR. F. MONKS AND THE ALLEGATIONS OF "SECRECY."

Mr. F. Monks presided at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee, which was held at the Town Hall on Monday evening. There were also present :—Alderman Bennett (vice-chairman), the Revs. Morley Stevenson, E. J. Willcocks, John Yonge and Father Wilson, Aldermen Sutton, Smethurst, and Pier- point; Councillors Tinnion Wilkinson, Brougb, Maginn, Hulse, Dbvies, Crailt, Burton, Ellison and Roberts; Major Buckton, Messrs. R. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, J. Fulton Smith, E. J. Guest, C. H. Unsworth, J. Upson, %V. Bibby, T. May, E. Plinston, G. Walker, J. Moore Murray (jirector of education), J. Fairhurit (borough treasurer), and Dr. Gornall (medical adviser). INCREASE OF SALARIES TO BE CONSIDERED. The CHAIRMAN said there was a matter which he wished to mention to the committee for consideration. First of all it was with reference to Mr. Fairhurst, their treasurer. No remuneration had been given to him for the extra work he had been called upon to per- form, and he thought it would be the wish of the General Committee that the Finance Committee should consider what extra remuneration should be given to him. Also, he wished to call attention to the fact that that Mr. Murray had been with them for a year, and though he did not wish to enter into discussion on the question of his salary he could not help but give ex- pression to his own feelings, and those of many others, which were that the present salary was inadequate for the work he bad to do. (Hear, hear.) Anyone who had seen the amount of work done by the Director in refer- ence to elementary and secondary education could not help but feel that his present salary at any rate was , inadequate, and he would be glad to move that the , question should be referred to the Finance Committee for their consideration, and for them to report at the next meeting as to what remuneration they thought should be paid to him. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH seconded.

Mr. T. MAY said he would like to propose also that the amount of the remuneration to Mr. Fairhurst should be reported to the committee at the next meeting, as well as the question of the Director's salary. They all knew how anxious he was that all matters should come before the whole committee, and not be delegated to a sub-committee. Although be should heartily 'second and support both the proposed extra remunerations— knowing the amount of work which the two officials did—he could not, in view of the opinion be held with reference to the management of the finances by the whole committee, second the proposal as it was in its original form. Alderman PIERPOINT : I think Mr. May ought to know that the proposed remunerations could not be passed except by the whole committee. Councillor TIN-mos remarked that the Borough Sur- veyor who was the surveyor of the schools, had done a considerable amount of extra work, and there was nothing to prevent his salary being considered at the same time. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Longdin, in his opinion, and in that of many others, was one of the most effi- cient officials of the town and it was only right, con- sidering he had extra duties to perform, that he ought to be considered in the same way as the others. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN : He is purely a servant of the Cor- poration and his salary will come up for consideration in February. Councillor TINNION said the Surveyor's increased work and responsibility were not really for the Town Council to deal with as they were due entirely to the serviceshe had performed for the Edttcation Commit- tee. He thought it wouldicolue with better grace if the suggestion for an increase came from that com- mittee. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said he, was quite willing to alter his resolution to inclnde the three officials. The resolution as altered by the Chairman was then carried.

MR. MAY AND "SECRET SERVICE MONEY." Mr. JOLLEY moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee which appeared in our last issue. At a later meeting it was resolved "That the tender of Messrs. W. and A. Ashton, amounting to ,E9B 12s. 6d., for the alteration of the Old Vicarage in Sankey-street for use as an office for the staff of the Education Com- mittee be accepted." _ _
Alderman PIERPOINT sw=onded. Mr. MAY sard he would like to call attention to the item which might be described as "secret service money." He noted with pleasure it had been reduced te £65 this month.

A VOICE: What are you referring to? Mr. MAY: The item termed "general " in the Finance Committee's accounts, which amounts to £65. It is much more satisfactory than when it amounted to £l,OOO, which more than two-thirds of the Committee knew nothing about. Continuing, he said that although he was not going to "launch forth" —(hear, hear, and laughter)—as he had done on previous occasions, he would like to, say that he had every confidence in the gentlemen on the Finance Committee. What he objected to was their methods. Last month he was told he -would be welcome to go to any of that committee's meetings, but as they were held at no particular time or day they were virtually secret, and it was practically impossible for anyone not notified as a member to get to them. He thought that in view of the prospective expenditure on new schools the whole committee ought to take the finances in hand themselves as early as possible. The CHAIRMAN said) that as Mr. May's remarks went forth to the public, and as on two or three occasions he had referred to "secret service" or something of the soh he (the Chairman) wished to say publicly that there was no attempt in any form to cook the accounts or suppress any item. (Hear, hear.) Whatever Mr. May might say, the impression he gave to The town was a wrong one, and one which was unjust to the Finance Committee who, as far as he had been able to see—and this remark applied to every conunittee-- had given the fullest, pessible information it could give (Hear, hear). He thought it was unfair to the Finance Committee for such remarks as " secret service com- mittee," or" things that had been hidden "to be made because it was not so. (Hear, hear.)
The minutes were agreed SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEI

The minutes of this committee which included a com- plete scheme of education for Warrington and the arrangement of a conference with a Board of Education. representative with respect to the co-ordination of higher education were confirmed. The discussion is reported in another column. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

Councillor ELLISON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, and alluded to a visit paid to the Blind and Deaf and Dumb Asylum. All the visitors were agreeably surprised with the progress that was being made in teaching the chil- dren to speak. Ho asked several of them questions,and got_ answers.

Mr. PLINSTON seconded, and said he was quite of opinion that it would be well to pay the increased money for the reception of children at Henshaw's Blind Asylum rather than withdraw the children. The educa- tion given was of a very high order. The children were very well looked after, and an amount of good was being done.
Mr. UPSON inquired why there was no monthly re- turn of the attendance at school.

Mr. May pointed out what a painful duty it was to deal with parents who were wilfully culpable. There was a large number of children in the borough whose education was being.. neglected, partly because there was no proper provision made for them in the element- ary schools. An educational system was a pyramid which ought not to rest on its apex—it ought not to be upside down, and in any system adopted they must pro- vide for every child in the borough obtaining a good primary education before they talked about se .ondary education. With regard to elementary education for the borough, it had been so badly neglected . The CHAIRMAN; We are discussing the School Attendance Committee's minutes. • Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH asked how many childreu from the Borough were in the Blind Asylum. Councillor ELLisoN : One. With reference to the monthly return, its absence that evenlit was an over- sight.
The minutes were ar!reed to. NEW SCHOOLS

The MAYOR made -a: brief Waiement with reference to the proposed new schools, one of which will be situated near the, Cheshire Cheese Tun, at Latchford, and the other at Brick-street. They were, he said, arranging for the sites. The CHAIRMAN : 'Provision will be made for 900 children.

div.p: CARETAKERS OF SCHOOLS,

THE REV. J. YONGE'S MOTION WITHDRAWN. The Rev. John Yonge had given notice of his inten- tion to move" That resolution A 16, July 20th, 1903, section 1, he reconsidered, with a view to special con- sideration of its relation to cases of caretakers in charge of schools previous to appointment under this author- ity." Mr. Yonge, in asking leave to -withdraw the motion, said it had been represented to him that as a ,matter of general policy, the procedure he advocated in the notice of motion might be undesirable espe:tially in some directions. That was why he had consentlod to withdraw it. (Hear, hear.) THE DATE OF THE NEXT MEETING.
The CTIAIRMAN moved "That the next meeting of the Education Committee be held on the 22nd instead of the 15th February."
The motion mis seconded by the MAYoR and carried.

KING JOSEPH COMMISSION.
WHY KING EDWARD WA",
SUPEnSEDED.
AN IMPARTIAL COMMISSION USELESS

The Joke of the Century. IT is growl for us that the "big fight " on the Fiscal question has not been without its humorous aspects. Politics are to many of us not only r,erious, but sacred also The im- perative duty which rests upon every Man and woman not merely to make the best of their life, but also to !Lake the best of the national and social life 1,, which they below, involves heavy respmisibilities which cannot o lightly borne. We ought to be the more thankful, therefore, to anybody who intTcduces a humorous side to our national disputations, even though the humour may not be intended. It is many yt•ars since the nation was treated to a political j• be of such a high order and gigantic dirrvti,ions as - Mr. Chamberlain's "Commission " on the Fiscal question. The best Innro;lr is often the least obvious. Mr. Chamberlain claim the distinction of hav- ing perpetrate?: a political joke which has been so well ecneealtql that only now are we beginning to awake to its merits. It is indeed the joke of the century.

A More Than Royal Edlct. THE F, ve Trade Press and Free Trade leaders, the Iran in the street and the man in the house, every man, though perhaps not many woman, who read Mr. Chamberlain's famous, more than Royal, edict calling for a Commission on Tariffs, seemed struck dumb with arrazHeent At the audacity of the proposal rather than with the enormity of the joke. Even Mr. Chamberlain may have begun to catch the prevailing opinion, and take himself seriously as a sort of arch-king of the'Empire who overrules not merely the puny will of the Prime Minister, but also sets aside the prerogative of King Edward VII. If re are to take Mr. Chamberlain seriously at all, it is really time we bean to take him seriously for what he is worth as a prancing platform politician and nothing more. His latest fantastic caper in assuminc, more than the Royal right of appointing a ''Commission upon British trade, without consulting Par- liament, should be simply regarded as an immense joke. Lie only serious way to look at the appointment of this Commission is to treat it as a serious effort to outshine all the humorists of all the ages.
Citizen Chamberlain

AFTER all, the average Briton who takes his politics as well al his pleasures seriously must he pardoned if he did not at once realise the magnitude of the joke of King Joseph's Com- missions. Commissions, when they are appointed, are appointed by the King at the instigation ef Parliament. The average Briton cannot readily appreciate the impu- dent audacity of Mr. Chamberlain in superseding not merely Parliament but King Edward VII. as well. The average man can hardly yet satisfy himself that the late Colonial Secretary is not acting within the rights vested in hit; late office, and in accordance with the rules of the British Constitution. The average Briton does not yet understand that Air. Uhamberlam has no higher place or 'power within the British Empiie than that of an ordinary citizen whose name may he John Jones or Ben Brown. The man in the street has got into the way of thinking of Mr. Chamberlain as a powerful and important person in the Government of the nation, and he forgets that this same Mr. Chamberlain has to-day no more power or right to appoint a Commission to arrange Tariffs than has any socialistic Dick, Tom, or Harry who may like to employ his idle hours by appointing a committee of his mates to play at dividing between themselves the wealth of the Bank of England.

King Edward Too Slow., WHEN King Edward VII., by the advice of Parliament, appoints a Commission to inquire into the workings of any part of British social, national, or commercial life, one golden rule is always observed. An attempt is made to appoint a Commission which represents all sections of the community concerned, and in this manner a. fairly impartial tribunal is secured whose verdict will gain the respectful attention of the nation. Perhaps the best- known Commission of recent .years was that which was presided over by Lord Peel, and which inquired into the question of public- house licences. Upon that Corn Mission were representatives of the brewers, the publicans, the temperance societies, the magistrates, employers of labour, labour leaders, and every section of the cOnmunitg interested in the question. This Commission heard a mass of evi▪ dence from all .sorts and conditions of men _the trade, the temperance people, .the magistrates, the police, ministers of various religious denominations, representatives of philanthropic and social organisations—in fact, from everybody who had any information to give. The result of all this was the collection of an enormous amount of most valuable evi▪ dence, every word of which had been care- fully sifter), and has passed under the most searching cross-examination. It is only in this way that the truth upon any great national question can be 'secured. But the methods of the Connristions appointed by King Edward VII. are far too slow for King Joseph. Ho wants a Con-mission whose verdict he can himself dictate, and whose opinion will not be influenced by the evidence it may secure, but by the or)inions an statements of Mr. Chairberlain.
The Examiner, Saturday, January 23, 1904.

div.p: King, Joseph's Rule,

UNDER King Joseph's rule his Commission has been carefully chosen So as to exclude everybody who dees not agree with King Joseph. Lai our has been left out. becanse the only rupreentativE who Was asked to be present said he could net spare the time! That representative evidently likes his jokes shori; the Cominiss:ion is likely to be long. TheTeople and tr:-,tlc.: who suffer by Protec- tion have been ignored. The people who con- sume but do rot manufacture, these who have to buy food, drink, clothes, goods, houses, but do not soil them, these are left out. Only those who would profit by the imposition of taxes upon the necessities of life—only those are appointed by King Joseph. We might as well appoint a conunittee of cats to decide ncn the government of a colony of mice; or a council of burglars to direct the operations of the police. But neither of these suggestions would ro grand a joke as Mr. Chamberlain's commission of • confederates to contrive a scheme, of taxing everybody but themsciWC3.
