div.head: Warrington Bridge.
div.p: Warrington Bridge.

Sir,—Mr. Edwin Woods is rather late in the day with his proposal to construct a new bridge, seeing that the Town Council hae.already decided to widen the exist- ing bridge by means• of cantilevers. The cantilever scheme has been adopted on two occasions at least, but there seems to be a determination in certain quarters to thwart the scheme and have a new iron and steel bridge at all costs. In their zeal for this project, the advocates take good care to -place the estimated cost of a new bridgeat a minimum, whilst the estimate for the cantilevers is placed at a maximum. No mention is made either of the addi- tional cost per annum to the ratepayers which a steel bridge would . entail for painting, &c. A cantilever .acheme has been thought good enough for the widening of London Bridge where the traffic is much greater than at Warrington, and as long as the existing railway bridge is allowed to remain, it is of little use spending a large sum of money on a single span bridge for the purpose of making it easier for navigators of The river.—Yours &c.
RATEPAYER.

div.head: Unemployed.—A Warrington
div.p: The Unemployed.—A Warrington
Labour Bureau Wanted.

Sir,—lt is with mingled feelings I read in your current issue, reference to the unemployed. Sad because such asquestion exists; pleased because it is a day's march nearer—the grave. There can be no doubt as to the state of things when one reads the reports of the various Trade Unions, Boards of Guardians, and several other'bodies which are closely connected with the rise and fall of the labour market. Yet these bodies. I submit, cannot gauge accurately the number of unemployed. Before we apply the salve, we must locate and know the extent of the wound. Therefore, I think Warrington should follow the example of -Liverpool, Bradford, Manchester, Eccles, and West Ham, and open a bureau,where the unemployed residents could register and state how long out : how many dependents; and class of work used to. If when this was done the Corporation would form a works committee, aid, cont- inence such work as inneedful. in different parts of the town, and also to give preference to tliose who had signed much would be done. I believe, to ease the dis- tress that prevails. The above question is the one that in the near future will have to be solved, for men will not always lie down to be trampled upon in such a manner. Starva- tion in a land of plenty ! Men, women, and children want boots and shoes: factories and shops full; so it would aid the day to discuss in your columns the case for and against a Labour Bureau: Yours, Ste., TED HORROCKS.

div.head: The" Political plunger and Gambler."
div.p: The" Political plunger and Gambler."

Sir,—l hope and believe it will be superfluous to draw the attention of any of your readers to the characteristically vigorous letter from Mr. John Burns to the electors of Gateshead, which T have just been .reading in Monday's papers. There is no need to en- large at any length upon the letter which speaks for itself, and every line of which is an appeal, a powerful and, I had almost said, impassioned appeal to our most intelligent artisans, not only in Gateshead but through- out the United Kingdom. But before the post goes, which should resell you on Friday, may I say a brief word or two on the -state of things in South Africa to which Mr. Burns alludes. During the course of the war you were good enough to publish some letters of mine in one of which I men- tioned that a very large and powerful merchant in the Orange Free State and the Transvaal had told me in 1894 or 1895, that in the natural course of events if we did not.seekto force the pace, both the Free State and the Transvaal would within a generation fall like a ripe 'alum into John Bull's mouth. Everything pointed, as 1 •bave shown in your cdiunans, at no very distant date to the Federation of South Africa, and this without any resort to force and bloodshed. My friend urged this about tiesame time on Mr. Chamberlain, .and I happen to know that the latter was much of the same way of thinking•up to the spring of 1899. After that he was unquestionably misled by an unscrupulous group of alien capitalists on the Rand, and his diplo- matic methods, if such reckless appeals to the gallery deserve that description at all, rapidly went from bad rto worse, and were, as I asserted during the war, the chief cause of it. Mr. Burns alludes to its consequences, and as regards South Africa the same friend to whom I have just re- ferred, recently returned from the Transvaal and Free State,and gave me a vivid description of the sadstate of affairs there. More recently still a very able man and acute, observer, whose business has taken him through the whole of South Africa, has described to me what he saw there. Even if we ignore the ruin and desolation that has been spread far and wide in the Transvaal and Free State,-the effect upon trade and commerce in the the rest of South Africa and the mutual hatred and suspicion between Dutch and English in Cape Colony which have been the inevitable consequences of the war are appalling. And be it remembered that prior to 1899 there were no more loyal subjects of the Empira than the Dutch of Cape Colony. Nowhere in all the domin- ions of the Queen was the picture of her Majesty to be found more frequently banging in the homes of humble folk. Time alone can efface the wreckage of what Mr. Burns only too truly calls "this tragedy." But is not -his allusion to it very much to the point. Are we indled to allow this politigal plunger.and gambler" (as Mr. Burns with no less accuracy than force de- scribes in his trenchant way the chief author of this '.measureless calamity" that tuts befallen South Africa) "to cover up that tragedy by plunging the British Empire into the turnmoil of a Tariff War which is as unnecessary "as it would be unprofitable, pernic- ious and disastrous to the Nation. Mid-Devon gave a pretty satisfactory answer to that question, and the magnificent victory at Norwich is a still more emphatic reply.—Yours faithfully,
A. H. CROSFIELD.
Cannes. January 20th, 1904. [We regret that pressure on our space this week pre- cludes us from publishing Mr. Burns' trenchant epistle. ED. "Ex."]

div.head: Class Legislation : The Land Laws.
div.p: Class Legislation : The Land Laws.

Sir,—The land laws of England, as they exist to-day, appear to be so leavened with sel2shness and injustice that one may well wonder how tlfe inhabitants have so long and so patiently borne with them. Inpeopling the world'it seems to have been the Creator's will and pur- pose that all who live upon the earth should have an inheritance in it. But unfortunately, so far as this country is concerned, this wise and just arrangement has been completely reversed. Instead of dealing with the land as the common property of the people, class legislation has so contrived that nearly the whole acreage of England is vested ma handful of aristocratic families to the exclusion of the rightful owners. And in order that this small fraction of men and women may live in idleness and luxury and enjoy their own peculiar amusements they are legally entitled to draw an enormous revenue through rents levied upon the ground and the coal and iron under it. The injustice and cruelty of this mono- poly are too transparent to need any comment, but a few observations upon some of the evils resulting from it may not be out of place at the present time, and it is remarkable that the very classes in whose interest the land laws were made are the first to feel their evil effects. Idleness and the possession of vast wealth for which others toiled and sweated are not natural conditions of life. And where nature is disregarded the tone of society is lowered, and demoralization generally ensues. Hence it is, presumably, that so many of the aristocracy are addicted to such pursuits as dog racing, horse racing and gambling, and find their greatest "sport" in killing and maiming defenceless birds and animals. Then the rents and royalties extorted by the Classes are grievous burdens upon the industry of the country, and entail degradation and poverty among multitudes of tile toiling class. Upon farmers who have ample capital and the power of sub-letting, the rent impost does not press heavily. But the rank and file of the farming class who are not so favourably circumstanced find rent to be a heavy burden indeed. in good times they may, by hard workand the strictest economy, manage to "put a little to the good. But when seasons are bad and crops scanty, severe self- denial is needed to meet the demands of the landlord; and not a few of them succumb under the pressure. And if this be true regarding struggling farmers what must be the condition of the labourers who have to bear the heat and burden of the day to satisfy the requirements both of the farmers and the landlords? 'Their earnings are so small and so precarious at all times that hopeless poverty is their normal condition. I And when the poverty becomes more acute than usual many of them find their way into the towns with aview to better themselves; but only in reality to swell the number of unemployed and wretched labourers already there! But even worse still, not content with levying rents for the use of the soil class legislation thrusts its flesh hooks into 'the very bowels of the earth! There, under conditions of labour so horrible as to move the hardest heart, the miners, old and young alike, are "sweated" until their lives become a burden to them in order to swell the unearned incrementj of the landowner. And the same unrighteous and cruel laws which thus oppress the farmers, labourers and miners in the country operate in

the towns and cities as well. Their exorbitant rents and royalties diminish the profits of every industry.' manufacturing and commercial. And as manufacturers and merchants must hold their positions in the markets it follows that the workers cannot and do not receive fair reward for their labours. And as these workers have not yet obtained the long promised blessing of "three acres and a cow," they have neither field nor garden produce of their own to fall back upon when work is slack and wages low. Their clubs are their only resource under such trying circumstances. But there are, unfortunately, multitudes of workers, also landless,l whose wages are too small to enable them to make any provision whatever for times of adversity. When these I arise the cold hand of public charity and the still colder one of the Board of Guardians • are their only refuge from destitution. And, as might be expected. the living places of the great majority of our workers are in keeping with their oppressed circumstances. In the rural districts the housing of field and other labourers is of the humblest description, yet fairly supplied with light and air. But in the towns and cities most workmen dwellings are so contrived and huddled together that sunbeams and ventilation are almost ex- cluded. And this dangerous and degrading state of things is largely due to the ground rents of the land- lords. And what have our class legislators, who are so generous in pensioning one another out of the public funds, done for the aged and infirm workers who spent their strength in build- ing up, the wealth of the nation? The answer to this question is found in England's workhouses, mainly supported as they are by rates on the urban population, where multitudes of our fellow creatures unable to work are no longer treated as men and women but as paupers! Once more and finally, class legisla- tion extends even into the grave. The lords and the squires are not likely to charge themselves with sites for family vaults in their own land. But the middle class, and the poor who have not worn the official badge of pauperism must pay for a few feet of their mother earth wherein to bury their dead! In view of all this surely it must be admitted that a recasting of our land laws on the lines of right and justice is one of the most pressing needs of our time. Yours truly, TO NA. January 1904.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
ALLEGED ATTACK ON A SISTER.

At Runcorn, on Monday, Thomas M'Donald, aged fifteen, was charged. with doing grievous bodily harm to his sister Ellen,aged eleven. Superintendent Ennion stated that the 'boy during an altercation with his sister struck her in the eye with a table knife. The eye- ball had been removed in hospital, where the girl was still detained. The table kiiife was somewhat worn and had a sharp point —The prisoner was remanded for a week.

SMALLPDX AT WIDNES. On Saturday afternoon a case of smallpox was dis- covered in a lodging-house in Marsh-street, Widnes. The victim, a woman had been residing there for some time. She was removed to the Smallpox. Hospital, and all the inmates of the house have been re-vaccinated. On Monday afternoon it was found that a girl residing in Alpha-street was suffering from the dread disease and she was removed to the hospital. _ PECULIAR DROWNING CASE.

_ On Sunday night John Cunnington. aged 21 years, mate on the sandflats Coronation and Ann, belonging i to Messrs. Abel, of Runcorn, was drowned n the iron- ore basin of the Bridgewater Canal. Deceased left the house of his captain, Albert Smith at 7.30 p.m., and three-quarters of an hour later Joseph Davies and Christopher Lewis, captain and mate of the Rochdale Canal Company's flat Frederick, heardshouts of some- one in the water, and,proceeding to the spot, recovered the body of the deceased by means of a boat-hook after a quarter of an hour's search. Instead of landing the body the men attached a rope to it and went away. Afterwards a lock-tenter came and landed the body Daviesand Lewis state that the man was quite dead and they thought thevihad no right to remove the body. from the water until the police were present. Had the man been alive, they allege they would have taken him from the water. ALLEGED BURGLARY BY A YOUTII. On Monday at the Widnes Police Court, 'a young fellow, named John Grimes, Wellington-street, was charged with breaking and entering the office of the Hutchinson Trustees, at West Bank Dock, and stealing 9s. The evidence showed that the foreman, named Lawton' who had the key of the office, went there on Saturday evening, and found that the door of the office had been forced open, apparently with an iron bar, and the money stolen. Prisoner, on being apprehended, said he had won the money playing cards at the West Bank Dock. He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. The magistrates, addressing one of the repre- sentatives of the Hutchinson Trustees, said something ought to be done to put a stop tp the persistent gam bling that went on at the dock. The inquest was held on Tuesday when the evidence showed that the deceased had evidently fallen into the water between his boat and the canal wall.—Joseph Davies, captain of the flat Frederick, belonging to the Rochdale Canal Com- pany, deposed that he heard the deceased's cries, and he and his mate, Christopher Lewis, went to the place and pulled him to the surface with boathooks. The deceased would then have bean in the water from a quarter to half an hour. Witness seized hold of the deceased's hand, but he was dead and quite stiff.—The Deputy Coroner (Mr. Fisher) said he could not be stiff in that short time.—Davies said he and his mate tied a rope to the body and left it in the water. They thought they ought not to remove the dead body from the water until the police arrived.—The Deputy Coroner told witness this idea was quite wrong. Hepught to have at once landed the body and attempted to restore life without waiting for the police. He ought not to have left the man in such a position that he would certainly die.—Mr. Bylield (captain of the Runcorn Grappling Corps) said he had known cases where a man bad been revived after being in the water threequarters of an hour.—Davies said that in future he would at once land the body.—The jury returned an open verdict of ' "Found Drowned."

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

MORE SMALLPDX AT Sr. HELENS. On Wednesday the health authorities discovered three more cases of smallpox—one at Greenbank and one at Eldon-street, where previous cases have arisen, and a fresh casein the district •of Gerard's Bridge. This makes six eases in the hospital, to which they have been removed during the past few days. %EXTRAORDINARY DEATH' OF A CHILD. The St. Helens police have received a notification of the death of acbild at Thatto Heath under extraordinary circumstances. Dr. Gray was on Wednesday, called to a house and found a child of three and a half years,who was said to be suffering from the effects of drinking whisky. It is alleged that some one gave the child a sip out of a glass of whisky and when it was put down the child seized the glass and gulped down the whole of the contents. The doctor paid several visits during the day, but death took place on Wednesday night.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

POOR CHILDREN'S TREAT.—For several years a treat for poor children in Stockton Heath and Walton, has been organized by the members of the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour, in connection with Hill Ciiffe Baptist Church. Tt has always been of an unsectarian and undenominational character, the only qualification required being that the children were the childen of poor parents, struggling with a growing 'family, preference being given to fatherless and orphan children. The event for this year came off on Thursday afternoon, when about ,130 hungry children were provided with a substantial tea m the school- room. The promoters had much difficulty in selecting suitable cases,there being such a large number of appli- cants, and both the room and the means at their dis- posal being limited the tables were crowded, and it was wonderful how the ample stores provided dis- appeared, as soon as the army of the hungry began to operate upon them. Happily there was sufficient for all. The tea was in charge of Mrs. Hughes, Mrs. Joseph Moss, Mrs. Willia'tns, Mrs. Pemberton, and the Misses Moss, Jones, Hall, Dodd, England, Moreton, and Simpson. After tea there was an enter- tainment, to which the Sunday scholars and friends had been invited, and there was a very full attendance. The Rev. J. S.Hughes, as president of the society, pre- sided, and spoke a few words of welcome and goodwill to the children, explaining the circumstances of the treat, and the regret they all felt that they could not accommodate more. Then Mr. T. Williams gave selec- tions on his beautiful and up-to-date phonograph, and which could be easily heard all over the schoolroom, and was in itself a capital entertainment. Mr. Williams is always ready to give his services, and he is quite a favourite amongst the children of this neighbourhood, from whom he had a hearty reception. Messrs. George and Septimu.s Moss sang " Larboard Watch "and " All's well" in good style, and several views were shown by the magic lantern by Messrs. Cobb and Knight. Mrs. Hughes and Miss Jones acted as accompanists. The children gave three cheers for the donors, entertainers. tea makers, singers, collectors, 84c., on the motion of Mr. Joseph Moss, jun., seconded by Mr. Wheeler.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 23, 1901

" tubbing" anywhere since it was discontinued at the Ragged School. That the Ragged School Mission is a thoroughly alive institution may be judged from the fact that there are many useful institutions connected with it. There are two healthy Christian Endeavour Societies, a flourishing band of hope, a drum and fife band, a choir, as well as the Sunday School. On Sunday even- ings a mission service is held. Mr. Skelland has 36 fatherless girls on the books and several orphans. There are between 200 and 300 children altogether attending the school. . There have been more in former years, but other churches and institutions are now doing more for the poor and destitute children of the town than was the case when Mr. Skelland took up the work. He has the satisfaction of knowing that he has in- fluenced many poor children for good and that after all is something to be proud of. PRESENTATION TO MR. JAMES SKELLAND. The teachers and workers connected with the Ragged School and Mission made a presentation to Mr. James Skelland, the fonnder and superintendent of the Mission at a social gathering on Monday evening. The presenta- tion took the form of a framed illuminated address and ti-in gift is to be supplemented by framed photo- graphic groups of the teachers of the school and also a framed photograph of some of the children. The chair was taken by Mr. F. G. Owen (assistant superin- tendent). The presentation was made by Mr, H. Osborne, who has been associated with Mr. Skelland in the work from the outset. The text of the address is as follows :- -" To visit the fatherless and widows in their afflic- tion.' The Ragged School and Mission. To Mr. James Skelland, founder and superintendent. Dear sir,—We, the teachers and workers at the above mission desire to express our deep appreciation of your great and noble work among the poor and destitute children of Warrington during the past 17 years. You founded the Ragged School in 1887, and since then have worked un- ceasingly and with an indomitable spirit for the cause you have so much at heart. Many a young mon and young woman at the present' day rejoice for the teaching and guidance you have given them in their early years, and thank God that they were lifted from their miserable home copilitions by the influence they receivedat the Ragged SZhool. We pray that your valu- able life will be spared for many years to come.and that God will give you health and strength to enable you to continue your labours in this neglected corner .of His vineyard. The harvest is great, but the labourers are few. With heartfelt sympathy in the work, we beg to remain, very sincerely yours, Henry Osborne, Francis J. Owen, Edmund Osborne, Agnes B. Monks, Clara Skelland, Thomas Johnson, Frank Owen Walter E. Wright, Harry P. Wright, Sarah A. Titchard, Joseph Marsh, Albert G. Odell, John Johnson, William Parton, Harold Elwell, Annie Leadbetter, Phcebe Worsley, John W. Howarth." The address had been beautifully illumin- ated by. Messrs. Brooks and Son, and framed by Mr. 'David ()wen, of Golborne-street. Mr. Osborne in making the presentation paid a tribute to the services of Mr. Skelland to the poor children of the town. Mr. J. W. HOWARTH, financial secretary, read the following letter from Mr. J. Charlton Parr : " Grappenhall Heyes, Warrington, January 16th, 1904. Dear sir,-1 much regret that I shall not be able to attend on ;Monday next, on the very interest- ing occasion of the presentation to Mr. Skelland. I feel that this kind recognition of his great services to the Ragged School will he most agreeablel to him, and,hehas well deserved any tribute that the workers and those engaged in the carrying on of the school are able to offer him. Please give him my very sincere con- gratulation on this proof of esteem and regard, for him and his labour of love, and assure him of my hearty appreciation of the good work he has done, may say, in establishing as well as maintaining this school among the poorest of the poor in Warrington.—Believe me, yours faithfully, J.CHARL- TON PARR, president. Mr. John Howaith, financial secretary, Ragged School." Mr. Howarth added that he was pleased to be present to assist in doing honour to their worthy superintendent. When he was asked to join the ranks of the Ragged School workers he did so with pleasure, and though his name appeared last on the list appended to the address, he could assure his co-workers that he was by no means the least in his feeling of admiration for Mr. Skelland for his labours in the past, and also for what he was doing at the present time. •(Applause.) Despite the abuse Mr. Skelland had received in the town he had continued his good work, and he (Mr. Howarth) hoped he would be spared for many years to come to still further carry it on. (Applause). , I Mr. EDMUND OSBORNE said he knew the difficulties Mr. Skelland had to contend with when the school was , formed, but during the whole of the time he (Mr. I Osborne) had been connected with the' work, he had never known Mr. Skelland to flag in .his zeal for the betterment of the poor children who lived in hovels that were not fit to be described as homes. If it had not been for Mr. Skelland's services there would have been no ragged school eetablished in Warrington. The cost of the building and alterations was £1,500. which had all been defrayed, and now Mr. Skelland had prac- tically presented the town with a building worth £1,500 intrinsically, but which was worth considerably more so far as the social betterment of the town was con- cerned. (Hear, bear.) Tributes to Mr. Skelland's work were also made by Miss Monks and the Chairman.

In acknowledging the gift, Mr. SKELLAND assured those present that he had always tried to do his duty. He had never cared for anyone's smiles or feared any- one's frowns. He had tried to please God and not man. Man was a second thought in his mind, although his desire was to be conscientious in everything he did. He had striven to make it ea.ly for these poor children to do right, and hard to do wrong. and he firmly believed all things worked together for those who served God. Many difficulties had been overcome, and his object was to establish a Ragged School for Warrington. He was glad he had succeeded, and hoped that those who followed him would do all they could to carry on the mission and make it a continued. success. He thanked his workers, without whom no success could have been achieved. The address is now on view in Mr. Birtles' window, together with two groups of children taken in 1837. One group shows the children as they first appeared in the Ragged School and the other shows them after being under Mr. Skelland's care.

div.head: CHAT ABOUT THE RAGGED SCHOOL.
div.p: A CHAT ABOUT THE RAGGED SCHOOL.
MR. SKELLAND'S REMINISCENCES.
An Unsympathetic Corporation Committee.

The genial founder and superintendent of the War- rington Ragged School Mission has this week been the recipient of an illuminated address in recognition of his seventeen years' labours on behalf of the poor and destitute children of Warrington. To Mr. Skelland the work has been a labour of love and as he looks back on the small beginnings of the work which he commenced in 1887 he must be agreeably surprised at the success which has attended his philanthropic efforts. A reporter of the " Examiner" had a pleasant hour's chat with Mr. Skelland one day this week and learned from him the troublous and chequered career of the Ragged School Mission .in Warrington. Lang before 1887—in which year the Mission was founded—Mr. Skelland had a warm corner in his heart for the ragged children whom no one seemed to care for. Whilst superintendent of a Sunday school which he conducted at Dallam-lane Chapel, he deter- mined to seek out some of these ragged children and bring them into the school. In order to have greater freedom he resigned his position of superintendent, and went out into the alleys and courts and "black spots" of Warring,ton,and induced a number of chil- dren to accompany him to the Sunday school. There were about thirty. in all, and in their dirty and unkempt condition they made their first acquaint- ance with a Sunday school. On the following Sunday the number was increased to fifty, but ,on the third Sunday a crisis arrived. Some lof the officials of the school looked with displeasure on the introduction of these youthful denizens of the slums into the school and threatened that they would not let the scholars, who usually, attended sit beside them. Mr. Skelland saw that it was impossible to continue the work against the wishes of the officials, and relinquished it for a time, fully determined that when he saw his way clear he would start a ragged school.

An opportunity presented itself some time after- wards, on the Dallam-lane chapel becoming vacant. Mr. Skelland determined to make a start. The conditions were very unpromising and would have /daunted a less determined man. He found himself in possession of a mission room without a scrap of furniture, with no funds to buy any, and no workers to help him in his self-imposed task of rescuing poor and destitute children. In relating these circumstances, Mr. Skelland said : " I turned matters over in my mind and talked of my difficulties to those at home. At last, a daughter of mine offered to give me the contents of her money-box-3s. 6d. I believe it was—as a start. I was so encouraged by this act of practical sympathy that I determined to commence the school and trust to the generosity of friends and sympathisers for financial support. My first duty was to provide seating accommodation, and in providing the necessary forms, I was generously helped by three friends. Mr. R. A. Nalor protided the timber at half cost, Mr. Smethurst supplied the iron castings also at half cost, and Mr. Joseph Moan- field put the materials together free of charge. In the meantime I had cleaned the interior of the building myself and on the Ist Sunday in January, 1887, the first Ragged Sunday school in Warrington was opened. I recollect the occasion very well. I was assisted by Mr. Robert Dale and my daughter. Shortly after two o'clock when the other schools in the town had opened, we went out towards Town's-end to gather together some poor boys and girls for the school. On the way there we met two girls who had heard that a ragged school was to be opened and were desirous of finding it. We took them with us, and as we stood opposite the Rodney, many suspected that the girls had been taken into custody for a misdemeanour and gathered round us. We announced our intentim of starting a ragged school and invited the children to come with us. Many responded and in less than half an hour we had with us over one hundred of the poorest children in the town. Some were without hats and jackets and were com- pletely destitute of the comforts of life. It was pathetic to see them crouch round the stove and fall asleep, under the influence of the heat. We sang a hymn land talked kindly to them. The school has been undenominational from the first and I hope it will remain so. In a circular issued at the time there occurs the following sentence : 'This school is in- tended for the poor ragged and destitute children of the town and is open every Sunday afternoon at 2.30. All children of this class, who do not attend anywhere are affectionately invited to the school, where-they will meet with kind friends and a hearty welcome."

In alluding to his early experiences, Mr. Skelland referred to the encouragement which the late Mr. John Walker, of this journal.gave him in the press. "After the first:Sunday,' continued Mr.Skelland, 'the children came readily enough and in a short space of time we had 200 scholars on the books. A number of earnest workers gathered round me and we visited the chil- dren in their homes. Some of them were fatherless, others orphans, whilst many had parents who had little or no regard for their responsibility to their off- spring. We have had to do what their parents neglected to do. We have clothed them, fed them,and even washed them. Our object has been to teach them to be sober and honest, industrious and clean. We have always impressed upon them that whatever ' was worth doing was worth doing well." Asked as to whether he thought they had succeeded Mr. Skelland said his long experience convinced him that they had. Many of the boys and girls who had passed through the school were now in situations and were doing well. A few of the oldest scholars had become active workers in the school. The financial difficulties which were experienced in the earlier years of the school's history threatened to bring the institu- tion to an untimely end. At the close of the second year the school was indebted to the amount of £2O, and some of the workers advocated that it should be closed. Mr. Skelland, however,said he would take upon himself the financial responsibility, and was determined to keep the institu- tion going. A drum and fife band was started, and this has proved one of the best stays the institution has had. "Were it not for the money raised by the drum and fife band," continued Mr. Skelland, the institution might long since have closed its doors. "The band has raised over £6OO towards the building fund, in addition to large sums towards the annual general income. Our sub- scription list last year only amounted to £24 35., whilst the donations and collections received by the band were £230, so that you will see the value of the band to the institution. Our band has visited all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire and has been kindly received wherever it has gone. Last year Mr. Owen and myself travelled 1600 'miles by rail with it and walked an additional 500 or GOO miles. I remember that the first town we visited was Wigan. The boys were not then well accus- tomed to their instruments, and PNV/IS afraid that they whuld break down, but somehow or other they played surprisingly well, and we came back to Warrington with 30s in hand for the funds of the institution. The lads have had several teachers, but they did not ' make much progress until a bandsman from the Barracks taught them to play simple tunes from ear. Since then the lads have prac- tised two nights a week and it is surprising what a good ear for music some of them have. They enjoy the journeys out of town, and during the intervals when the band is not playing, either Mr. Owen or myself,give short addresses to those who gather round. We also give the girls five or six outings to the seaside in the course of the summer. Some criticism was made on our conduct at the Police Court, where it was mentioned that a girl had been out collecting for us at Southport until eleven o'clock. As a matter of fact, the station- master at Southport refused to let all of us get into the train at eight o'clock and some had to wait until the last train. That was why the girl was out so late. She had not been collecting. Only the officials and older scholars are allowed to take the collecting boxes." In relating the circumstances which led to the acquire- ment of the Ragged School premises in Bank-street. Mr. SKF,LLAND stated that when the Government had no further use for them for County Court purposes, they were Offered for sale. The late Mr. Robert Garnett, one of the vice-presidents of the Ragged School, secured the premises for £BB5. It was decided to alter the building for the purposes of the school. The total cost was £1,450. This sum has now been paid off, but a further sum Of about £l5O is still required to renovate the building, to renew the flooring and window frames. In connection with the school, baths have been intro- dnced but owing to the action of an unsympathetic Water Committee the use of the baths has been discon- tinued. It came about in this way. The Water Com- mittee sent in a prettystiff bill for water. Mr. Skelland appeared before the committee and explained that the baths performed a useful sanitary purpose. The workers gave their time in assisting to wash the children, who were dirty in the extreme, and it was thought that the Water Committee might forego any charge for this purpose. The Water Committee decided to reduce the bill to £5 which was paid by the Ragged School Authorities, but it was decided to dis- continue this work of cleansing the unwashed on the ground of expense. Tt is now three years since the baths were used and Mr. Skelland has grounds for be- lieving that many of the children have not had a

div.head: ETCHING AND ENGRAVING.
div.p: ETCHING AND ENGRAVING.

This subject was capably dealt with by Mr: John Bowland, of Timperley,lin;the course of a lecture at the Warrington Museum on Monday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. Charles Madelev, curator and librarian, in the absence of Alderman 'Bennett. The lecturer congratulated the Museum authorities upon their success in obtaining from South Kensington the splendid collection of engravings now being shown in the art gallery. He believed :Warrington was the only municipal authority in England that had been so favoured. The Board of Education had sent them sufficient to form a miniature exhibition,comprising as it did examples of line engravings dating from the sixteenth century, etchings and mezzotint engravings d.ating from the 17th century, and coloured-engrav- ings, aquatints, and lithographs of a more recent date. He could only think they were favoured, because, it was thought that the „Lancashire town that had pro- duced a Luke Fildes and a Henry Woods, both mem- bers of the Royal Academy, would probably have within it latent talents of an undeveloped Valentine Green, or Samuel Cousins; or a James McNeill Whistler. (Hear, hear.) Dealing with etching and engraving, Mr. Bowland said the present position of engraving was secondary to painting (though some engravings were much better than many paintings.) The engraver to-day was ' mostly occupied in translating the works of painters. By his intervention the engravings could be widely circulated and give pleasure and profit to thousands who might never see the original painting. There were several varieties of engraving, the chief of which were represented in their collection. First there was line engraving on metal plates, usually copper or steel, in which the line was always incised or cut in; secondly, there was etching, also on metal, in which the lines were corroded by means of acid ; thirdly, there were mezzotints in which there were no lines whatever, but only shades produced by roughening the surface of the metal;' lastly, the woodcut, on whioli the lines which print black had .to be left in relief, whilst the surface round them was cut away. These various processes were fully described by the lecturer, who illustrated his subject with lantern slides, and at the close exhibited a number of engrav- ed plates and tools,lent by Mr.J.B.Pratt,one of the fore most mezzotint engravers of the day. —The lecturer was thanked for his services on the preposition of Mr. W, H. J. Jenkins, seconded by Mr. W. H. Woodcock.— Mr. Dean's services as lanternist were also acknow- ledged. We are glad to record that the collection of objects with which the lecture was illustrated has, by the kindness of the above-named gentlemen, been deposi- ted for a few days in the Art Gallery. Etching is illustrated by (1), a, cipper plate. prepared with smoked ground, and with a mrtion of a landscape drawn thereon, and by some f the needles used. (2) Etched plates completed, including three land- snipes etched by F. Goolden, of Timperley; with ennrayer's proof impressions from the same. Line engraving is represented by a large finished steel plate of" Cerito," a celebrated greyhound, with the resulting print alongside. This plate has a ruled background. A number of burins or gravers, bur- nishers, &c. .accompany this plate. Mezzotint is more fully shown by three copper-plates, by Mr. J. B. Pratt himself, in various stages of incompleteness, along with several " rockers," the peculiar toothed' chisels with which the "ground " is produced.—We may mention that the loan collection of British engravings now in the gallery will remain on view only a fort- night longer.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Baptist Church, Golborne-street. The Pastor's text at the evening service was taken from Daniel lc. Bv. "Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself," the chief point emphasized being that sin was not only a wronr, committed against the law of the universe, against God and against one's fellow men, but a grevious wrong to one's own soul, a degradation to one's manhood and an outrage to ones own nature. To overcome temptation and liven virtuous life required purpose of heart and that devision of character which was displayed by Daniel. St. Paul's Church.

At this church on Sunday services were held on behalf of the Church of England Incorporated Society for .providing homes for Waifs and Strays. The preacher was the Rev. Hawley Sharp, organising secretary, who gave a large number of instances in which poor, ragged, neglected children had been rescued from their miser- able homes in the slums, and were now occupying respectable situations. He told the congregation about a Warrington girl who, after the conviction of her father, was taken into one of the homes and was now doing well. To show her appreciation of the work of the society she had sent a large number of carefully finished aprons, prepared by herself, and which were in use in some of the homes. The collections at the three services amounted to the handsome sum of .214 10s. At the "pound" service in the afternoon 2801b5. of tea, sugar, soap, currants, oatmeal, flour, 8:3., were given to the officiating clergy, and the goods will be utilized in some of the homes.

Holy Trinity Church. There were large congregations at this church on Sunday on the occasion of the choir festival. The preacher, morning and afternoon,was the Rev. A. Inglis while in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Vicar. At the morning service Maunder's Te Deum " in B flat was sung. A musical service was given in the afternoon by the choir and a number of friends. Mrs. A. Booth gave a finished rendering of " I will extol Thee," while Mr. T. Amos in "The Lord God of Abraham" and Mr. C. Hoult in the song "The Heavenly song," acquitted themselves well. The choir sang with good effect the anthem " The Son of God." The pro- cessional hymn was " All people that on earth "and the recessional hymn" Forward be our watchword." In the evening other special hymns were sung, and the choir repeated the anthem "The Son of God." Mr. Percy Randall presided at the organ. The collections realized about £9. • Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. _ -

The usual P.A. meeting was held (in Sunday and was presided over by Mr. J. Holland, who congratu- lated the members upon the. privilege of meeting together, StAday by Sunday, in such large numbers. A pleasing feature was the large number of young men present.—ln the absence of Mr. Thomson, of Liverpool, Mr. W. Jenkins very kindly consented to relate the very pleasing and interesting life story of "Thomas Williams, Botanist and Poet." Mr. Williams, In said, was born in humble circumstances. Yet in early life he showed signs of thought and study. Born in Ludlow, he afterwards removed to Anglesea, and then to Liverpool, and from thence he went to a little -village near Wigan. He was a gardener by trade, and became a general student of botany, and often found treasures for the mind on the Sand Hills between Liverpool and Southport. To him everything in nature was beautiful, and he could see right through nature up to nattre's God. The poetic tendency of his mind, caused him to write, thin:, and speak of God's handywork. His home was lowly and humble, yet to him was heaven on earth. God's works around him filled him with reverence and admiration. The more he knew the less he felt he knew. Williams was a Wesleyan local preacher, but did not succeed in that direction. To him everything around were sermons and he was delighted to think of God in His natural world. He was a self made man,"and he being dead yet speaketh." It could be said of him, "He did what he could." At the close,Mr.Farrar(the secretary) specially thanked Mr. Jenkins for his kindness in so willingly coming to help them at such short notice. The Lyric Quartette Party consisting of Miss Woodland, Miss Fairhurst, Mr. George and Mr. Cook very pleasingly rendered two pieces which delighted the brethren, "God is a Spirit" and " Sleet) gently sleep." Mr. Payton, Mus. Bac. presided at the organ. Mr. Healey and the Secretary also took part in the meeting. There was a very large attendance,and a hearty welcome was extended to a new member.

div.head: NEW TURBINE LINER,
div.p: A NEW TURBINE LINER,
A Big Experiment _in Trans-Atlantic
Service.
THE NEW ALLAN LINER "VICTORIAN."

Much interest his been Awakened in passenger circle 8 by the new departure in Atlantic steamship propulsion that has been announced by the Allan Line The new steamers they are now building for their improved Canadian Mail Service are, it appears, to be propelled' by Turbines instead of by the usual reciprocating steam engine, and it is claimed for this method—adapted, as it is to be, in an especial manner for Atlantic navigation that it will so greatly change: for the better the move- ment of large vessels at sea as to bid fair to revolu- tionize Atlantic passenger travel. The first of these steamers, named the "Victorian," is now well advanced in the building yard of Messrs. Workman' Clark and Co., Ltd., Belfast, and is to be ready for her station in the autumn of the present year. The." Victorian" will be by far the largest steamer, as she will also be the swiftest, of the Allan Fleet. She , will be fitted in the most modern style for upwards of 1,500 passengers,, and is expected, by reason of the absence of the throbbing movement inseparable from the ordinary steam engine, and the rapidity and unbroken steadiness of revolution in her shafting and propellers, to be at once noiseless and steady in a sea- way, even while exertingp all her great power. The first compound steam Turbine engine was built SO long ago as the year 1884 by the Hon. C. A. Parsons, i F.R.S., and was applied to the driving of a dynamo Iwith satisfactory results- The evolution of the Turbine was rapid, and ten years later the PiGneer Marine Syndicate was formed. The famous " Turbinia" under- went her initial trial in 1891. She was fitted with one shaft, which in 189 G gave place to three shafts with three propellers on each, making nine in all. The vessel developed a great speed, and excited particular atten- tion in naval circles. Another vessel had four shafts with three propellers on each, making in all twelve pro- pellers. Following upon these earlier vessels came the two coasting passenger steamers, that for the last two years have been runnin€, with great success on the Clyde. Attracted by the remarkable results achieved by these vessels, Messrs Allan resolved to see how far they could adapt the system to ocean steamers, which had not only to contend, at times, with weather conditions unknown in inland waters, but which called foran amount of pro- pelling power enormously in excess of anything pre- viously attempted, and which also required, as an indis- pensable concomitant, great atoppine, backing, and steering power, with the least possible liability to take injury at sea. The result has been that Mr. Parsons has devised a modification hi his earlier designs to suit Atlantic requirements. Great power will be attained both for forward and backward movement; it will be transmitted through shafting,and by means of propellers of special strength and design, runat aspeed mo,Zerated to the conditions of Atlantic work, and contrive to give steady efficiency without undue strain, and free from all vibratory disturbances. The Turbine machiaes for the "Victorian," to Mr. Parsons' designs, and under his , supervision, are to be constructed at the Belfast Works 1 of Messrs. Workman, Clark and Co., Ltd., who have se- cured the privilege of constructing such engines, and special care is being taken that the workmanship shall be of the highest class, the boiler power ample, and the pumps, valves condensers, and other allied parts be specially adapted to the wonderfully ingenious design of its originator, Mr. Parsons. For the benefit of those to whom the name "Turbine" does not convey any clear idea, it maybe explained that the mode of producing rotary motion in the shafting and its attached propellers is, in principle, the same aal that of the oldfashioned windmill, the force in the Turbine, however, being steam instead of wind, and the angled arms and sails of the windmill being represented Tin theurbine b y metallic vanes set on the service of ft conical casting, which forms, by attachment, the for- ward end of the propeller shafting ;these vanes,working into counterpart flutings on a fixed, surrounding,hollow casting, complete the device. The steam, entering a the forward end of this combined arrangement of bladet can only find passage by forcing the parts attached tos the shafts into rapid revolution. Rushing along with the momentum due to its volume and boiler pressure at one end, supplemented by the withdrawal of atmospheric i paessure by means of powerful air pumps operating at the other end, the steam imparts a steady,. unceasing, rotatory movement to the propellers, utilizing to the heat advantage the whole boiler power of the ship. Then there is a special arrangement that has been de- vised by Mr. Parsons in the" Victorian," whereby a re- versing power equal to that of the forward propelling power can be imparted to the machinery, securing almost instant arrestment of the ship's forward motion, and speedy backing in case of need. In this matter the "Victorian" is designed to surpass the ordinary engine-propelled steamer. The wide-spread arrangement of her propellers, of which there are three in number, each on a separate shafting, and the rapidity with which power can be directed upon each of the outer shafts separately, in any direction, will greatly assist the ship's manoeuvring power. A Marconi telegraphic apparatus has been fitted on board, and there is in the 'tween decks a complete 'printing outfit. All the accommodation is provided with heating arrangements on the most approved principle. and in all the public rooms and passages are fitted numerous radiators of an elegant and up-to-date design. The ship is fitted up throughout with a first class installation of electric light, the generating powerfor which is provided by means of a pair of engines and dynamos. The speed of the "Victorian" will be a great advance ' on any other steamer on the route, and it is confidently 1 expected that under favourable conditions the voyage to Canada will be shortened by over a day, so that this i vessel will prove an important factor in the develop- ment of our premier Colony. •

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: THE LICENSING SESSIONS.

At a meeting of magistrates held on Tuesday, -the following were selected to form the licensing com- mittee :—Mr. F. Monks, Mr. C. White, Alderman'''. H. Sutton, Mr. T. Birchall, Mr. J. Geddes, Mr. H. Roberts, and Dr. Fox. The sessions will be held at the Court House, Arpley-street, on •Friday, February sth and notice has been given of two applications, Mr, Benjamin Kenyon, the licencee of the "Green Man." Inn, Green-street, will make another effort to obtain a full licence and Mr. Richard Sanson, of Hall- street, will apply for a full licence in respect of a new house propsed to be erected by the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) on a plot of land at the juncture of Lovely-lane and Dalamere street, and let to Mr. Sanson as tenant.
THE ABOLITION OF BARMAIDS. _ MAGISTRATES PETITIONED.

A petition against the employment of barmaids was presented to the Warrington magistrates at the meet- ing held on Tuesday for the purpose of electing the Licensing Committee. A deputation from the British Women's Temperance Association, consisting of Mrs. Garnett (president), Miss Bessie Dutton (ex-president), Mrs. Norman (vice-president), Mrs, Carson (treasurer and. Mrs. Simpson (sec retaryl,wai ted upon the Bench and was very kindly received. Mr. F. Monks was in the chair. The Chief Constable had made preparations for the visit of the deputation and had also compiled valuable statistics, which he submitted to the Bench, with refer- ence to the employment of barmaids inWarrington. Mrs. Garnett presented the petition which was signed by manyof the clergyand ministers and other promin- ent townsmen. The magistrates were asked to do all that lay in their power at the forthcoming Brewster- Sessions,to suppress the employment of girls as bar maids. It was contended that the work had a deterior- ating effect upon the health and morals of girls. Miss Bessie Dutton also spoke, and pointed out that barmaids were almost unknown in countries on the Continent, and few were employed in Scotland and Troland. The services of barmaids in this country were often dispensed with at a comparatively early age, and thus women were thrown upon their own resources, being almost unfit for any other kind of work after serving such long hour at the public- houses. Some were employed tbetween 90 and 100 hours per week, whereas the limit for women workers in ' factories was 56 hours. It was hoped that the magistrates would do all in their power to put a stop to the employment of any more barmaids in Warrington. The Chairman said the Bench would do what they could to help the Association im the matter. We are informed that most of the magistrates appeared to be in favour of the petitioners' requests.

div.head: IMPROVED TRAIN SERVICE FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: IMPROVED TRAIN SERVICE FOR WARRINGTON.
London and North Western Railway Company Waking Up.

For many years there have been loud complaints as to the passenger train service of the London and North— Western Railway from and to Warrington. Hitherto the complaints have fallen upon deaf ears but some con- cessions have been recently made which seem to indicate that the railway company are determined to give War- rington a train service more in keeping with the re- re- quirements of such a busy industrial centre as Warring- ton has now become. .

T. Williams, the new district superintendent, has already shown himself to be fully alive to the importance of developing for the benefit of his com- pany, to a greater extent than hitherto, the large volume of Warrington traffic, both passenger and goods, which competing lines have mid° heavy encroachments Upon during past years. Mr. Turnbull, the traffic manager, recently paid a visit to Whrrington and some of the grievances of Warrington against the London and North-Western Company were laid before him by the Town Clerk.

As the result of his visa the following alterations will be made in the week day service of trains from and to Warrington, commencing on February Ist next. The 8 28 a.m., Warrington to Over and Wharton, will leave at 8 10 a.m., call at Moore in addition to present stoppages, and connect at Hartford with the 8 0 a.m. Breakfast Car Express, Liverpool to London, due Euston, 12 0 noon. This will also give a connection to Birming- ham (New-street). arriving at 10 30 a.m. The 7. 20 a.m., Manchester (London-road) to Warring- ton, will leave at 7. 10 a.m, and arrive Warrington 8. 2 a.m. affording a connection with the 8. 10 a.m, from Warrington to Birmingham and London. A new express train, in connection with the 2.0 p.m express from Glasgow (Central) and Edinburgh (Princes- street), will leave Wigan at 7.1 p.m. and arrive War- rington 7.16 p.m. The 7.20 p.m., Warrington to Sand- bach, and 7.5 p.m., Warrington to Manchester (London road), will each leave at 7.25 p.m., so as to connect with this new service from Scotland.

The 2.20 p.m. Warrington to Lymm, which now runs on Saturdays only, will run daily and be extended to Broadheath, calling at all intermediate stations. A new train will leave Broadheath at 3.15 p.m. for Warrington and Widnes, calling at all intermediate stations.
The 12.33 p.m., Warrington to Lymm, which is now extended to Broadheath on Saturdays, will run to Broadheath daily.
The 2.5 p.m., Lymm to Warrington, which now starts from Broadheath.on Saturdays only at 1.50 p.m., will start from that station at 1.50 p.m., daily.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT EARLESTOWN. Richard Buckley, Sankey-street, Earlestown, was charged at the Warrington Coui.ity,Seissions on Wednes- day with attempting to comma suicide on Saturday night. Inspector Foster stated that the prisoner had been very unsteady during the past twelve months, and in consequence the relatives of the Young woman with whom he kept company objected to him. He was the worse for drink on Saturday night and some unpleasant- ness took place at his young lady's house. When he went home prisoner apPeared to bl 3 very much upset. His parents went to bed, leaving him in the kitchen. Hearing a riche, his father came down stairs and found prisoner suspended by a muffler from the banisters. He was cut down but was so violent that the police had to be called in. He now promised not to repeat his rash act and to sign the pledge. Under the cir- cumstances he asked the magistrates to discharge the prisoner. The bench agreed to this course.

div.head: WELCOMING A NEW MINISTER,
div.p: WELCOMING A NEW MINISTER,

Wycliffe Annual Congregational Tea Meeting. A public welcome was given to the Rev. Harry Wall (late of Nottingham Institute) who has undertaken the duties of assistant minister at Wycliffe Congregational Church, with the special oversight of Cockhedge Mission at the annual Congregational tea meeting hold in con- nection with the church on Thursday evening. About 300 persons partook of tea which was served in the schoolroom. The tables were presided at by the lady members of the congregation and Mr. William Beswick very efficiently discharged the onerous duties of making the preparations. The subsequent proceedings were held in the Wycliffe Memorial Building and the Pastor (Rev. John Yonge) presided. He was accompanied on the platform by the Rev. Harry Wall (assistant minister) and the Rev. J. S. Langley, of Kirkham, near Preston, Mr. Wall's late pastor. There was a crowded attendance, many being unable' to get a seat in the. mom.

In the course of a few interesting remarks, the Pastor- said the presence of many Cockhedge friends at that meeting showed their interest in the advent amongst them of the Rev. Harry Wall and their desire to give him a warm and social welcome. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Yonge proceeded to refer sympathetically to the absence, through illness, of Mr. Joseph Podmore. Mr. WALLINGTON was called upon to extend a hearty welcome to Mr. Wall, on behalf of the congregation, and in complying said he did so with great pleasure and cordiality. Mr. Wall, he said, was a Lancashire man and therefore did not need to be assured of the hearti- ness and w2rmth of a Lancashire welcome. He might take it for granted that he could feel at home with them at once. Whilst Mr. Wall's work would lie more particularly at Cockhedge, the people connected with Wycliffe Church would be very glad to have his presence and help at any time. They would be glad to see him in their homes, and at their social and religious gatherings. The Young People's Society, the Sunday school, the P.S.A. Society and all the other organisations connected with Wycliffe would be glad of any, assistance he could render. He could assure Mr. Wall that in all the work he undertook he- would have their good wishes and their help. (Applause). - -

Mr. B. HALL, speaking on behalf of the Cockhedge friends, said they had great hopes for the success of Mr. Wall's labours amongst them. The district was an extensive one and provided a vast field for labour. He hoped the time was not far distant when the Mission at Cockhedge would blossom forth into a second Congregational Church. (Hear, hear.) In any efforts which were put forth in that .direction he trusted the Wycliffe congregation would lend assist- ance. (Hear, hear.)

The CHAIRMAN observed that so far as he had yet got to know Mr. Wall he believed they would have in him a man who would do .them good service. (Hear hear). He was genial in disposition, pleasant in speech and comely in appearance. (Hear, hear). They looked with interest and hopefulness to important develop- ments at Cockhedge 'under his ministry. Mr. Yonge pointed out that it was not intended that Mr. Wall should do any of his (Mr. Yonge's) work Lut no doubt Mr. Wall would help him and take advice from him. They must not expect too much from Mr. Wall. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion Mr. Yonge extended a very hearty and loving welcome to Mr. Wall.

Mr. WALL, who had a hearty reception, stated that since coming to Warrington he had never felt that he had-been amongst strangers. People asked him how he liked Warrington and when he told them they seemed a bit disappointed. He could not help that, and he had tried to make amends by telling them that the people were a good deal better than the place. (Hear, hear.) When he came to Warrington he was surprised at the cordiality with which he was greeted. He had very great hopes of Cockhedge developing. As Congregationalists he thought they were sometimes behind the times in not being more aggressive. He trusted that something more would be done at Cock- hedge, and:that in course of time they would be able to move out of the present mission room to a larger and more commodious place. He appreciated the work that lay before him at Wycliffe and Cockhedge, and he was determined to do all he could to extend it. (Hear, hear.)

The Rev. J. S. LANGLEY, of Kirkham spoke of Mr. Wall's connection with the Congregational Church there, and said they were very sorry to part with him He brought with him the best wishes and prayers of the church and Christian Endeavour Society at Kirk- ham for Mr. Wall's future success. He trusted that Mr. Wall would receive the sympathetic assistance of the Congregationalists and friends at Wacringt on. (Hear, hear.) An interesting programme of vocal and instrumental music was submitted. Mr. R. H. Pearson played with his usually good taste and skill a violin solo "Tarantelle " (Pappini). Solos were contributed by Miss Ethel Roberts, Miss Lizzie Knowles, Mr. Bowman Hibbert and Mr. A. Cotterill, and all the artistes sang in such good style as to secure hearty receptions. Another pleasing item was a duet by Miss Ethel Roberts and Miss Annie Williams. The accompaniments were played with marked ability by Mr. NV. H. Payton, IVlus Bac . Mr. H. M. Ashton delighted the audience with a humor- ous:reading from his extensive repertoire. A vote of thanks was tendered to all who had taken part on the proposition of Mr. Thomas Wallington,. seconded by Mr. David Owen. A pleasant evening's entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the Doxology.

- • At Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday,.Tames Melia of Manchester-row, Vulcan Village, Earlestown, was charged with the theft of two hens, the property of Mary Peake, value 6s.—lnspector Forster stated that prosecutrix lived at 470, Wargrave-road, Earlestown, and she had a fowl cote on Vulcan Brow, not far from her house. The cote was next to a stable occupied by hernephew, a coachman, named Litherland. Miss Peake saw the cote door quite safe on Saturday evening the 9th inst., about 8.30. Shortly afterwards, Litherland, who was attending to his horse mthe stable,was attracted by the barking of his dog and on going to ascertain the reason saw prisoner just about to leave the fowl cote with two hens lying at his feet. He sent for P.C. Hughes, who found feathers and whitewash on defen- dant's coat antl cap. On being charged defendant denied the offence.—Miss Peake and Walter Litherland gave evidence to support the charge. Prisoner pleaded guilty. but said that if he had not had drink he would never have done such a thing.—A fine of 20s. including costs was inflicted, and in default prisoner went to gaol for 14 days.

FOUNDRY TIMEKEEPER'S SAD DEATH. Crushed Between a Lurry and a Wall. THE CORONER AND THE MAYOR. . The circumstances attending the death of Thomas Williams, aged sixty-six, residing at 2, St. Peter's-place, and employed as a timekeeper by Whyman's Foundry Co. Ltd., Dallam-lane, formed the subject of an inquest conducted at the Police Station on Monday afternoon by Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner. Mr. A. Lewis, inspector of factories for the district, was in attendance and Mr. steel,solicitor,represented deceased's relatives. Detective Inspector W. Harter was present on behalf of the Great Northern Railway Company. The police report, read by the Coroner, stated that on Saturday morning deceased opened the works gates to allow two railway lurries which had cotne for materials to pass in. The first vehicle passed into the yard without mishap but the second, belonging to the Great Northern Railway Company, caught deceased and pinned him against the wall. He did not appear to be much hurt at the time, but shortly afterwards he became worse and was removed to the Infirmary where he died. Hugh Williams son of the deceased, said his father had been employed at the works twelve months last October. His eyesight and sense of hearing were good. —ln answer to Detective Inspector Harter, witness said , deceased met with an accident sixteen or sevmteen i years ago, when he fell from a lurry to the ground and hurt his shoulder, backand head. Nt ribs were broken. Nurse Robinson said deceased was admitted to the Infirmary at 11.30 on Saturday morning in a state of collapse, and died a quarter of an hour later. William Moseley, the driver of the lurry, said he was leading the horse by the head as steadily as he could. He was taking particular care that the vehicle did not come into contact with the corner of the wall, and he did not notice the deceased. Mr. Whyman called out. and when he stopped the lurry he found that deceased had been pinned between the comer of the vehicle and the wall. The Coroner had some difficulty in obtaining full explanations from the witness. Havingasked one ques- tion he casually remarked "I know my intellect is dull at times. There is authentic information in Warring- ton that no one takes any notice of what I say. The Mayor said that the other night. Let me see whether my intellect is worth anything or not." At a later stage when witness seemed not to pay sufficient attention to the questions, he was told by the Coroner that he and the Mayor would be very good company. When another explanation was offered Mr. Brighouse remarked "I know pretty well about it, notwithstand- ing what the Mayor says." Mr. Thomas Whyman, manager of Whyman's Foundry Company Limited, also described the acci- dent. He said that when the horse and lurry in charge of the last witness passed through the gates he noticed that the rein was broken. The horse's foot was on the rein and this had naturally pulled the animal somewhat to one side. Witness called Moseley's attention to the rein and the driver picked it up. At the same time he saw that he was going too near the corner and drew the horse towards the other side. Witness noticed that the vehicle was getting near Williams's feet and called out to the driver to turn the horse away. Moseley im- mediately did so but the point of the lurry caught the deceased. mThe foreman of the jur*y (Mr. Cherry) said he believed d ost of • the jurymen wer3 of the opinion that the river took too sharp a tun in entering the yard and the result was that he had to bring the horse close to the wall. The Coroner pointed out that if the driver was iyak- ing particular care to avoid the corner and did no tsee Williams he could not be blamed. The jury returned a verdict of aAccidentaj death'.
